Accessory Navicular

Pediatrics · 1 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidencenormal variant in up to 12% of population (Orthobullets) · 2–21% (OB explanation) · majority asymptomatic

Sexmore commonly symptomatic in females

Genes & lab markers

Inheritanceautosomal dominant

Pathoanatomy

Lesionplantar medial enlargement of the navicular
✗ Wrong options: dorsal medial · dorsal lateral · plantar lateral · central

Formsseparate accessory bone or completely ossified extension of navicular

Origintuberosity develops from a secondary ossification centre that fails to unite in childhood · accessory navicular does not ossify before age 8

Normal navicularsingle ossification centre · ossifies age 3 (girls) / 5 (boys) · fuses ~13 yr

Associatedflat feet (pes planus) · posterior tibial tendon insufficiency (rare)

Anatomy & tibialis posterior insertion

Tibialis posteriorinserts on medial tuberosity of navicular · innervated by tibial nerve
✗ Wrong options: deep/superficial peroneal · medial/lateral plantar

PTT functioninverts hindfoot + assists ankle plantarflexion
✗ Wrong options: dorsiflexion = tibialis anterior · plantarflexion = gastrocsoleus · eversion = peroneus brevis

Other insertions (distractors)FDL → bases of 2nd–5th distal phalanges · FHL → base of great-toe distal phalanx · PB → base 5th MT · PL → plantar medial cuneiform + lateral base 1st MT

3Presentation

Symptomsusually asymptomatic · medial arch pain, worse with overuse/after practice · may follow a perceived inversion injury / ankle sprain

Pain sourcerepeated microfracture at the synchondrosis or PTT insertional inflammation

Examfirm, tender medial-plantar navicular prominence · ± swelling · pain with resisted inversion

Rigid arch supportsrub on the prominence → worsen pain → use soft, cushioned inserts

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

RadiographsAP, lateral, external oblique · best seen on external oblique view

Findingbony enlargement or accessory ossicle at medial navicular · no periosteal reaction / destruction / matrix
✗ Wrong options: biopsy · MRI + chest CT

MRIonly to evaluate other pathology · not needed for work-up
✗ Wrong options: "obtain MRI" as next step

Radiographic classification

Type Description Image
1 Sesamoid in substance of tibialis posterior insertion
2 Separate accessory bone attached via synchondrosis
3 Complete bony enlargement (cornuate navicular)

5Management

Symptomatic accessory navicular
  • First line→activity + shoe modification, orthotics, NSAIDs, PT
  • Failed above→short cast immobilization
  • Failed extended nonop→excision through synchondrosis
    • Flatfoot is primary problem→add MCO + PTT reattachment

Nonoperative care – orthotics & casting

First lineactivity restriction, shoe modification, non-narcotic analgesics/NSAIDs, PT (✓ even after acute sprain)

UCBL orthosisinverts heel during walking → offloads prominence → ↓ symptoms

Orthotic rulemust offload the accessory navicular or it exacerbates symptoms

Cast immobilizationnext step after failed activity + shoe modification
✗ Wrong options: continued activity modification · MRI · ORIF

Outcomemost become asymptomatic at skeletal maturity

Surgery – excision ± PTT advancement; with flatfoot correction

Indicationrecalcitrant pain after extended nonoperative management

Proceduremedial approach (distal talus → medial cuneiform) · reflect PTT / tendon-splitting approach · excise ossicle through the synchondrosis · trim navicular body flush with medial border of medial cuneiform

PTT advancement (Kidner)Orthobullets: do NOT advance PTT (no added benefit, ↑ morbidity) · OB: simple excision = Kidner in outcomes · ✓ "split PTT and excise prominence"
✗ Wrong options: PTT advancement · hindfoot osteotomy · osteosynthesis of ossicle (does not shrink prominence)

Flatfoot is the primary problem (flexible, hindfoot valgus, symptomatic Type II) — MCO + excision + PTT reattachment · otherwise flatfoot not corrected at the same time
✗ Wrong options: isolated excision (fails) · FDL transfer · lateral closing wedge · subtalar fusion

6Complications

Most commonpersistent medial prominence and pain → navicular body not trimmed enough

X vs Y

Simple excision Kidner (+ PTT advancement) MCO + excision + PTT reattachment
Use / evidence Isolated ossicle · relieves pain · = Kidner Historical · no added benefit, ↑ morbidity Flexible flatfoot + hindfoot valgus primary

How it's asked

"Accessory navicular excision — tendon elevated is innervated by?"tibial nerve

"Function of muscle attached to the ossicle?"inverts hindfoot, assists plantarflexion

"Rigid arch insoles make medial foot pain worse — which tendon inserts there?"posterior tibialis

"Underlying anatomy?"plantar medial enlargement of navicular

"Failed 6 months activity + shoe modification — next?"cast immobilization
✗ Wrong options: MRI · continued modification

"Symptomatic after sprain / incidental ossicle — initial treatment?"activity modification, orthotics (UCBL), PT
✗ Wrong options: cast 6 weeks · excision + PTT advancement

"Failed orthotics + casting — next?"excise medial prominence including synchondrosis
✗ Wrong options: ORIF / bone stimulator for "nonunion"

"Best surgical procedure?"split PTT, excise prominence
✗ Wrong options: Kidner advancement (no outcome difference)

"Symptomatic accessory navicular + flexible flatfoot with hindfoot valgus?"MCO + excision + PTT reattachment

"Most common complication of excision?"persistent prominence/pain — inadequate trimming

Achondroplasia

Pediatrics · 2 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Most common skeletal dysplasia80–90% of all dwarfism (TO)
✗ Wrong options: diastrophic · MED · nail-patella

Incidence1 in 15,000–30,000 (Orthobullets) · 1/30,000 live births (OB)

Sex / timingno sex predominance · diagnosed in utero or early infancy · short stature apparent at birth

Risk factoradvanced paternal age (>50 yr: 1 in 1,875; >35 yr still ↑)

FGFR3 genetics, inheritance & affected physeal zone (proliferative)

Inheritancesporadic 80% (de novo) · autosomal dominant 20% · 100% penetrance · once present → AD transmission, 50% risk per child (TO) · "most common inheritance pattern" → ✓ AD
✗ Wrong options: AR · X-linked · mitochondrial

GeneFGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3, not FGF-3 the ligand) on chromosome 4p

Mutationpoint mutation Gly → Arg in transmembrane domain · G380R (OB) = nucleotide Gly1138Arg (Orthobullets) · always the same site
✗ Wrong options: COL1A1 (>200 sites)

Effectgain of function ("turned on") → ↑ tyrosine kinase activity → ↑ inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation + differentiation (TO)

Zoneproliferative zone of physis (TO) · quantitative cartilage defect · defect of endochondral ossification

Intramembranous ossification normalnormal skull vault, clavicles, diaphyseal width (TO)

Mechanism detailmutation stabilises FGFR3 dimers → escapes ubiquitin degradation → persistent signalling

PathwaysSTAT1 (inhibits chondrocyte proliferation) · MAPK · PLCγ · PI3K-AKT

ModulatorC-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) → NPR-B → ↑ cGMP → ↓ FGFR3 activity → basis of vosoritide

Genes & lab markers

Condition Gene / defect
Achondroplasia FGFR3 gain of function, chr 4p, ↑ tyrosine kinase
Hypochondroplasia FGFR3 Asn540Lys
Thanatophoric dysplasia FGFR3 Lys650Glu — lethal (respiratory)
SADDAN FGFR3 Lys650Met
Apert syndrome FGFR2
Pseudoachondroplasia COMP, chr 19
MED COMP (chr 19)
SED · Kniest COL2A1 (type II collagen)
Osteogenesis imperfecta Type I collagen (COL1A1 / COL1A2)
Diastrophic dysplasia SLC26A2 (DTDST), chr 5 — sulfate transport, AR
Cleidocranial dysplasia RUNX2 (CBFA1)
Fibrous dysplasia GNAS activating → ↑ cAMP
Marfan Fibrillin
Gaucher Glucocerebrosidase
Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia PTHrP
Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia Type X collagen (AD)
Larsen syndrome Filamin B (AD form)

Physeal zone associations (distractors)

Zone Pathology
Epiphyseal bone MED
Reserve / resting Gaucher, diastrophic dysplasia, pseudoachondroplasia
Proliferative Achondroplasia ✓
Hypertrophic SCFE, physeal fractures, enchondroma, rickets
Primary spongiosa Metaphyseal corner fractures (abuse), scurvy
Secondary spongiosa SCFE in renal osteodystrophy

Labelled-figure questionsletter varies (B or C in different stems) → always choose the proliferative zone

3Presentation

Clinical features – rhizomelia, frontal bossing, trident hand

Rhizomelic dwarfismproximal segment shortest (humerus < forearm, femur < tibia) · disproportionate short stature · normal trunk (TO)

Heightadult ~50 in (male 4′4″, female 4′) · 6–7 SD below normal

Facemacrocephaly, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge

Handsbrachydactyly · trident hand = all fingers same length, divergent middle and ring fingers (TO)

Upper limblimited elbow extension · radial head subluxation/dislocation · posterior humeral bowing

Lower limbgenu varum · hypermobile hips and knees · muscular hypotonia · long fibulae
✗ Wrong options: genu valgum

Spinethoracolumbar kyphosis · lumbar hyperlordosis (up to 80%) · lumbar stenosis · foramen magnum stenosis

Neuro / developmentnormal intelligence · delayed motor milestones

ENTotitis media 90% before age 2 · hearing loss · tonsillar hypertrophy · obesity

NOT a featurecervical spine instability (→ pseudoachondroplasia) · atlantoaxial instability (→ Morquio MPS IVA, Down) · dural ectasia (→ NF, Marfan) · cauliflower ear (→ diastrophic)

Dwarfism by segment

Type Segment short Example
Rhizomelic Proximal (humerus, femur) Achondroplasia
Mesomelic Middle (forearm, leg) Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis
Mesoacromelic Middle + distal Ellis–van Creveld
Acromelic Distal (hands, feet) Peripheral dysostosis
Category (TO) Examples
Short trunk Kniest, metatrophic dysplasia, SED
Proportionate Diastrophic, cleidocranial dysplasia, mucopolysaccharidoses
Disproportionate (short limb) Achondroplasia, metaphyseal chondrodysplasias

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical + skeletal survey in most · FGFR3 molecular testing only if atypical / to distinguish similar disorders

PrenatalUS 2nd/3rd trimester: short long bones, wide metaphyses, ↑ biparietal diameter (>95th centile) · cell-free fetal DNA

Sleep studyall infants (screen for apnea)

Key radiology findings

Viewsskeletal survey · AP pelvis + femur (most diagnostic features)

Spine↓ interpedicular distance L1 → S1/L5 (pathognomonic) · short pedicles · posterior vertebral scalloping · T12/L1 apical wedging · bullet-shaped vertebrae in infants · hyperlordosis with flat sacrum

Pelvischampagne-glass pelvis (wider than deep) · squared ("ping-pong paddle") iliac wings · narrow sciatic notch · flat horizontal acetabula

Limbsshort thick bones · metaphyseal flaring · inverted-V distal femoral physis · proximal femoral radiolucency · epiphyses normal

MRIFMS: obliterated posterior subarachnoid space, cord "nicking/waisting", T2 signal change, syrinx · also lumbar stenosis

5Management

Thoracolumbar kyphosis – natural history

Most common dysplasia with TLKachondroplasia
✗ Wrong options: Trevor · MED (normal spine) · Larsen (cervical kyphosis) · diastrophic (cervical)

Causeflexible, forward slouching with unsupported sitting · 50–100% born with TLK

Natural historyresolves by 12–18 months (OB) · 1.5–2 years (TO) as child walks and gains trunk strength · resolution 90% by 18 months · ~70% by age 3 (OB) · prevalence ~87% at 1–2 yr → ~10% at 5–10 yr

Thoracolumbar kyphosis in achondroplasia
  • Flexible (most)→observe; no unsupported sitting
  • Fixed >30° / anterior wedging→TLSO until walking
  • Neuro deficit / failed brace / >45–60° (>50° TO)→posterior fusion ± anterior decompression
    (delay to age ≥4 for instrumentation)

Observationfirm-backed seating · avoid C-position · no sitting >60°

Bracing (TLSO)fixed component >30° (prone lateral) · substantial anterior wedging · posterior apical displacement · worn until independent walking · mean residual 8°

Fusionneuro compromise · kyphosis >45–60° (Orthobullets) · fixed >50° (TO) · failed brace · wait until age 4 · corpectomy if severe anterior cord impingement

Foramen magnum stenosis – sleep apnea

FMS → central sleep apnea → SIDS (2–5% mortality in 1st year) (TO)

Central vs obstructiveadenotonsillar hypertrophy → obstructive apnea, no hypotonia · FMS → central apnea + hypotonia

Signsclonus, hypotonia, hyperreflexia, clumsiness, dysphagia (lower CN), weakness

Work-upsleep study all infants · MRI/CT if abnormal exam or sleep study

Foramen magnum stenosis
  • No central apnea, no compression, neuro intact→observe, repeat MRI 6–12 mo
  • Central apnea / cord compression / neuro deficit→foramen magnum decompression + upper cervical laminectomy ± duraplasty
    (intra-op US; 10% recurrence)

Lumbar stenosis

Prevalence37–89% · 25% need surgery · disability in 3rd–4th decade

Causesshort thick pedicles · ↓ interpedicular distance L1→L5 · hyperplastic disc + ligamentum flavum

First lineweight loss, PT, corticosteroid injections

Surgerysevere neurogenic claudication · failed nonop · neuro symptoms at rest → multilevel laminectomy + fusion

Technique3 levels above block → at least S2 · no sublaminar wires / laminar hooks (narrow canal) · pedicle screws preferred but pedicles cranially directed, ~10 mm shorter, smaller sagittal diameter

Post-laminectomy kyphosiscommon despite >50% facet preservation → fuse if ≥5 levels or skeletally immature

Operative criteria

Problem Surgery when
TLK — brace Fixed >30°, anterior wedging
TLK — fusion Neuro deficit · >45–60° (Orthobullets) / >50° (TO) · failed brace · age ≥4
FMS Central sleep apnea · cord compression · weakness, hyperreflexia, clonus
Lumbar stenosis Severe claudication · failed nonop · neuro symptoms at rest
Genu varum Progressive severe deformity · fibular thrust
Upper-limb lengthening Bilateral humeral shortening preventing perineal / head hygiene (TO)

Extremities & stature

Genu varumbracing generally unsuccessful · tibial ± femoral osteotomy at CORA for progressive deformity / fibular thrust · TO: osteotomy > growth modulation

Growth hormonecontroversial · +6–8 cm over 5 yr

VosoritideCNP analogue · daily injection · age ≥5 yr with open physes

Lower-limb lengtheningvery controversial · early adolescence or two stages (age 7 + 12) · gain ~20.5 cm

Upper-limb lengthening

Indicationbilateral affection with humeral shortening limiting perineal hygiene (TO)
✗ Wrong options: unilateral LLD (upper limb non-weight-bearing, cosmetic)

Gainhumerus ~10 cm

Complications25–43%: fracture, early consolidation, nonunion, malalignment, stiffness, infection (TO)

6Complications

Hydrocephalusshunt in 5%

ENTotitis media 90% < age 2 · 50% need tympanostomy tubes

Spinal surgeryrecurrent FMS · CSF leak · malpositioned screw (abnormal pedicles) · neuro injury (overcorrection, wires/hooks) · post-laminectomy kyphosis

Life expectancy~61 yr (10 yr less) · highest mortality <4 yr (FMS)

X vs Y

Achondroplasia Pseudoachondroplasia Hypochondroplasia
Gene FGFR3 (chr 4p) COMP (chr 19) FGFR3 (Asn540Lys)
Face Frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia Normal face/skull Milder
Onset At birth Normal at birth, diagnosed 2–3 yr Often puberty (no growth spurt)
Spine Spinal stenosis, ↓ interpedicular distance No stenosis (normal interpedicular distance); C1–C2 instability (odontoid hypoplasia) Craniocervical issues less common
Epiphyses Normal Epiphysis + metaphysis involved, early hip dysplasia Similar X-ray to achondroplasia
Other Normal IQ — Taller; seizures/cognitive issues more common
FMS Adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Apnea Central Obstructive
Hypotonia Yes No
Test Sleep study → MRI/CT Sleep study

✗ Wrong options: COMP chr 19 · RUNX2/CBFA1

"Most common dysplasia with thoracolumbar kyphosis?"achondroplasia

"Associated with achondroplasia?"(central) sleep apnea (TO)
✗ Wrong options: genu valgum · LLD · atlantoaxial instability · dural ectasia · cauliflower ear

"Hypotonic 3-year-old with central apnea — work-up for?"foramen magnum stenosis

Adolescent Blount's Disease

Pediatrics · 3 / 112

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Definitionprogressive pathologic genu varum centred at proximal tibia, onset >10 years · idiopathic proximal tibia vara

Risk factorsobesity (causative) · African-American descent · more common in males (OB)

Associatedhypertension (often undiagnosed, under-treated, modifiable) · vitamin D deficiency prevalence = healthy children
✗ Wrong options: rickets

Onset vs diagnosisdeformity often begins 4–10 yr · diagnosed as adolescent form after age 10 (OB)

Pathophysiology

Causedyschondrosis of medial proximal tibial physis (posteromedial) · mechanical overload in genetically susceptible child

Deformitygenu varum + procurvatum + internal tibial torsion

Associated deformitydistal femoral varus + distal tibial valgus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: compensatory distal femoral valgus (that's infantile)

3Presentation

Hallmarkgenu varum, usually unilateral · obesity · "waddle"

OtherLLD secondary to deformity · mild–moderate MCL laxity · medial knee pain

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis – obesity & late-onset tibia vara

Diagnosisclinical genu varum + radiographic ↑ metaphyseal–diaphyseal angle

Differentials ruled outcongenital hypothyroidism (presents earlier) · metabolic syndrome (normal A1c, TGs) · primary varus gonarthrosis (adult) · vitamin D deficiency/rickets (bilateral femoral + tibial bowing)

Physiologicgenu varum normal <2 years

Key radiology findings

Viewsstanding long-cassette AP both lower limbs, patellae forward (internal tibial torsion common)

Findingsnarrowing of tibial epiphysis · widening of medial tibial physis · occasional widening of lateral distal femoral physis · metaphyseal beaking less common than infantile

Metaphyseal–diaphyseal (Drennan) angleline through metaphyseal beaks vs perpendicular to tibial axis · >16° abnormal

Tibiofemoral anglefemoral vs tibial longitudinal axes

Classificationno radiographic classification for adolescent form (Langenskiöld = infantile) · severity graded mild / moderate / severe by mechanical axis deviation (MAD)

5Management

Rulesurgery (TO) · observation/bracing unlikely to work — progressive, never resolves spontaneously · untreated → medial pain, altered kinematics, early arthritis
✗ Wrong options: orthotics

Adolescent Blount
  • Mild–moderate, growth remaining (>2 yr)→lateral tibial ± fibular hemiepiphysiodesis
  • Severe / near or at maturity (<2 yr growth)→proximal tibial osteotomy
    • No LLD→focal dome osteotomy at CORA
    • LLD corrected by opening wedge→medial opening wedge HTO + plate
    • LLD too large→osteotomy + external fixator (gradual)

Distal femoral varus ≥8° → distal femoral osteotomy or epiphysiodesis

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Mild–moderate + significant growth remaining Lateral tibia + fibula hemiepiphysiodesis (8-plate / staple / permanent)
Closed physes / insufficient growth (e.g. 15 yr ♀, triradiate fused) Osteotomy (✗ Wrong options: growth modulation)
Varus + LLD 2 cm, physes closed Medial opening wedge HTO + plate
LLD not correctable by opening wedge Osteotomy + external fixator
Distal femoral varus ≥8° Distal femoral osteotomy / epiphysiodesis
Goal Neutral mechanical axis (✗ Wrong options: overcorrection into valgus (that's infantile))

Treatment – hemiepiphysiodesis (failure) & osteotomy

PrincipleHueter-Volkmann law: lateral tether slows lateral growth → medial "catches up"
✗ Wrong options: flexible nails = secondary healing · VDRO · Ilizarov distraction · lag screw = primary healing

Transient hemiepiphysiodesis8-plate or staple · removable · needs significant growth · watch for physeal arrest or rebound growth

Permanent hemiepiphysiodesislateral physeal ablation · overcorrection uncommon · no rotational correction · does not preclude later osteotomy

Residual deformityup to 25% need formal osteotomy

Acute HTO + internal fixationclosing, opening, dome, serrated, inclined osteotomies · immediate correction · risks neurologic injury (acute lengthening) + compartment syndrome → consider prophylactic fasciotomy · PWB 6–8 wk

Gradual correction (Taylor Spatial Frame / Ilizarov)12–18 wk · limits NV compromise + compartment syndrome · all planes + length · cons: pin-site infection, duration, bulk

Paley osteotomy rules (tibia vara)

Rule Osteotomy vs ACA/CORA Result
1 Osteotomy through ACA-CORA Pure angulation, no translation
2 ACA through CORA, osteotomy elsewhere Angulation + bone-end translation, axes collinear
3 Osteotomy through ACA, CORA at another level No bone-end translation, axes parallel but translated

Best osteotomyfocal dome centred on CORA → restores alignment, minimal axis translation + shortening, least bone-end translation, most bone contact
✗ Wrong options: intra-articular (chondral/cruciate risk) · horizontal (translates ends + axes)

6Complications

Most common complication of growth modulationimplant failure (screw breakage) (TO)

Ankle Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 4 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence25–40% of all physeal injuries (2nd most common) · 5% of pediatric fractures

Demographicsmales 2:1 · age 8–15 yr

Risk factorssports · ↑ BMI

PatternsSH I, II · SH III → Tillaux, medial malleolus · SH IV → triplane, medial malleolus

Anatomy – physes

Distal tibial physis35–40% of tibial growth, 15–20% of limb growth · 3–4 mm/yr · growth until 14 yr girls / 16 yr boys · closes over 18 months

Closure ordercentral → anteromedial → posteromedial → lateral (basis of Tillaux, triplane)

Distal fibular physiscloses 12–24 months after distal tibia

Ligamentsorigins distal to physes → physis fails first

Ligament Attachments Note
AITFL Chaput (anterolateral tibial epiphysis) → Wagstaffe (anterior fibula) Avulses Tillaux / transitional fractures
PITFL Volkmann tubercle → posterior fibula —
Inferior transverse Posterior fibula across posterior tibial plafond Posterior labrum
Deep deltoid — Primary restraint to lateral talar shift

2Mechanism

Mechanismdirect trauma · twisting about a planted foot

High-energy abduction injuries (e.g. skateboarding) → ↑ physeal closure risk

3Presentation

Symptomspain, inability to bear weight

Examswelling, ecchymosis, deformity if displaced · distal fibular physeal tenderness = nondisplaced SH I

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP, mortise, lateral · full-length tibia to rule out Maisonneuve

CTdisplacement (best post-reduction), articular step-off, pre-op planning

Physeal widening after reduction → interposed periosteum

Salter-Harris classification

Type Freq. Description Note
I 15% Through physis Nondisplaced: fibular tenderness only
II 45% Physis + metaphysis (Thurston-Holland) Most common
III 25% Physis + epiphysis Tillaux, medial malleolus · ↑ arrest
IV 25% Metaphysis + physis + epiphysis Triplane, medial malleolus shear · ↑ arrest
V 1% Crush Diagnosed late at growth arrest
VI Rare Perichondral ring Lawnmower / iatrogenic

Dias & Tachdjian (mechanism) classification

Mechanism Injury
Supination–inversion Gr 1: fibular SH I/II avulsion · Gr 2: + medial malleolus SH III/IV
Supination–plantarflexion Tibial SH I/II, epiphysis displaced posteriorly, posterior Thurston-Holland · no fibular fracture · hard to see on AP
Supination–external rotation Gr 1: tibial SH II, fragment posteromedial, line runs proximal-medial on AP · Gr 2: + low spiral fibula
Pronation/eversion–ER Tibial SH I/II + transverse fibula, displaced laterally · ± diastasis
Axial compression SH V — diagnosed late

Operative criteria

Fracture Nonop CRPP ORIF
Isolated distal fibula <2 mm → boot / NWB SLC 4 wk · >2 mm acceptable CR → NWB cast 6 wk >2 mm, failed CR, >2 yr growth >2 mm, failed CR, <2 yr growth
Distal tibia SH I/II Acceptable CR → NWB cast 6 wk Unacceptable CR + >2 yr growth Unacceptable CR + <2 yr growth
Distal tibia SH III/IV — <2 mm after CR >2 mm after CR

Acceptable SH I/II tibiano varus · <10° valgus · <10° recurvatum/procurvatum · <3 mm physeal widening

Acceptable tibial reduction<2 mm · confirm on mortise

Displaced distal tibial physeal fracture
  • CR acceptable→long-leg NWB cast 6 wk
  • Irreducible / residual physeal gap→open reduction, remove interposed periosteum
    • Stable after open reduction→cast
    • Unstable→internal fixation (smooth wires across physis)

Irreducible fractures – interposed periosteum & open reduction

Closed reductionadequate sedation + relaxation · max 2 attempts (repeated attempts injure physis)

Block to reductionperiosteum on the tension side · also tendon, NV structures
✗ Wrong options: compression side · comminution · unrecognised fracture line

Failed CR under sedation → ORIF
✗ Wrong options: repeat CR under GA · cast and follow-up · admit

Why openinterposed periosteum → premature physeal closure (makes bone, cartilage or fibrous tissue in physis)
✗ Wrong options: "to prevent nonunion" (nonunion rare)

✗ Wrong options: "rare"

SH III/IV medial malleoluslarge cartilaginous portion (bigger than X-ray fragment) → articular incongruity → ORIF avoiding physis and joint
✗ Wrong options: casting · CAM walker

Fixationtransepiphyseal, parallel to physis · 2 parallel epiphyseal screws (medial malleolus shear) · cannulated screws parallel to physis (Tillaux, triplane) · transverse metaphyseal screw if large fragment · smooth K-wires if crossing physis
✗ Wrong options: screw crossing physis

Follow-uplong-term (high growth-arrest rate)

6Complications

Physeal arrest risk – residual gap

Ratepremature physeal closure 8–50% after distal tibial physeal fractures

Highest growth disturbancemedial malleolus SH IV

Risk factor for premature physeal closure
Residual physeal gap — greatest risk >3 mm (Orthobullets, OB) · >2 mm (OB) — read the options
Initial displacement +15% per 1 mm
Entrapped periosteum Yes
High-energy (abduction, skateboarding) Yes (✗ Wrong options: football)
SH III / IV Yes (all types at risk)
Age >8 yr NOT a risk factor
Number of reductions, ORIF vs closed not associated if anatomic

Partial arrestdistal fibular arrest → valgus · medial tibial arrest → varus (continued fibular growth)

Complete arrestLLD

Physeal bar – resection, osteotomy & fibular epiphysiodesis

Distal tibial physeal bar
  • <50% area + >2 yr growth→bar resection + interposition (fat)
    (add osteotomy if angulation >10–20°)
  • >50% + ≥2 yr growth→complete epiphysiodesis + ipsilateral fibular epiphysiodesis
  • Skeletally mature with deformity→osteotomy

Bar resection<50% physis, >2 yr (or 2 cm) growth, angulation <20° (Orthobullets) · interpose fat, cranioplast, bone wax, cartilage, muscle, silicone · via metaphyseal window
✗ Wrong options: through the joint (bar not visible)

Osteotomyangulation >10–20° (won't remodel after resection) → osteotomy + bar resection through osteotomy site

Fibular epiphysiodesisbar >50% + ≥2 yr growth + open fibular physis → prevents varus + lateral impingement

Bar typesperipheral (angular deformity, resectable) · elongated (SH III/IV, middle) · central (tents articular surface) · small <25% central = best prognosis

LLDbar resection if <50% + >2 yr growth · contralateral epiphysiodesis near maturity

Rotational malunion

Unrecognised deformityexternal rotation through physis, noticed months after walking (↑ foot-progression angle)
✗ Wrong options: internal rotation · procurvatum/recurvatum (seen and corrected initially) · valgus

Anterolateral Bowing & Congenital Pseudoarthrosis of Tibia

Pediatrics · 5 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidenceextremely rare · 1:140,000–190,000 (Orthobullets) · 1 in 250,000 live births (TO)

Continuumanterolateral bowing → congenital pseudarthrosis of tibia (CPT) = same disease
✗ Wrong options: calcaneovalgus · fibular hemimelia · CTEV · CVT

Pathophysiologypseudarthrosis is not congenital · develops post-natally from fracture nonunion

NF1 association & natural history (fracture/pseudarthrosis)

NF1most common association · in 50–55% of anterolateral bowing/CPT (Orthobullets, TO) · 50–90% in large series (TO)

Reverseonly 6–10% of NF1 patients have anterolateral bowing (TO: ~6%)
✗ Wrong options: 20% · 50% · NF2

Fibrous dysplasia15%

First signpresents in 1st year → may be first recognised manifestation of NF1 · NF does not change union rate or outcome (TO)

NF1 geneticsneurofibromin, chromosome 17, usually spontaneous mutation · café-au-lait spots

NF1 orthopaedic manifestationsscoliosis (dystrophic + non-dystrophic), CPT, soft-tissue tumours · nerve sheath tumours (neurofibromas) → "not associated with NF1?" → none of the above (TO)

Natural historydoes not self-resolve · spontaneous fracture at site of bowing → nonunion · once fractured, low chance of spontaneous healing
✗ Wrong options: resolution by 2 yr · no change · spread

Three types of tibial bowing

Bowing Cause Natural history
Anterolateral NF1 / CPT Fracture → pseudarthrosis; no remodelling
Posteromedial Physiologic (intrauterine packing) · calcaneovalgus foot Resolves over 5–7 yr · LLD 3–4 cm · rarely fractures
Anteromedial Fibular hemimelia (deficiency) —
Posterolateral No specific association —

3Presentation

Onsetbowing in first year of life

Examanterolateral deformity · café-au-lait spots + other NF stigmata

Fibuladysplastic fibula / fibular pseudarthrosis in two-thirds (TO) · one-third (other TO explanation) — read the options

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Radiographsanterolateral bow · intramedullary sclerosis / narrowed or obliterated canal at apex (prefracture stage) · cystic change · hourglass constriction · tapered, sclerotic ends

Treatment-guiding criteria

ClassificationsBoyd, Andersen, Crawford: none guide management or predict outcome

Two practical criteriafracture present or absent · age at fracture: early onset <4 yr, late onset >4 yr

Boyd classification (TO)

Type Feature Prognosis
I Anterior bowing + tibial defect at birth —
II Anterior bowing + hourglass constriction; fracture <2 yr ("high-risk tibia"), sclerotic, canal obliterated Most common, NF-associated, poorest
III Congenital cyst (middle/distal third junction) Recurrence less than II
IV Sclerotic segment, no narrowing; stress fracture Good
V Dysplastic fibula Good if confined to fibula
VI Intraosseous neurofibroma / schwannoma Extremely rare

Crawford classification (TO) — all anterolateral

Type Feature Prognosis
I Preserved canal, cortical thickening at apex Good, may never fracture
II Thinned canal, cortical thickening, trabeculation defect —
III Cystic lesion Early fracture → early treatment
IV Established pseudarthrosis (tibia ± fibula) —

Andersendysplastic, cystic, sclerotic, clubfoot types · El-Rosasy–Paley–Herzenberg — I atrophic mobile, no surgery · II atrophic mobile, previous surgery · III broad ends, stiff · Choi fibula — A (fibula intact) · B (fibular pseudarthrosis, B1–B3)

5Management

Anterolateral bowing / CPT
  • Bowing, no fracture, ambulatory→brace (clamshell / PTB / AFO anterior shell) to maturity
    (TO: 8-plate guided growth for cystic, unfractured tibia)
  • Fracture or pseudarthrosis→resect, realign, graft, IM rod ± frame / vascularised fibula / 4-in-1
  • Multiple failed unions, severe LLD→Syme / Boyd amputation

Bracing to prevent fracture

Indicationambulatory (weight-bearing) child with bowing, no fracture/pseudarthrosis

Braceclamshell orthosis · patellar tendon bearing (PTB) orthosis · AFO with anterior shell · until skeletal maturity

Goalprevent further bowing + fracture
✗ Wrong options: correct deformity (bowing is not brace-correctable)

Contraindicatedosteotomy for bowing alone (→ nonunion)
✗ Wrong options: observation · IM rod · vascularised fibula · PT

Posteromedial bowing case"pseudarthrosis, brace" is the false statement · observation only, LLD, calcaneovalgus association (TO)

Growth modulation for deformity

Unfractured anterolateral bowing with cystic changedistal tibial anterolateral 8-plate (guided growth) → gradual cyst resolution + correction (TO, Laine 2020)
✗ Wrong options: osteotomy + IM nail/plate (nonunion) · 4-in-1 (for established pseudarthrosis)

Surgical indications & NF1 association

Surgical indicationpseudarthrosis or fracture (TO)
✗ Wrong options: bowing >45° · failure of brace to correct

Goalsresect pseudarthrosis to normal bone · correct alignment · bone graft + stabilise · intramedullary splinting

Technique Key point
IM rod + bone graft Resect, shorten tibia, rod, graft
Free vascularised fibula (Farmer) Contralateral fibula (ipsilateral involved) · when IM nailing + graft fails
Ilizarov / circular frame Lengthening or bone transport
4-in-1 (Choi) Resect both sclerotic ends + cortical onlay grafts → tibiofibular cross-union · for Choi B2/B3 fibula · + Ilizarov lengthening if shortening >2–3 cm (TO)
Fibula Resect fibular pseudarthrosis (↑ union) · osteotomise intact fibula

Amputationafter multiple failed unions, severe LLD, dysfunctional deformity · Syme or Boyd (ankle disarticulation) preferred over amputation at pseudarthrosis

Refracture≥50% even after union · decreases with age, ceases after maturity

Othervalgus deformity · LLD ~5 cm at maturity · no treatment gives predictable results

Fracture risk High Rare —

Arthrogryposis

Pediatrics · 6 / 112

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Definitionnon-progressive congenital disorder · multiple rigid joints in all 4 limbs · a physical finding in ~300 disorders (TO)

Incidence1:3000 live births (TO)

Coursecontractures do not worsen with growth
✗ Wrong options: "progressive, peak at maturity"

Etiology

Mechanismfetal akinesia (↓ movement in utero) → symmetric contractures · movement needed from 8 weeks' gestation (TO)

Neurogenic vs myopathicneurogenic 90%, myopathic 10% (Orthobullets) · neurologic 70–80% / 80% (TO)

Pathophysiologymaternal antibodies vs fetal acetylcholine receptors → ↓ anterior horn cells · anterior horn cell disease (Werdnig-Hoffmann, SMA)

Other causes (TO)connective tissue (diastrophic dysplasia, Larsen, Beals) · myopathies · uterine space limits (oligohydramnios, fibroids, multiple pregnancy) · vascular compromise · maternal disease (diabetes, MS, myasthenia, myotonic dystrophy, rubella, CMV, toxoplasma)

No genetic predisposition for classic form (OB)

Classification

Type Description
I Single localised deformity (e.g. forearm pronation)
II Full expression — absent shoulder muscles, thin limbs, elbows extended, wrists flexed + ulnar deviated, intrinsic-plus hands, adducted thumbs, no flexion creases
III Type II + polydactyly + non-neuromuscular systems

By neurological function (TO)normal: amyoplasia, distal arthrogryposis, fetal crowding, systemic tissue disorder, multiple pterygium · abnormal neurological function

Amyoplasiamost common recognisable form · sporadic, symmetric · normal/above-average IQ · midline facial hemangioma · hip involvement ~80%

Distal arthrogryposis & related syndromes (TO)

Distal arthrogryposishands + feet, large joints spared · ulnar-deviated fingers at MCP · "cup-like" palm, single crease · flexed adducted thumb · equinovarus or vertical talus · better prognosis

Freeman-Sheldoncommon variant of type 2 distal arthrogryposis · whistling face (pursed lips, deep eyes)
✗ Wrong options: Larsen · Escobar

Pterygium syndromesskin webs across joints · Escobar = multiple pterygium (neck webs, vertebral anomalies) · popliteal pterygium variant

Larsenfilamin B · hypermobility · congenital dislocation of multiple joints (anterior knee dislocation) · cervical kyphosis/injury · normal IQ

Bruck syndromeOI + congenital contractures

3Presentation

Clinical characteristics

Region Classic finding
Shoulder Adducted, internally rotated (absent deltoid)
Elbow Extended, no flexion creases (deficient biceps, brachialis) · rarely flexed
Wrist Flexed + ulnar deviated (TO)
Hand Intrinsic plus · IP flexion + relative MCP extension · adducted thumb / thumb-in-palm
Hip Flexed, abducted, externally rotated · subluxation / teratologic dislocation
Knee Extended (classic) but most often flexed · weak quads · dimple over patella
Foot Clubfoot (most common deformity) · vertical talus rarer
Spine C-shaped neuromuscular scoliosis — 33% (Orthobullets) · 28–67% / 10–30% (TO) · long thoracolumbar curves

Normalintelligence, facies, sensation, viscera

Otherfractures 25% · limbs cylindrical/fusiform with ↓ skin creases · nonambulatory 25%

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis & upper-limb pattern

Diagnosisclinical: multiple symmetric contractures (e.g. stiff fingers with few creases, IR arms, flexed-ER hips, stiff clubfeet) → arthrogryposis
✗ Wrong options: Larsen · CP · Down

Studies at 3–4 monthsneurologic studies · enzyme tests · muscle biopsy · genetic testing

Prenatal US (TO)lack of movement, fixed flexion, abnormal position, ↑ nuchal translucency, polyhydramnios-type signs, thin ribs, diaphyseal fractures

5Management

Principlemultidisciplinary · stretching + casting first → soft-tissue release / osteotomy · correct alignment, preserve ROM, tendon transfers for active motion

Operative criteria

Region Indication / timing
Upper limb surgery After age 4 (independent eating) (Orthobullets) · after ambulation, 3–4 yr; not >8 yr (TO)
Elbow extension contracture Triceps V-Y lengthening + posterior capsulectomy at 1.5–3 yr
Unilateral hip dislocation Open reduction ≥6 mo (Orthobullets) · 6–9 mo (OB) · before 1 yr (OB)
Knee flexion contracture >30° → hamstring release at 6–9 mo (Orthobullets) · not corrected by 6–12 mo (TO)
Hip flexion contracture >45° → surgical release (TO)
Knee extension contracture Failed casting by 6–12 mo → quadricepsplasty (TO)
Foot Around time of standing (↓ recurrence) (TO)

Upper limb – passive manipulation & casting

Goalsdrive electric chair, use computer devices · one elbow extended (positioning, perianal care) + one flexed (feeding)

First linepassive manipulation + serial casting (13-month-old, good triceps)

Deformity Procedure
Elbow extension Triceps V-Y lengthening + posterior capsulectomy (passive flexion) · active flexion: bipolar pectoralis major / latissimus transfer, long-head triceps transfer, Steindler flexorplasty
Stiff flexed elbow Not severe → no surgery (TO)
Wrist palmar flexion + ulnar deviation FCU release/lengthening/transfer to wrist extensors · dorsal carpal closing-wedge osteotomy · fusion = salvage · ideal 5–20° dorsiflexion
Thumb-in-palm, syndactyly Z-plasty, adductor release, syndactyly release
Finger deformity PIP arthrodesis
Shoulder IR External rotation humeral osteotomy (TO)

Hip dislocation – open reduction (not Pavlik)

Teratologic hip68–80% · dislocates early in utero → stiff, rigid

Pavlik / abduction braceunlikely to succeed → US still shows dislocation (α ~40°, β unmeasurable) · Pavlik in dislocated hip prevents posterior wall development

Closed reductionrarely successful (skin/skeletal traction not helpful)

Arthrogrypotic hip dislocation
  • Unilateral→open reduction (prevent pelvic obliquity, scoliosis)
    • <1 yr (6–9 mo)→medial approach ± femoral shortening
    • Older child→anterior approach + femoral shortening ± pelvic osteotomy
  • Bilateral→observe (controversial; many ambulate)
    • Good arc of motion (e.g. 80°)→bilateral medial open reduction (OB)

Approachmedial (good results 80%; Szoke) · anteromedial or anterolateral both good (OB) · anterior reserved for older children

Prerequisitereasonable flexion/extension arc + active lower-limb movement

Riskresulting hip flexion contracture worsens gait

Sequence conflictknee releases before hip reduction to help maintain reduction (Orthobullets; TO: correct knees before hip) · "hip first, knee second" (other TO explanation) — read the options

Knee contractures

Flexion contractureserial splinting/casting → hamstring release (>30°, early) · ambulation possible with residual 15–20° · supracondylar femoral extension osteotomy at maturity · guided growth with osteotomies (may not fix poor quads) · Ilizarov for severe

Extension contracture / dislocationearly stretching + casting · open quadriceps tenotomy at 4–6 mo · late V-Y quadricepsplasty · reduce knee dislocation first

Most common deformity in AMCtalipes equinovarus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: CVT · knee flexion · IP flexion

Newbornstart serial stretching + splinting immediately (TO)
✗ Wrong options: wait for weight gain · wait 1 month

Ponsetieffective but more casts than idiopathic · high relapse (27% at 2 yr) (TO)

  • Early→Ponseti casting (more casts)
  • Rigid / failed Ponseti→posteromedial + posterolateral release
  • Recurrence after release→talectomy (child) / triple arthrodesis (adolescent)

CVT in arthrogryposissoft-tissue release first · talectomy if recurrence

CVT associationship dislocation 43–50% (✓ "congenital hip dislocation") · myelomeningocele, arthrogryposis, trisomy 18, Cri-du-Chat · familial HOXD10 · 60–85% have associated anomalies
✗ Wrong options: amniotic band · fibular hemimelia · PFFD · polydactyly

Typeovergrowth syndrome

Locuschromosome 11p15.5

Mechanismoveractivity of IGF-2 (growth factor) and/or loss of active CDKN1C (cell-proliferation inhibitor)

Inheritancesporadic 85% · AD with incomplete penetrance 15%

Labneonatal hypoglycemia (✗ Wrong options: hyperglycemia) from pancreatic islet cell hypertrophy (✗ Wrong options: pancreatic insufficiency) → repeated bouts → spasticity, altered development

3Presentation

Diagnostic criteria

Major Minor
Overgrowth (large for gestational age, gigantism) Hemihypertrophy — 10–20% (Orthobullets) · ~15% (OB)
Abdominal wall defects incl. omphalocele Ear anomalies (linear lobe creases)
Macroglossia Neonatal hypoglycemia
Nephromegaly

Exammacroglossia · midface hypoplasia · infraorbital creases · anterior linear ear-lobe creases · visceromegaly · exophthalmos · hemihypertrophy (whole side incl. foot)

No skin markingsabsence of nevi / vascular markings excludes NF, Proteus, Klippel-Trenaunay as causes of hemihypertrophy

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisphysical exam + genetic testing

Key radiology findings

Radiographscomparison view of affected vs contralateral limb (LLD)

Bone ageinaccurate when very young · later useful to time epiphysiodesis
✗ Wrong options: as initial study at age 2

5Management

Wilms tumour screening

Predispositionembryonal tumours: Wilms tumour (most common), hepatoblastoma, adrenal neoplasm · hemihypertrophy from BWS → 40% malignancy risk (OB)

Screeningrenal + abdominal ultrasound every 3–6 months until 5–8 years (Orthobullets) · until ~7 years (OB) · intervals ≤4 months ↓ late-stage disease

Tumour sidemay be contralateral to hemihypertrophy

Child with hemihypertrophy (BWS)
  • Screening→abdominal/renal US q3–6 mo until 5–8 yr (Wilms)
  • LLD→serial limb radiographs, bone age later
    • Predicted significant LLD→epiphysiodesis of affected (longer) limb

Operative criteria

Epiphysiodesisgrowth arrest of the affected (overgrown) limb for LLD

Multidisciplinaryorthopaedic, abdominal and overgrowth issues

How it's asked

"Large-for-dates neonate with hypoglycemia, now right hemihypertrophy + 2 cm LLD — next imaging?"renal and abdominal ultrasonography
✗ Wrong options: left-wrist bone age · MRI spine/brain · hip US

✗ Wrong options: hearing loss · hyperglycemia · pancreatic insufficiency · vision loss

"Cause of infantile hypoglycemia in BWS?"pancreatic islet cell hypertrophy

"Treatment of BWS limb overgrowth?"epiphysiodesis of affected limb

Bipartite Patella

Pediatrics · 8 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence2–3% (Orthobullets) · ~2% (TO) · "1 in 20" (OB)

Sexno sex predilection (Orthobullets) · M:F 9:1 (TO) — read the options

Bilateral50% (Orthobullets, OB) · "most patients" (TO)

Locationsuperolateral (Saupe type III) most common

Etiology & anatomy

Naturenormal variant, failure of fusion of accessory ossification centre · often confused with patella fracture

Ossificationpatella = largest sesamoid, single nucleus · ossifies 4–5 yr ♂ / 3 yr ♀ · accessory centre at 8–12 yr · fragment joined by fibrocartilage

Painful bipartite patellatrauma disrupts fibrocartilaginous zone → cannot unite (no arterial penetration to fragment) · vastus lateralis traction → separation/nonunion

Blood supplypredominantly distal → proximal · 6 arteries: superior + inferior medial/lateral geniculates (popliteal), supreme geniculate (SFA), anterior tibial recurrent

Associatednail-patella syndrome

Histology

Interposed tissuefibrocartilage > fibrous > hyaline · avascular

Adjacent bonescalloped, osteoclasts, well vascularised

3Presentation

Symptomsmostly asymptomatic, incidental · only 2% symptomatic: anterior knee pain after direct trauma (fall, kick) or overuse (cycling, hill climbing) · worse squatting, jumping, stairs · giving way

Examtenderness over fragment (superolateral) · hematoma · quad inhibition · palpable defect / large patella

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

AP kneebest view to see bipartite patella

Skylineprone (non-weight-bearing) vs squatting (weight-bearing) → ↑ separation of fragments on squatting view

Contralateral kneesimilar findings in 50%

Bipartite vs fracturesuperolateral · smooth, rounded borders · often bilateral

MRIpainful bipartite patella → edema around fragment = pain source

Bone scanequivocal X-ray: ↑ uptake superolateral · controversial

CTshows fragment, not edema

Saupe classification

Type Incidence Location Image
I 5% Inferior pole (transverse split)
II 20% Lateral margin (longitudinal)
III 75% Superolateral pole (oblique)

5Management

Bipartite patella
  • Asymptomatic / benign exam→reassure, symptomatic Rx, RTP as tolerated
  • Symptomatic→rest, NSAIDs, isometric quads, brace 30° flexion, ± steroid ≥6 months
  • Failed >6 mo / displaced / significant impairment→excision of fragment
    • Superolateral fragment→± lateral release or subperiosteal VL release

Location & nonoperative care

Incidental with benign examreassurance + observation · symptomatic treatment, return to play as tolerated
✗ Wrong options: MRI · ORIF · cast 6 wk · immobilise 120° (that's quad contusion)

Nonop ≥6 monthsrest/sport restriction · NSAIDs · isometric quadriceps strengthening · brace in 30° flexion · local corticosteroid · less successful in young athletes (compliance)

Operative criteria

Indication for surgery
Failed nonop >6 months
Displaced fragment needing reduction
Direct trauma causing onset of pain
Significant impairment of daily activities
Procedure Note
Open excision Most common, good results · poor if large articular fragment (PF incongruity)
Arthroscopic excision Faster recovery, spares quad tendon
Lateral retinacular release Superolateral fragment — removes VL traction
Subperiosteal VL release Superolateral; avoids long lateral release; arthroscopic = quicker, less effusion
ORIF Large fragments · controversial

6Complications

PF maltrackingexcision of large fragment / lateral release → PF degeneration

Otherseffusion (arthrocentesis) · persistent pain (after lateral release) · quad weakness · osteonecrosis

Differential – dorsal defect of patella; double-layered patella (MED)

Double-layered patellapathognomonic of MED · two segments split by coronal septum · anterior in quad/patellar tendons · posterior articulates · painful snapping, locking, dislocation → fusion of segments (best) or resection (TO)
✗ Wrong options: CDP · SED · achondroplasia

Dorsal defect of patellaround, lytic, well-defined subchondral lesion, superolateral quadrant, sclerotic rim, no matrix, no periosteal reaction · MRI: T2 bright, no marrow edema · usually incidental, self-limited → activity modification · rarely curettage + graft (TO)
✗ Wrong options: OCD · chondroblastoma · Brodie abscess

X vs Y

Bipartite patella Patella fracture Dorsal defect of patella
Site Superolateral Any Superolateral, subchondral dorsal
Edges Smooth, rounded Sharp Sclerotic rim, lytic
Bilateral 50% No —
Treatment Symptomatic Per fracture Self-limited

How it's asked

"Knee pain after fall, benign exam — which X-ray warrants reassurance?"bipartite patella
✗ Wrong options: patellar dislocation · patella alta/tendon rupture · Segond · GCT

"Helmet to knee, benign exam, bipartite patella on X-ray — next?"symptomatic treatment, RTP as tolerated
✗ Wrong options: MRI · ORIF

"Most common location?"superolateral (Saupe III)

"Double-layered patella is pathognomonic of?"MED (TO)

"12-year-old, superolateral dorsal subchondral lucency with sclerotic rim?"dorsal defect of patella (TO)
✗ Wrong options: OCD · chondroblastoma · Brodie abscess

I Primary bladder closure Newborn

Both Bone Forearm Fracture - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 10 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence~40% of all pediatric fractures · males > females

Locationdistal physis 14% · distal metaphysis 60% · midshaft 20% · proximal third 4%

Peakduring peak bone turnover (remodelling mismatch)

Associatedfloating elbow (ipsilateral supracondylar) 15% · nerve injury 1%, most often median

Anatomy

Bowingphysiologic apex-lateral radial bow · apex-posterior ulnar bow

Deforming forcesbiceps + supinator flex/supinate proximal fragment · pronator teres + quadratus pronate distal fragment · brachioradialis dorsiflexes + radially deviates distal fragment

Periosteumintact on concave side · interosseous membrane taut in neutral to slight supination

2Mechanism

Mechanismfall from height, sport, playground (monkey bars)

3Presentation

Symptomsforearm pain, refuses to use arm

Examswelling, deformity, ecchymosis · subtle poke-hole open wounds · check elbow + wrist · NV exam · compartment syndrome

4Diagnosis & Classification

Typesincomplete: greenstick, torus, plastic deformation · complete · proximal / middle / distal third · apex volar or dorsal

Assessing rotational alignment

View Landmarks 180° apart when aligned
AP Radial styloid + bicipital tuberosity
Lateral Ulnar styloid + coronoid

Other cluesfragment diameters and cortical thickness should match

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral forearm + orthogonal elbow and wrist

Findingsboth bones fractured · one fracture + plastic deformation of the other · atypical bowing without fracture = plastic deformation

5Management

Acceptable alignment & remodelling by age

Age Angulation Malrotation Bayonet apposition
<10 yr <15° <45° Yes if <1 cm short (100% translation OK)
≥10 yr <10° <30° No
<2 yr growth left 0° 0° No — adult tolerances

By level (girls ≤8, boys ≤10)distal third 20° · middle 15° · proximal 10° · remodelling ↓ distal → proximal

Bayonetacceptable (esp. distal radius) if angulation ≤20° and ≥2 yr growth remain

8-year-old, 12° dorsal angulation at 1 week → acceptable → no sequelae
✗ Wrong options: ↓ rotation · malunion · nonunion

Operative criteria

Indication Treatment
Unacceptable alignment after CR (beyond table) Fixation
Bayonet apposition >10 yr Fixation
Both-bone fracture <13 yr Elastic IM nails
Both-bone fracture >13 yr (near maturity) ORIF (plate)
Open fracture, refracture ORIF
Comminuted / segmental, highly displaced ORIF (relative)
Malunion with callus + lost rotation (missed follow-up) ORIF (open callus removal) (✗ Wrong options: brace · recast · repeat CR · cast wedging)
Pediatric both-bone forearm fracture
  • Acceptable after CR→cast, weekly X-rays
  • Unacceptable / lost reduction
    • <13 yr, simple midshaft→elastic IM nails
    • >13 yr, comminuted, open, refracture→ORIF

Casting technique – cast index & loss of reduction

Closed reductiontraction (finger traps), thumb pressure, rotation, 3-point bending · apex volar → pronate · apex dorsal → supinate

Plastic deformationaccept if ≤20° · reduce with slow steady 3-point bending (abrupt force → fracture)

Short vs long arm cast (distal BBFF) — no difference in loss of reduction · SAC fewer complications
✗ Wrong options: more swelling, pain, remanipulation

Cast indexlateral inner width ÷ AP inner width · >0.8 → loss of reduction
✗ Wrong options: pain · physeal arrest · nonunion · swelling

Remanipulation riskinitial fracture displacement (angulation + translation) · same-level radius + ulna fractures · cast index >0.8 · residual deformity
✗ Wrong options: mechanism · distal location · below-elbow cast · cast index <0.7

Swellingbivalve cast (compartment syndrome)

Operative fixation – intramedullary nails vs plates

Ulnar nailolecranon tip or through anconeus (protect ulnar nerve)

Radial nailjust proximal to radial styloid or dorsal distal radius proximal to physis · dorsal central start risks EPL

Techniquereduce easiest bone first · open the fracture after 2–3 failed passes · nail removal at 3–4 months

Elastic IM nails ORIF plate
Time Shorter Longer
Blood loss Less More
Union, radial bow, rotation Equal Equal
Refracture Lower (no screw holes) Higher after plate removal
Best for Midshaft, transverse/oblique, minimal comminution, acute (pre-callus) Comminution, older, open

6Complications

Complication – loss of forearm rotation

Most common long-term after IM fixationloss of pronation/supination (soft-tissue injury, stripping)
✗ Wrong options: infection · malunion · refracture · nonunion

Refracture5–10% · risks: plate removal, greenstick pattern → ORIF

Malunionloss of rotation · from initial reduction or delayed diagnosis → corrective osteotomy

Compartment syndromehigh energy · multiple reduction / nail-passage attempts → fasciotomy

Synostosisrare · head injury, high energy · resection rarely helps

"7-year-old acceptable alignment at 1 week?"observation
✗ Wrong options: repeat CR · ORIF · IMN

"Short vs long arm cast after anatomic CR of distal BBFF?"no difference in outcomes

"Cast index 0.95 — risk?"loss of reduction

"Factor predisposing to remanipulation?"initial fracture displacement

"IMN vs plate — true statement?"radial bow restoration similar
✗ Wrong options: IMN higher nonunion · more blood loss · longer surgery

"Missed follow-up, 6 weeks, healed malaligned, lost pronosupination?"ORIF radius + ulna
✗ Wrong options: cast wedging · repeat CR

"Radiographic rotational alignment?"AP: radial styloid + biceps tuberosity 180° apart

1Basics

Epidemiology

Not required if foot flexible enough to exclude CVT

Plantarflexion lateraldistinguishes from CVT · before navicular ossifies (age 3) use 1st metatarsal as proxy · calcaneovalgus: 1st MT lines up with talus · CVT: talar axis passes plantar to 1st MT on standard + plantarflexion laterals

Flexible flatfootyears after resolution

Calcaneovalgus Congenital vertical talus
Flexibility Flexible, passively correctable Rigid
Hindfoot Calcaneus (dorsiflexion) Equinus + valgus
Midfoot Normal Dorsal TN dislocation, rocker-bottom, medial talar head

Weak Plantarflexors (S1, S2), invertors (L5)

Cavovarus Foot in Pediatrics & Adults

Pediatrics · 13 / 112

1Basics

Deformity components

Componentscavus (high arch) · plantarflexed 1st ray + forefoot pronation · hindfoot varus · forefoot adduction

Etiology

Neurologic~67% (two-thirds) · identifying the neuro cause is critical

Unilateral → rule out tethered cord / spinal cord tumour · Bilateral → most commonly Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT), often hereditary/congenital

Idiopathicsubtle, bilateral (subtle cavus, no weakness)

Traumatictalus fracture malunion · compartment syndrome · crush injury

Conditions with cavovarusCMT · cerebral palsy · Friedreich ataxia · spinal cord lesions · polio · amniotic band syndrome

Pathomechanics (PL vs TA, PB vs PTT) & Charcot-Marie-Tooth

Pair Strong (spared) Weak Result
PL vs TA Peroneus longus (hypertrophic) Tibialis anterior Plantarflexed 1st ray (cavus) — primary deformity
PTT vs PB Tibialis posterior Peroneus brevis Hindfoot varus + forefoot pronation
Extrinsics vs intrinsics Long flexors + extensors Lumbricals, interossei (first affected) Claw toes (intrinsic minus)
EHL recruited for weak TA EHL TA 1st MTP hyperextension, windlass drives 1st MT down

Sequence (forefoot-driven)plantarflexed 1st MT + pronated forefoot → medial forefoot strikes first → subtalar joint supinates for tripod contact → compensatory hindfoot varus → flexible at first, rigid with time

Forefoot positionpronation
✗ Wrong options: supination (the EXCEPT answer)

CMT geneticsHMSN · PMP22 duplication, chromosome 17 · weak TA + PB, normal PL + PT

Overactive muscle with cavusposterior tibialis
✗ Wrong options: TA (causes DF + inversion) · toe flexors/extensors

Gait effecttransverse tarsal joint locks in stance → lateral column overload

3Presentation

Historyrecurrent ankle sprains, lateral ankle pain (peroneal pathology) · lateral foot pain (5th MT stress fracture) · calluses under 1st + 5th MT heads · plantar fasciitis

Exampeek-a-boo heel (varus heel seen from front) · prominent 1st MT fat pad · Silfverskiöld (gastrocnemius tightness common) · unstable gait, ↑ double-limb stance

Neuro clues1st dorsal interosseous wasting of hand → CMT · scoliosis → CMT · spinal dysraphism · high-steppage gait

Coleman block test – hindfoot flexibility & forefoot-driven deformity

Used forcavovarus foot (TO)
✗ Wrong options: CVT · planovalgus · metatarsus adductus

Testshindfoot flexibility
✗ Wrong options: forefoot flexibility · ankle instability · Achilles tightness (that's Silfverskiöld)

Technique1–1.5 inch block under lateral foot + heel → 1st ray drops off medially → removes forefoot contribution

Flexibleheel corrects to neutral or valgus → forefoot-driven → forefoot procedures only

Rigidheel stays in varus → lateralising calcaneal osteotomy + forefoot procedures

Other signs (distractors)"too many toes" = forefoot abduction in flatfoot · inability to single-heel-rise = PTT insufficiency

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Viewsstanding AP + lateral ankle · standing AP, lateral, oblique foot

View Measurement Cavovarus value
AP foot Talocalcaneal (Kite) angle <20° (nl 20–45°) → hindfoot varus
AP foot Talonavicular coverage >7° overcoverage → forefoot adduction
AP foot Metatarsal overlap Forefoot pronation
Lateral foot Meary's (talo–1st MT) angle >4° apex dorsal (1st MT line passes dorsal to talus)
Lateral foot Calcaneal pitch >30°
Lateral foot Sinus tarsi see-through, double talar dome Hindfoot ER relative to cassette
Lateral foot Bell-shaped cuboid · ↑ 5th MT base–medial cuneiform distance —
Oblique MT stress fractures, CN coalition —

Work-up – electrodiagnostic studies

CMT diagnostic algorithmneurologic exam → EMG/NCS → genetic testing (genetic first if family member has known CMT)

Bilateral cavovarus, lateral pain, hand intrinsic wasting, family history → electrodiagnostic studies next
✗ Wrong options: muscle biopsy (dystrophies) · nerve biopsy (only if inconclusive) · CK/aldolase · echo

5Management

Cavovarus foot
  • Mild, flexible→orthotic (lateral posting + recessed 1st ray)
  • Failed nonop, flexible hindfoot (Coleman corrects) → plantar release + 1st MT DF osteotomy ± PL→PB transfer
  • Rigid hindfoot (Coleman stays varus)→add lateralising calcaneal osteotomy
    • Painful rigid arthritic→triple arthrodesis (rarely; poor long-term)

Orthoses – lateral hindfoot posting & recessed first ray

Supple adult cavovarusfull-length semi-rigid orthotic with 1st-ray recess + lateral hindfoot posting/wedge · not indicated in children (Orthobullets)
✗ Wrong options: medial posting (flatfoot) · walker boot · accommodative · lace-up

Other orthotic matcheshallux rigidus → Morton's extension · midfoot arthritis → rocker-bottom shoe · flexible planovalgus → medial posting · rigid cavovarus → orthoses don't work

More severeSMO · AFO if dynamic equinus (equinocavovarus) · lace-up brace / high-top if rigid bracing not tolerated · accommodative shoes rarely enough

Surgery – first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy, plantar release, calcaneal osteotomy, EHL transfer

Problem Procedure
Cavus Plantar fascia release · Steindler stripping (short flexors off calcaneus)
Plantarflexed 1st ray PL → PB transfer (↓ 1st-ray PF without losing eversion) · 1st MT dorsiflexion osteotomy
Flexible hindfoot varus (Coleman corrects) 1st MT DF osteotomy ± plantar release — calcaneus spared
Rigid hindfoot varus (Coleman fails) Lateralising (lateral slide / Dwyer closing-wedge) calcaneal osteotomy + 1st MT DF osteotomy
PTT overpull / TA weakness PTT transfer to dorsum
Equinus Gastrocnemius recession (less weakness, with plantar release) · TAL staged weeks after plantar release
Chronic lateral ankle instability Broström (fails unless deformity corrected)
Clawed hallux Modified Jones: EHL → 1st MT neck + IP fusion
Lesser toe clawing Extensors → 2nd–5th MT necks
Painful rigid arthritic hindfoot Triple arthrodesis — almost never (poor long-term)

Clawed hallux distractors✗ Wrong options: EHL to proximal phalanx / FHB tenotomy (worsen MTP hyperextension) · original Jones (EHL to neck only — inadequate) · FHL tenotomy alone · MTP + IP fusion (stiff ray) · Keller · metatarsal head resection

Flatfoot procedures (distractors)✗ Wrong options: medial calcaneal slide · lateral column lengthening · FDL transfer · 1st TMT fusion in plantarflexion

Equinus – gastrocnemius recession (Silfverskiöld)

SilfverskiöldDF ↑ with knee flexion → isolated gastrocnemius tightness → gastrocnemius recession · tight in both positions → Achilles/soleus → TAL

Diabetic equinus after castingtoe-drag in swing + DF improves with knee flexion → gastrocnemius recession
✗ Wrong options: Thompson positive · too-many-toes · fixed dorsiflexion

6Complications

Ankle instabilitylateral ligament reconstruction fails if cavovarus not corrected · → varus ankle arthritis

Stress fractures5th MT base (Jones) · 4th MT · navicular · medial malleolus (↑ medial compression; ↑ nonunion → cast NWB)

Othershallux sesamoiditis (plantarflexed 1st MT) · peroneal tendon pathology (PB most common) · plantar fasciitis · metatarsalgia, calluses

NOT caused by cavovarushallux valgus (→ planovalgus)

X vs Y

Flexible hindfoot Rigid hindfoot
Coleman block Heel → neutral / valgus Heel stays varus
Driver Forefoot (plantarflexed 1st ray) Fixed hindfoot
Orthotic Lateral posting + recessed 1st ray Not effective
Surgery 1st MT DF osteotomy + plantar release ± PL→PB + lateralising calcaneal osteotomy

"PL→PB, Broström, lateralising calcaneal osteotomy — supporting exam?"↑ inversion vs other side + no change on Coleman

"Equinus — when is gastrocnemius recession right?"DF improves with knee flexion

Cerebral Palsy - Foot Conditions

Pediatrics · 14 / 112

1Basics

Foot deformitymost common deformity in CP · forms: equinus, hallux valgus, equinoplanovalgus, equinocavovarus

Deformity Typical CP type Muscle imbalance
Equinus All; isolated in hemiplegia Spastic/contracted gastrocsoleus vs dorsiflexors
Equinoplanovalgus Spastic diplegia + quadriplegia, bilateral Spastic peroneals + heel cord, weak PTT, lax ligaments
Equinocavovarus Spastic hemiplegia Invertors (PTT ± TA) overpower peroneals
Hallux valgus Diplegics with equinus + planovalgus Adductor hallucis overactivity + external forces

Lever-arm dysfunctionplanovalgus and cavovarus both disrupt push-off / second rocker

3Presentation

Equinus

Symptomsshoe wear, tripping (poor clearance), instability

Examforefoot calluses · toe walking, no heel strike · compensatory knee hyperextension · late equinoplanovalgus

True equinus gaittoe walking with lack of heel strike at initial contact · plantarflexion moment in stance
✗ Wrong options: ↑ DF in stance/swing · DF moment

SilfverskiöldDF ↑ with knee flexed → gastrocnemius tight · equal → Achilles tight · DF is worse with knee extended when gastroc spastic (crosses knee)

Planovalgus trapuncontrolled subtalar joint overestimates ankle DF → correct heel valgus first before testing for Achilles contracture

Equinoplanovalgus

Findingsbilateral · valgus heel · talar head callus in arch · midfoot break · hallux valgus develops over time

Equinocavovarus

Findingslateral-border / 5th MT calluses (ulcers) · in-toeing · foot drop if TA weak · supination on TA firing = TA is main source

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Deformity Views Findings
Equinus Not required unless hindfoot malalignment —
Equinoplanovalgus WB AP ankle (rule out ankle valgus) + foot ↓ calcaneal pitch · negative talo–1st MT angle · talar head uncovering
Equinocavovarus WB foot + ankle Metatarsal overlap · ↑ calcaneal pitch
Hallux valgus WB series ↑ HVA, IMA, DMAA, HVI

5Management

Equinus – botulinum toxin, serial casting & gastrocnemius recession

Treatment Indication
Serial casting Mild, dynamic, young · unbraceable foot (can't reach neutral) after botox → cast, then brace
Botulinum toxin A (gastrocnemius) Mild spasticity, delays surgery · prevents presynaptic release of acetylcholine (ACh) · not more often than every 3 months
Hinged / articulated AFO Mild, passively correctable, no myostatic contracture · not if excessive midstance DF
Solid AFO Mild–moderate, partly correctable, mild contracture · not if heavy, ≥12 yr, rigid malalignment
Gastrocnemius recession Silfverskiöld positive (isolated gastroc) · less immobilisation, higher recurrence
TAL Gastrocsoleus (Achilles) tight · rarely isolated except in hemiplegia · walking cast 4–6 wk

Botox mechanism distractors✗ Wrong options: binds nicotinic receptor (curare, succinylcholine) · destroys receptor (myasthenia) · sarcolemma instability (dystrophy)

Surgery timingdelay equinus surgery until ≥4 yr (OB) · ≥6 yr to prevent recurrence (OB) — read the options

Hemiplegic 3-year-old, toe-walking, DF short of neutral after botox → serial casting of affected side
✗ Wrong options: bilateral AFOs (unaffected side toe-walks in compensation) · heel-cord lengthening · repeat botox at 1 month · baclofen pump (diplegia)

Gastrocnemius recession techniqueposterior/posteromedial incision · protect sural nerve · incise aponeurosis transversely or U-shape · cast in neutral

Equinovarus – split tibialis posterior transfer

Flexible equinocavovarus (hemiplegia)
  • PTT EMG continuous→SPOTT (split PTT to peroneus brevis), age 4–7
  • PTT EMG out-of-phase→whole PTT transfer to dorsum (lateral cuneiform)
  • Spastic TA (supination on TA firing)→SPLATT ± TAL + PTT lengthening
  • Fixed deformity→add calcaneal osteotomy / arthrodesis

SPOTTpassively correctable · age 4–7 · spastic hemiplegia · continuous PTT EMG · posterior half rerouted behind tibia (anterior to NV bundle) → woven into PB · more consistent than whole transfer
✗ Wrong options: athetosis (unpredictable) · rigid deformity · quadriplegic/diplegic valgus

SPLATTpassively correctable + spastic TA · lateral half → cuboid tunnel · not for weak TA / foot drop

Bonylateral slide or lateral closing-wedge calcaneal osteotomy (fixed varus) · triple arthrodesis (severe fixed; recurs if soft tissues not balanced)

Bracingsupple only · rarely successful, worsens calluses

Equinoplanovalgus

Flexible → bracing

Pain / pressure sores despite bracing → soft tissue + bone

Soft tissue Bone
TAL · peroneus brevis lengthening · PTT advancement Medial slide calcaneal osteotomy · lateral column lengthening (Evans) (trapezoidal graft anterior to middle facet) · Grice (extra-articular subtalar, does not affect tarsal growth) · subtalar arthroereisis (plug; breakdown)

Hallux valgus – first MTP arthrodesis

Painless, shoes OK → observe

Painful (failed accommodative shoes) → 1st MTP arthrodesis — highest success in ambulatory + nonambulatory CP
✗ Wrong options: double/crescentic MT osteotomy · modified McBride · night orthotics (recurrence unacceptably high)

Valgus interphalangeus → Akin proximal phalanx osteotomy

6Complications

Planovalgus surgeryovercorrection into varus (most common) · sural nerve injury · overlengthened lateral column → lateral forefoot overload · CC joint destabilisation

Cavovarusrecurrence if all components not addressed

X vs Y

Equinoplanovalgus Equinocavovarus
CP type Diplegia / quadriplegia Hemiplegia
Imbalance Spastic peroneals, weak PTT PTT ± TA > peroneals
Callus Talar head Lateral border / 5th MT
Calcaneal pitch ↓ ↑
Surgery LCL, medial slide, Grice, arthroereisis SPOTT / SPLATT, lateral calcaneal osteotomy

How it's asked

"5-year-old hemiplegic, flexible equinocavovarus, lateral ulcers, continuous PTT EMG?"split posterior tibial tendon transfer
✗ Wrong options: PTT to lateral cuneiform (out-of-phase) · triple · calcaneal slide (fixed)

"Best candidate for SPOTT?"6-year-old spastic hemiplegic, flexible equinovarus
✗ Wrong options: athetosis · rigid

"Spastic diplegic with true equinus gait — expected?"toe walking, no heel strike

"Botulinum toxin mechanism?"prevents presynaptic ACh release

"3-year-old hemiplegic, DF −5° after botox 1 month ago?"serial casting of affected side

"Isolated gastrocnemius recession best when?"DF 15° knee flexed vs neutral knee extended
✗ Wrong options: too-many-toes · Thompson · equal DF · no single heel rise

"15-year-old CP community ambulator, painful hallux valgus?"1st MTP arthrodesis

Cerebral Palsy - Gait Disorders

Pediatrics · 15 / 112

1Basics

Gait disorderprimary reason for orthopaedic consultation in CP

Ambulatory prognosis & milestones

Independent walkingexpected 12–18 months
✗ Wrong options: towers of 4 blocks = 2–3 yr · transfers toys = 6–9 mo · jumping = 2–3 yr · overhand throw = 18–24 mo

Good prognostic sign for walkingpositive parachute reaction (reaches toward floor when lowered prone)

Poor signsMoro beyond 6 months · asymmetric tonic neck reflex, extensor thrust, absent foot placement (abnormal at any age)

Pathophysiology – deviations

Level Definition Examples
Primary Direct CNS insult Spasticity, weakness, ↓ proprioception
Secondary Growth-related from abnormal loading Myostatic contractures, femoral anteversion, hip subluxation, equinoplanovalgus
Tertiary Compensations for secondary deviations —

Modern approachdefine deviation, plane (sagittal, coronal, transverse) and level (hip, knee, ankle)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Gait patterns – crouch, jump & stiff-knee (rectus femoris)

Pattern Hip Knee Ankle Note
True equinus Normal Normal / hyperextended Equinus (foot < plantigrade) Isolated, hemiplegics · GRF anterior to knee
Jump gait Flexed Flexed Equinus + anterior pelvic tilt · diplegia
Apparent equinus Flexed Flexed Plantigrade-capable but toe-walks Proximal deviation (knee flexion)
Crouch gait Flexed Flexed Excess dorsiflexion (calcaneus) GRF posterior to knee · diplegia, quadriplegia at puberty
Stiff-knee gait — ↓ swing flexion — Rectus femoris out of phase
Asymmetric Each limb in a different group —

Crouch causesiatrogenic isolated TAL in jump gait · pubertal growth spurt → ↓ strength-to-weight · breaks plantarflexion–knee-extension couple → very inefficient, tiring

Stiff-knee gaitrectus femoris overactive in pre-swing + early swing · EMG: quadriceps active from terminal stance through swing · compensation from hip deviation → surgery won't help
✗ Wrong options: adductor magnus · gluteus medius · sartorius · TFL

Descriptive classificationsfail to classify up to 40% of patterns

Key radiology findings & gait analysis

Quantitative gait analysismore accurate than observation · physical exam (spasticity, contractures, torsion) · kinetics (forces, moments) · kinematics (3-plane motion) · pedobarography · dynamic EMG · video

Planessagittal: pelvic tilt, hip/knee/ankle flexion · coronal: pelvic obliquity, hip ab/adduction · transverse = least reliable (rotation, foot progression)

5Management

Equinus management – AFO, serial casting & gastrocnemius recession

Orthosis Indication
Solid AFO Flexible equinus — ankle passively correctable to neutral (subtalar neutral) · stance + swing control · excessive midstance DF
Posterior leaf-spring (PLSO) / hinged Absent heel strike + excessive swing plantarflexion + some passive DF (~5°)
Floor-reaction AFO Crouch gait
KAFO Knee instability in minimally ambulatory/standers
SMO Flexible coronal hindfoot supination/pronation

3-year-old diplegic (PVL, walked at 2), mild contractures, gastroc tightness → ankle bracing + therapy
✗ Wrong options: percutaneous/open TAL (surgery not indicated at this age) · steroids (dystrophy)

Botulinum toxin Atemporise / primary · hamstring spasticity without fixed deformity in ambulators

Silfverskiöld + popliteal angle — choosing surgery

DF knee extended DF knee flexed Popliteal angle Procedure
−5° +20° 25° (normal) Gastrocnemius recession only ✓
−5° +20° 55° Gastroc recession + hamstring lengthening
−10° −10° 25° TAL (Achilles)
−20° −20° 55° TAL + hamstring lengthening
+20° +20° 55° Hamstring lengthening only

Normal popliteal angle ~25° · >50° = significant hamstring tightness

Gastrocnemius recessionSilfverskiöld positive · protect sural nerve (superficial to fascia) · divide tendon only · goal 10° DF

TALrigid (not correctable to neutral), true equinus, Silfverskiöld negative · contraindicated in spastic diplegia → weakness, calcaneus/crouch

Operative criteria — SEMLS

SEMLSgold standard · correct all primary + secondary deviations at multiple levels in one operation (avoids iatrogenic worsening) · AFOs + aggressive PT · ~1 year recovery

Deviation SEMLS procedure / criterion
↑ Femoral anteversion (lever-arm) External rotation proximal femoral osteotomy
Hip flexion contracture Intramuscular psoas lengthening
Mild knee flexion (<5° fixed), young Medial hamstring fractional lengthening (✗ Wrong options: lateral (excess weakness))
Knee flexion 10–25°, ≥2 yr growth Guided growth (anterior distal femur)
Knee flexion 10–30° + quad lag, at/near maturity Distal femoral extension osteotomy ± patellar tendon advancement
Stiff-knee gait Distal rectus femoris transfer posterior to knee axis (better than release)
Equinus TAL or gastrocnemius recession
Flatfoot Reconstruction

Selective dorsal rhizotomy

Permanent tone reductionselective posterior (dorsal) rhizotomy
✗ Wrong options: tone-reducing AFOs · botox (wears off 3–6 mo via axonal sprouting) · single intrathecal baclofen injection (pump gives prolonged reduction) · fractional lengthening

Rhizotomy drawbacksexcess weakness · hip dislocation · spinal deformity

Recurrent hamstring contractureesp. jump gait

Patella altamultiple releases without gait analysis · hard to treat

Knee painTAL without gait analysis

Jump gait Crouch gait
Ankle Equinus Excess dorsiflexion / calcaneus
Hip + knee Flexed Flexed
GRF at knee Anterior (early) Posterior
Cause Spastic gastroc + hamstrings + psoas Isolated TAL, growth spurt weakness
Orthosis — Floor-reaction AFO
