Cerebral Palsy - General

Pediatrics · 16 / 112

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Definitionnon-progressive UMN disease (static encephalopathy) from injury to immature brain · onset before age 2 · musculoskeletal picture worsens with growth (bone grows faster than spastic muscle)

Incidence2–3 per 1000 · most common cause of chronic childhood disability

Risk factorsprematurity (most common) (Orthobullets) · prenatal causes most common (70%) (TO) — TORCH, toxins, Rh (kernicterus), malformations · perinatal: anoxia, traumatic delivery, chorioamnionitis · postnatal: meningitis, encephalitis, HIE, NAT

Brain MRIperiventricular leukomalacia (PVL) most frequent (56%) (preterm, spastic diplegia) · grey matter 18% · malformations 9%

Manifestationsprimary: abnormal tone, spasticity, loss of motor control, impaired balance · secondary: contractures (dynamic → static), hip subluxation, spine deformity, foot deformity, gait disorders, fractures

Classification & ambulation prognosis

Physiologic Feature
Spastic Most common (80%) · velocity-dependent ↑ tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski · agonist-antagonist co-contraction · most amenable to surgery
Athetoid (dyskinetic) Slow writhing involuntary movements · normal reflexes · contractures uncommon
Choreiform Continuous purposeless distal movements
Rigid Lead-pipe/cogwheel, no hyperreflexia · most hypertonic
Ataxic Cerebellar · wide-based, drunken gait, tremor
Hypotonic Precedes spastic/ataxic for 2–3 yr
Mixed Spastic + athetoid, total body
Anatomic (geographic) Feature
Diplegia Legs > arms · usually ambulatory · near-normal IQ · most common (TO)
Hemiplegia One side, arm > leg · ~50% mentally retarded (TO)
Quadriplegia All four, nonambulatory, low IQ, ↑ mortality
Paraplegia Legs only, arms spared
Double hemiplegia All four, arms > legs
Monoplegia One limb (rare)
Total body + absent head control, drooling, dysphagia

Lower > upper limb → diplegia
✗ Wrong options: paraplegia (arms spared) · double hemiplegia (arms > legs)

GMFCS (best motor-function score)

Level Ability (age 6–12)
I Walks without limits · runs, jumps · stairs without rail
II Walks with limits — difficulty uneven ground, inclines, long distances · stairs with rail · minimal run/jump
III Walks with handheld mobility device (walker, crutches) · wheeled mobility for community/long distance
IV Self-mobility limited · powered mobility / pushed wheelchair
V Transported in manual wheelchair · dependent in all care

Best score for motor functionGMFCS · EDACS = eating/drinking
✗ Wrong options: MACS (upper limb/hands) · CFCS (communication) · PEDI

Motor plateaulevels I–II by ~5 yr · III by ~8 · IV–V by ~7, may decline in adolescence

Ambulation prognosis

Most reliable predictorindependent sitting by age 2 (OR 26:1)
✗ Wrong options: creeping · rolling · CP pattern · motor type

Poor prognosisno sitting by 4 yr · not walking by 8 yr (without severe contracture) → unlikely ever

Bleck poor signsasymmetric tonic neck reflex · persistent Moro · strong extensor thrust on vertical suspension · persistent neck-righting reflex · absent parachute reaction after 11 months → "all EXCEPT" = presence of parachute reaction (TO)

3Presentation

Historyperinatal, development, function (sitting, standing, hands, communication, hearing, vision)

Spinescoliosis flexibility, pelvic obliquity · hamstring contracture → ↓ lordosis · hip flexion contracture → ↑ lordosis

Hipflexion + adduction contractures · dislocation may be missed as "contracture" → thigh length sitting, Galeazzi

Footequinovarus, planovalgus · toe walking, knee hyperextension for heel contact · Silfverskiöld

Foot & knee deformity patterns (recurvatum, foot deformities)

Common CP footequinocavovarus (hemiplegia) · equinoplanovalgus (diplegia in crouch) · hallux valgus · isolated cavus is NOT typical → think spinal dysraphism / CMT (TO)

Knee recurvatum causes (TO)quad–hamstring co-spasticity (quads stronger) · weakened hamstrings (over-lengthening/transfer) · gastrocsoleus weakness · ankle equinus · quadriceps weakness is NOT a cause

Recurvatum work-upprone rectus test (quad spasticity) · SLC/AFO at neutral: still recurvatum → not from equinus · treat with long-leg braces locked in 20° flexion

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

BaselineAP + lateral hips · standing spine films

Hip surveillance (TO)

Reimers migration percentage (MP)% of femoral head lateral to Perkin line (Hilgenreiner line through triradiates) · supine, hips together, patellae forward

MP Meaning
<30% Stable — monitor
>30% (surveillance) / >33% (Reimers) Displacement / subluxation
>60% High risk of dislocation · soft tissue alone fails
>100% Dislocation
Rise >10%/yr Red flag — rapid progression
GMFCS Hip displacement risk X-ray frequency
I ~0–5% (≈1%) Age 2, then if gait changes
II ~15% Age 2, then 2-yearly to 10
III ~35% Age 2, then yearly to 10
IV ~70% Age 2, then 6–12-monthly
V ~90% Age 2, then 6-monthly

Clinical red flagspassive abduction <30° (knee extended) · new pain with dressing/hygiene/sitting · new LLD

Hip at riskflexion contracture >20° + abduction <30° · ↑ neck-shaft angle (coxa valga) · ↑ femoral anteversion · acetabular dysplasia (posterosuperior in CP vs anterolateral in DDH)

Dislocation by type70–90% occur in quadriplegia

5Management

Spasticity management – botulinum toxin, baclofen (withdrawal) & SDR contraindications

Agent Mechanism Use / note
Botulinum toxin A Binds motor nerve terminal → enters → cleaves SNARE → blocks presynaptic ACh release (flaccid chemical denervation) Dynamic contracture, too young for surgery · little benefit in static contracture · lasts 2–3 mo (Orthobullets) / 3–4 mo (OB) / 3–6 mo (OB) → reverses by axonal sprouting · inject belly near nerve entry
Baclofen GABA-B agonist (spinal cord, central) Intrathecal preferred (oral → sedation, poor bioavailability) · nonambulatory GMFCS IV–V
Lidocaine Na⁺ channel block —
Acetylcholinesterase Degrades ACh —
Pyridostigmine / neostigmine AChE inhibitors → ↑ ACh —
Trihexyphenidyl Muscarinic antagonist —
Gabapentin Ca²⁺ channel —
Methacholine Direct cholinergic agonist —

Botox distractors✗ Wrong options: destroys ACh receptor (myasthenia gravis) · binds muscle receptor (curare, succinylcholine)

Baclofen withdrawal (pump failure)rebound rigidity, myoclonus, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis → ↑ creatinine, ↑ K⁺, ↑ CPK, multi-organ failure
✗ Wrong options: ↓ K⁺ · ↓ CPK · hypothermia · atony

Spasticity grading (TO)R1 = angle of muscle catch · R2 = passive ROM · R2 − R1 >20° = significant dynamic component → botox

Phelps testhip abduction ↓ only with knee extended → gracilis spasticity

5-yr GMFCS III diplegic, jump gait, DF R1 −10/R2 +20, popliteal R1 80/R2 40, abduction 45° flexed / 20° extended → botox to gastrocnemius + gracilis + semitendinosus + semimembranosus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: surgery · adductor release (abduction already 45°)

Selective dorsal rhizotomy

Proceduresection L2–S1 dorsal rootlets with abnormal response to stimulation

Ideal candidatespastic diplegia, ambulatory, age 4–8 (Orthobullets, OB) / 3–8 (TO), GMFCS II–III, voluntary + trunk control, pure spasticity, no fixed contractures, preterm, motivated family · improves one GMFCS level (TO)

Contraindicationsathetosis (unpredictable) · nonambulatory spastic quadriplegia (spinal deformity) · hemiplegia not recommended (TO)
✗ Wrong options: "hemiplegics benefit most before 5"

Complicationship subluxation/dislocation · lumbar hyperlordosis (esp. >60° preop) · scoliosis · spondylolysis/listhesis · weakness

Athetoid 5-year-old — contraindicated? → SDR
✗ Wrong options: botox · UE tendon transfer · SEMLS · intrathecal baclofen

Operative principles

Muscle behaviour Procedure
Continuously active Tenotomy (hip adductor) or lengthening (Achilles, hamstring)
Out of phase Tendon transfer (rectus femoris, tibialis posterior)

Soft-tissue surgeryage 3–5 with spasticity + voluntary control

Bony surgerylater childhood/adolescence

SEMLSone event, gait-lab guided · simple lengthenings "uncover" other contractures and worsen gait

Upper extremity surgery – voluntary control predicts outcome

Voluntary motor controlbest predicts improvement after wrist/hand tendon transfers
✗ Wrong options: botox · SDR · femoral/tibial derotation osteotomy

Hip subluxation in GMFCS V – adductor release

CP hip by migration percentage
  • MP 30–40%, dynamic, abduction <30°→adductor ± psoas release (preventive)
  • MP >40–60%, coxa valga, anteversion→VDRO (bilateral) ± femoral shortening
    • Acetabular index >25–30°→add Dega acetabuloplasty (posterosuperior)
  • Painful, deformed head, GMFCS IV–V→salvage: McHale / proximal femoral resection

Adductor releasegoal >60° abduction hips flexed, 45° extended · bilateral (avoid windswept pelvis) · then abduction splinting 6 mo · avoid excessive release in IV/V → abduction contracture

Psoasflexion contracture 15–30° → intramuscular recession over pelvic brim · >30° → add rectus, sartorius, TFL, anterior glutei release · ambulators: fractional at brim (complete lesser-trochanter release → flexor void, crouch)

VDROneck-shaft angle 110–115° · correct anteversion · shorten 1–3 cm if tight (↓ AVN, sciatic tension)
✗ Wrong options: 105° → abductor weakness, Trendelenburg

AcetabuloplastyDega / San Diego (incomplete trans-iliac, hinge on triradiate) → deeper posterior graft for posterosuperior coverage · Pemberton = volume-reducing, open triradiate
✗ Wrong options: Salter (anterolateral redirection, leaves posterior uncovered) · extra varus · isolated psoas tenotomy

GMFCS V, painful sitting, hygiene problems, coxa valga + unilateral dislocation, failed therapy → bilateral adductor release + bilateral VDRO ± pelvic osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: observe · soft tissue alone (MP >60% fails) · shortening alone · unilateral VDRO (asymmetry)

5-yr GMFCS IV, MP 18% → 31% in 1 yr, abduction 25° → 6-monthly X-rays + refer for preventive soft-tissue surgery (TO)
✗ Wrong options: annual surveillance · VDRO now · discharge at 5

Operative criteria

Situation Choice
Open reduction of dislocated hip — all 4 Moderately mature intellect · at least sitting potential · minimal/corrected pelvic obliquity · ideally unilateral
GMFCS IV, MP 100%, deformed head Femoral head resection (McHale: resection + subtrochanteric valgus osteotomy + interposition) over reconstruction (TO)
Schanz osteotomy Pelvic-support for sitting platform
THA Selected higher-function painful arthritic hips
Hamstring lengthening Popliteal angle >45–50° · medial preferred (lateral → ↑ ext. tibial torsion, lordosis)
DFEO — "rule of 15" Fixed knee flexion >15° (TO) · guided growth/soft tissue below
Guided growth (anterior 8-plate) FKFD with growth left (<11–12 yr)

Crouch gait & knee surgery (DFEO, patellar advancement)

PFKE coupleplantarflexion–knee extension couple: competent gastrocsoleus stops tibia falling forward · failure = iatrogenic over-lengthened Achilles / triceps surae weakness → crouch (TO)
✗ Wrong options: rectus spasticity · psoas contracture · hamstring shortening

Apparent equinus (toe-walking, ankle neutral, knee 35° + hip 20° flexion, patella alta Insall-Salvati 1.4) → DFEO + patellar tendon advancement (TO)
✗ Wrong options: TAL (causes severe crouch) · isolated hamstring lengthening · gastroc recession + AFO

Patellar tendon advancement/plicationmandatory with DFEO in chronic crouch to restore quad lever arm (TO)

Post-DFEO anterior knee pain / extensor shiftunaddressed patella alta with shortened femur (TO)

GRAFO (floor-reaction AFO)shifts GRF anterior to knee → knee extension moment (TO)

Hamstring activity throughout stance on EMG → hamstring lengthening likely to fail (TO)

Post-opearly weight bearing · night knee immobilisers for years

Stiff-knee gait – rectus femoris transfer

Rectus femoris transferdistal rectus → gracilis/semitendinosus · removes swing-phase restraint → ↑ peak knee flexion (TO)
✗ Wrong options: ↑ extension moment · pure hip extensor

Stiff knee + internal rotation in swing + anteversion (hemiplegia Winters IV, double-bump rectus EMG) → femoral derotation osteotomy + rectus femoris transfer (TO)

Equinus – gastrocnemius recession & lengthening zones

Zone Procedure Structures
Zone 1 Strayer (transverse, above junction) Isolated gastrocnemius — safest vs crouch
Zone 1 Baker (tongue-in-groove) Gastroc + partial soleus
Zone 2 Vulpius (inverted V at MTJ) Gastroc + often soleus fascia
Zone 3 Hoke triple hemisection / TAL Tendo-Achilles (TO)
Intramuscular Baumann Multiple deep gastroc recessions

Diplegia → usually isolated gastroc contracture · hemiplegia → gastrosoleus tight (TO)

8-yr diplegic, −10° knee extended, +15° knee flexed → Strayer (TO)
✗ Wrong options: percutaneous TAL (crouch) · Vulpius (weakens soleus) · SPLATT (varus)

Neuromuscular scoliosis surgery – evaluation, outcomes & complications

Pre-op work-upnutrition (weight) · pulmonary (PFT/sleep study/clinical) · swallow + GERD (aspiration) · valproate may impair coagulation (↓ vWF) · MRI NOT routine (only if neuro change or rapid progression)

Most predictable outcome↑ caregiver satisfaction (perceived comfort)
✗ Wrong options: cognition · nutrition · pain · mobility

Respiratory complication risk factorgastrostomy tube · resp. complications 15–28% · NMS has highest complication rate (congenital 10.6%, idiopathic 6.3%)
✗ Wrong options: lymphocytes <1000 · albumin <3.5 · reactive airway · Hb <8

Wound drainage 3 weeks after T2–pelvis fusion → culture + I&D + IV antibiotics + retain instrumentation
✗ Wrong options: oral abx · aspiration · hardware removal → rapid progression

Bone health – bisphosphonates for fragility fractures

Fragility fracturesnon-ambulators, low BMD (immobility, nutrition, anticonvulsants, contractures) · prevalence 6–50% · annual 4% → 7% after a fracture

IV pamidronate>3 fractures + DEXA Z-score <−2 SD (Orthobullets) · prevents refracture
✗ Wrong options: LLD · nonunion · malunion · contracture

Mechanismnitrogen-containing (pamidronate, alendronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (mevalonate pathway) → osteoclast apoptosis · non-N (clodronate, etidronate) → toxic ATP analogues

CROW walkerCharcot foot (TO)
✗ Wrong options: CP equinus · polio · spina bifida

X vs Y

Botulinum toxin A Baclofen SDR
Site Peripheral NMJ, presynaptic Central spinal GABA-B Dorsal rootlets L2–S1
Duration Temporary (months) Continuous via pump Permanent
Best for Dynamic, focal, young Nonambulatory GMFCS IV–V Ambulatory spastic diplegia 4–8
Avoid Static contracture Abrupt withdrawal Athetosis, quadriplegia
CP hip DDH
Deficiency Posterosuperior Anterolateral
Pelvic osteotomy Dega / San Diego Salter, Pemberton

Cerebral Palsy - Hip Conditions

Pediatrics · 17 / 112

1Basics

Hip surveillance – risk by GMFCS level & pathogenesis

Incidenceprogressive subluxation in up to 50% of spastic quadriparesis · rare in ambulators

GMFCS Risk of subluxation by age 7 (Orthobullets, OB) Hip displacement risk (TO surveillance table)
I <10% ~0–5%
II 10–15% ~15%
III (walks with assistive devices) 30–40% ~35%
IV 50–60% ~70%
V 70–80% ~90%

Pathogenesiships normal at birth · spastic adductors (longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis) + iliopsoas (psoas major, iliacus) → scissoring → coxa valga, anteversion, acetabular dysplasia → subluxation → dislocation
✗ Wrong options: sartorius · gluteus minimus · obturator externus · piriformis · rectus femoris

Directiondislocation posterior + superior (>95%) · acetabular deficiency posterosuperior

Degenerationfemoral head cartilage erosion → pain · 50–75% of dislocated hips become painful (OB) · pain by 2nd–3rd decade

Windswept hipsone hip abducted, other adducted → pelvic obliquity · adducted hip on high side at risk of dislocation · infrapelvic obliquity → compensatory scoliosis

3Presentation

Symptomship/groin pain · difficulty sitting · perineal care / hygiene / diaper difficulty

Examunreliable alone · ↓ ROM, pain with motion · lever-arm gait dysfunction · thigh-length discrepancy ("pseudo-Galeazzi")

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP pelvis + frog lateral if possible

Reimers migration index% of femoral head uncovered lateral to Perkin line · most accurate method to identify and monitor stability · <33% at risk · >33% subluxated · >100% dislocated

Natural historyhips will dislocate untreated if MI >60–70%

Acetabular index>25° (OB) / >27° (OB) → acetabular dysplasia → add acetabuloplasty

CToperative planning (3D acetabular correction) · CT scanogram for femoral version before derotation

Stages of hip deformity

Stage Characteristics Treatment
Hip at risk Abduction <45° + partial uncovering · MI <33% Botox (<3 yr) to delay · adductor ± psoas release, hamstring lengthening (3–4 yr) · avoid obturator neurectomy
Subluxation MI >33% Adductor tenotomy if abduction restricted · persistent → VDRO (5–6 yr) · pelvic osteotomy if acetabular insufficiency
Spastic dislocation MI >100% Open reduction + VDRO + femoral shortening + pelvic osteotomy
Windswept One abducted, one adducted Brace adducted hip ± tenotomy · release abduction contracture of abducted hip

5Management

Nonopobservation (mild) · PT never shown to prevent subluxation · abduction bracing alone does not ↓ dislocation, may cause windswept deformity

CP hip
  • Young (<4–6 yr), MI 25/33–60%, limited abduction→adductor ± psoas release
  • >4 yr or MI >60% (or >40% failing soft tissue)→VDRO + soft-tissue release
    • Acetabular index >25°→+ pelvic (Dega / San Diego) osteotomy, single stage
  • Painful, chronically dislocated, deformed head (GMFCS V)→salvage
    • McHale valgus-support osteotomy · Castle resection-interposition

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Adductor + psoas release Age <6 with MI >25/33–60% + limited abduction (Orthobullets) · <4 with MI >40% (OB) · progressive subluxation <8 yr · adjunct to bony surgery
Psoas lengthening Only with hip flexion contracture (positive Thomas)
VDRO ± Dega + soft tissue Age >4 or MI >60% · treat all at single stage
Add acetabuloplasty Acetabular index >25° (✗ Wrong options: age <6 · GMFCS V · neck-shaft angle (VDRO fixes that) · prior botox)
Proximal femoral resection / McHale Painful, chronically dislocated, deformed head, nonambulatory (GMFCS V)
Castle Chronic dislocation, adults, can't stand to transfer (GMFCS V)
THA Ambulatory or can stand to transfer · 85% 10-yr survival
Hip arthrodesis Young patients
Girdlestone No longer done — uniformly painful (proximal migration, no interposition)

Soft-tissue releases – adductor tenotomy indications & failure risk, obturator neurectomy

3-yr diplegic, abduction 20°, MI 20%, Thomas negative → bilateral adductor releases only · one of few surgeries in CP <4 yr
✗ Wrong options: psoas (no flexion contracture) · VDRO · pelvic osteotomy

Techniqueadductor longus tenotomy → sequentially gracilis, adductor brevis · psoas at lesser trochanter (nonambulatory) or pelvic brim MTJ (ambulatory) · goal >45° abduction

Failure riskpreop MI >40% · acetabular index >27°
✗ Wrong options: lack of bracing · no neurectomy · age

Obturator nerveanterior branch lies on adductor brevis/magnus after longus release (Ludloff) · supplies adductor longus, brevis, gracilis · pinch neurectomy → weak hip adduction · neurectomy does not improve results and risks abduction contracture — avoid (Orthobullets, OB) · sometimes used in nonambulatory spastic adduction (OB)

6-yr nonambulatory quadriplegic, subluxation >50%, abduction 20° → open adductor tenotomy + iliopsoas release + bilateral VDRO (too old for soft tissue alone)
✗ Wrong options: percutaneous tenotomy · oral baclofen · phenol · neurectomy

Reconstruction – VDRO with pelvic (Dega) osteotomy

VDROshortening varus derotation → corrects coxa valga + anteversion

Degaacetabular reshaping, incomplete trans-iliac · improves posterior coverage (neuromuscular hip needs posterior) · hinges on triradiate → triradiate must be open · bone graft placed · no fixation needed · San Diego = alternative
✗ Wrong options: salvage (shelf/Chiari are salvage)

Bilateral MI 70%/60%, AI 30° → combined bilateral VDRO + pelvic osteotomies + soft-tissue releases — lowest resubluxation
✗ Wrong options: soft tissue alone · VDRO alone · pelvic alone · closed reduction

8-yr wheelchair-bound, hygiene problems, abduction 5°/15°, bilateral dislocation + dysplasia → bilateral adductor release + varus femoral osteotomies + acetabuloplasties
✗ Wrong options: botox + PT · Pavlik · abductor release + valgus osteotomy

Salvage – proximal femoral resection

GMFCS Vno antigravity head/trunk control, transported

15-yr GMFCS V, painful sitting, flattened head on CT → proximal femoral resection
✗ Wrong options: open reduction (degenerate head stays painful)

Resection over reconstruction → GMFCS V, MI 100% + head deformity
✗ Wrong options: GMFCS IV MI 50% (reconstruct) · MI 25% (analgesia) · MI 100% normal head (osteotomy)

McHale (valgus support)resect head/neck (ligamentum teres left, sutured to psoas/capsule) + subtrochanteric valgus closing-wedge osteotomy → lesser trochanter articulates with acetabulum · relieves pain, ↑ abduction

Castleresect at lesser trochanter level · vastus oversewn over femur, abductors/psoas/capsule over acetabulum → large soft-tissue interposition (differs from Girdlestone)

6Complications

Osteonecrosis1–11%

Heterotopic ossificationradiation on POD 2–3 better than NSAIDs

Insufficiency fractures4–29% · distal femur after spica

Abduction contractureanterior obturator neurectomy

1Basics

Whohemiplegia and quadriplegia

Typical postureshoulder IR · elbow flexion · forearm pronation · wrist flexion + ulnar deviation · thumb-in-palm · finger flexion

Hygienic vs functional procedures

Hygienic Functional
Patient ↓ mental + physical function Voluntary control, IQ ≥50–70, good sensibility (position sense without vision)
Examples Releases, wrist arthrodesis + PRC Tendon transfers (FCU → ECRB), PT rerouting

Voluntary controlbest predictor of improvement after hand/wrist tendon transfer

3Presentation

Volkmann angle

Techniquefingers extended, wrist from maximal flexion → extend wrist · angle short of full extension = Volkmann angle
✗ Wrong options: fingers flexed (must stretch extrinsic flexors)

Meaninghigh Volkmann angle → extrinsic finger flexor contracture → correcting wrist alone gives clenched fist unless finger flexors also lengthened

Volkmann angle Severity / treatment
~15° Mild → FCU or FCR lengthening
~25°, correctable wrist FCU + FDS/FDP tenotomy + ECU → ECRB transfer
Cannot reach within 45° of neutral Severe → wrist arthrodesis + PRC
90° + palmar wounds (fingers-in-palm) PRC + wrist fusion + FDS → FDP

Distractorslocked IR shoulder + extended elbow = arthrogryposis · unstable thumb CMC = Blauth IIIB hypoplasia (pollicise) · constricting bands = constriction band syndrome

House classification (thumb-in-palm)

Type Deformity Treatment
I 1st MC adduction contracture Adductor release ± 1st dorsal interosseous release · Z-plasty 1st web
II + MP flexion contracture Adductor release
III + unstable / hyperextensible MP Adductor release + MP fusion or capsulodesis
IV + MP + IP flexion contractures Adductor release + FPB + FPL release/lengthening

Operative criteria

Deformity Procedure Indication
Shoulder IR Derotational humeral osteotomy and/or subscapularis + pectoralis lengthening >30° contracture interfering with hand function
Elbow flexion Lacertus fibrosus release, biceps + brachialis lengthening, brachioradialis origin release Elbow flexion contracture

Wrist flexion, mild FCU or FCR lengthening Good finger extension, little wrist-flexor spasticity
Wrist flexion, functional FCU → ECRB (Green) · FCU → EDC Supple wrist, voluntary control, IQ ≥50–70, sensibility · better long-term than botox/therapy
Wrist flexion, spastic FCU ECU → ECRB Avoids hyperextension from transferring spastic FCU
Wrist flexor weakening Flexor-pronator slide (from medial epicondyle) Severe fixed wrist + finger flexion (also post-compartment syndrome)
Fixed, non-supple Wrist arthrodesis ± PRC No volitional control · hygiene + function
Swan neck Correct wrist flexion first Intrinsic tightness + extensor overpull
CP wrist flexion deformity
  • Supple, voluntary control, functioning FCU
    • Good grasp→FCU to EDC
    • Poor grasp / weak extensors→FCU to ECRB (Green)
  • Supple but finger-flexor tightness (Volkmann 25°)→FCU + FDS/FDP tenotomy + ECU to ECRB
  • Rigid, no volitional control, palmar wounds→PRC + wrist arthrodesis (dorsal plate)

✗ Wrong options: anconeus, brachialis, brachioradialis, supinator

Wrist Supple Rigid

Criterion
Multiple sites of apparent osteomyelitis
Pathology + cultures negative
No response to antibiotics

<12 yearssling / shoulder immobiliser / figure-of-eight (no difference sling vs figure-of-eight) · no reduction attempted · ROM at 2–4 wk, strengthening 6–10 wk · callus bump fades 6–12 mo

✗ Wrong options: malunion with shortening · nonunion

Symptomatic maluniononly 10–20%
✗ Wrong options: 50%

Absolute Controversial
Open fracture Shortening >2 cm — not an indication <12 yr; debated in adolescents
Skin at risk from tenting —
Subclavian artery/vein injury —
Pediatric clavicle shaft fracture
  • Newborn→observe, careful handling
  • <12 yr (even 100% displaced, shortened)→sling
  • Open / tenting / vascular injury→ORIF (precontoured plate)
    (adolescent >2 cm shortening — controversial)

ORIFprecontoured plate (± recon / locking / IM rod) · sling 7–10 d · strengthening ~6 wk · sport ~3 mo

Principleabduct the foot, rotating it laterally around a fixed talus · counterpressure on lateral talar head (fulcrum)
✗ Wrong options: push against calcaneocuboid joint (Kite → rocker bottom) · manipulate heel directly

OrderC → A → V → E

Step Manoeuvre
1 Cavus (first cast) Forefoot SUPINATION — elevate 1st MT, align forefoot with hindfoot (✗ Wrong options: pronation → ↑ cavus, midfoot break)
2 Adductus + varus (together) Abduct foot around talar head; supination gradually ↓ to neutral
3 Equinus (last) Only when heel neutral/valgus + foot ≥60° abducted → percutaneous Achilles tenotomy → cast 3 weeks in max DF (15°)

✗ Wrong options: 30° abduction (the false statement)

Manipulated insupination + abduction (TO)
✗ Wrong options: pronation · adduction · dorsiflexion first

  • FAO 23 h/day × 3 mo→nights/naps to age 3–4

4Diagnosis & Classification

Tarek classification

Grade Radiology Passive flexion Treatment
I Simple recurvatum >90° Manipulation + casting
II Subluxation / dislocation 30–90° Casting if <1 mo; PQR if seen later
III Dislocation <30° Surgery (open V-Y quadricepsplasty)

5Management

Congenital knee dislocation
  • Newborn (Tarek I, early II)→weekly long-leg manipulation + flexion casting
    (knee + hip dislocated → treat KNEE first, then Pavlik)
  • Failed to gain 30° flexion by 3 mo / grade III / recurrent→surgical release
    • Grade II (later)→percutaneous quadriceps recession
    • Older, failed casting, grade III→open V-Y quadricepsplasty / open reduction

Serial casting vs quadricepsplasty/open reduction

Knee + ipsilateral hip dislocated (2-day-old) → manipulate + cast knee first — can't fit Pavlik on a hyperextended knee
✗ Wrong options: Pavlik first · spica · delay · quad lengthening

Casting failure90° not attained in 4 weeks (OB) · 30° not gained after 3 months (Orthobullets) → surgery

6-month-old, failed 3 mo casting, flexion 15°, hyperextension 25° (recurrent grade III) → open V-Y quadricepsplasty + above-knee cast
✗ Wrong options: cast in extension · more flexion casts · ACL division alone · percutaneous recession (for grade II at presentation)

7-month-old, can't flex >30° after casting, hips normal → open reduction — ideally ~6 months, before age 1
✗ Wrong options: observe · more casting · closed reduction · wait for walking

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
<30° flexion after 3 months casting Soft-tissue release
Tarek II after 1 month, III, recurrent Release
Goal 90° flexion
Options Percutaneous quadriceps recession (PQR) · V-Y quadricepsplasty / Z-lengthening · anterior capsule release · posterior transposition of hamstrings · collateral mobilisation
Post-op Cast 45–60° flexion × 3–4 weeks

ACL division + quad releaseonly fair results

Mild, resistant Abductor hallucis release

1Basics

Epidemiologyrare · Finland (carrier 1 in 70 Finns)

SLC26A2 sulfate transporter & phenotype

Genes & lab markers

Inheritanceautosomal recessive (both parents carriers)

GeneDTDST = SLC26A2, chromosome 5q → defective sulfate transporter → undersulfation of cartilage proteoglycan → abnormal cartilage matrix (ear, trachea, ligaments)

Ossificationfailure of secondary ossification centres (OB)

No commercial testmany mutations → clinical + radiographic + family history · prenatal US possible

Gene (distractors) Disorder
SLC26A2 / DTDST Diastrophic dysplasia ✓
FGFR3 Achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia
FGFR2 Apert (craniosynostosis + complex syndactyly)
CBFA-1 / RUNX2 Cleidocranial dysplasia (osteocalcin)
Gs α (GNAS) Fibrous dysplasia
COL1A1/2 OI (blue sclera, bowing)
COL5A1/2 Ehlers-Danlos (classic)
Lysosomal storage Hunter, Hurler
Lipid storage Gaucher

3Presentation

"Twisted dwarf"short-limbed (rhizomelic) dwarfism, diagnosed at birth

Feature Note
Cauliflower ears 80% · cystic swelling of pinnae · responds to early compressive bandages
Hitchhiker thumb Short 1st MC + radial subluxation of MCP (abducted)
Cleft palate 60% (59%)
Cervical kyphosis Severe, early · often resolves spontaneously
Thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis Progressive
Feet Rigid clubfeet (equinocavovarus) · skewfoot (TMT adductus + hindfoot valgus) · tarsal valgus 43%, MT adductus 37%
Lower limb Genu valgum (± dislocated patellae) · hip + knee contractures · hip dislocation
Hand Symphalangism (stiff fingers)
Other Tracheomalacia (can be fatal) · atlantoaxial instability (rare)

ViewsAP + lateral cervical and thoracolumbar spine · standing 3-joint lower-limb films

5Management

Mostobservation + supportive

Problem Surgery
Atlantoaxial instability + neuro symptoms Occipitocervical fusion (quadriplegia risk)
Cervical kyphosis not resolving Posterior cervical fusion
Progressive TL kyphoscoliosis ASF / PSF
Foot deformity after casting · severe hip/knee contractures Soft-tissue release
Progressive valgus, resistant clubfeet, fixed knee flexion, early hip subluxation Osteotomies (distal femoral extension, valgus intertrochanteric ± acetabuloplasty)
End-stage hip OA THA

Distal Clavicle Physeal Fractures

Pediatrics · 34 / 112

1Basics

Incidencerare · 5–10% of pediatric clavicle fractures

Equivalentchildhood "pseudodislocation" = adult AC separation

Pathoanatomy – intact periosteal sleeve

Injuryclavicle (metaphysis) displaces superiorly out of its periosteal sleeve, through the physis · inferior periosteal sleeve + epiphysis stay attached to intact CC + AC ligaments · AC joint intact

Healingnew clavicle forms within the sleeve → "Y-shaped" clavicle; displaced fragment remodels/resorbs

Anatomy & ossification

Claviclefirst bone to ossify (5th week in utero, intramembranous) · physes last to close

Medial physis80% of growth · ossifies 18–20 yr · last physis to close (20–25 yr) → teenage "SC dislocations" are physeal fracture-dislocations

Lateral epiphysisossifies ~18 yr

CC ligamentsvertical stability · trapezoid 2 cm, conoid 4 cm from AC joint · AC ligaments — horizontal stability

2Mechanism

Fall on side of shoulder / outstretched arm · direct blow · rarely child abuse

3Presentation

Exampain, distal clavicle tenderness, deformity, ecchymosis · rarely tenting

Newbornpseudoparalysis with intact reflexes (vs brachial plexus palsy)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP ± Zanca (intra-articular extension) · axillary lateral (type IV posterior displacement)

Laternew bone from intact sleeve inferior to the superiorly displaced fragment

Rockwood (Dameron-Rockwood) classification

Type Injury
I AC ligament sprain, periosteal tube intact
II Partial periosteal tube disruption
III Large split, superior displacement
IV Posterior displacement through trapezius
V Complete disruption, through deltoid + trapezius
VI Inferior, below coracoid

5Management

Pseudodislocation – intact periosteal sleeve & sling treatment

Most (even displaced, elite athletes) → sling immobilization
✗ Wrong options: CRPP · plate · CC reconstruction/suture · stress views · MRI

Operative criteria

Absolute (rare) Relative
Open fracture Severely displaced, near physeal closure
Skin compromise Fragment entrapped in trapezius
Displaced intra-articular extension Floating shoulder
NV injury needing surgery Some type III near maturity · types IV–VI (open reduction + sleeve repair)

Avoid pins around clavicle (migration)

6Complications

Subclavian vessel lacerationrare · rapidly expanding hematoma → vascular repair (thick periosteum protective)

Nonunionrare, after open reduction → fixation + iliac crest graft

"6-yr distal clavicle fracture, lateral fragment superior?"sling

"16-yr hockey player, likely injury pattern?"physeal separation, intact inferior sleeve, intact CC + AC

"12-yr elite gymnast, distal clavicle physeal fracture?"sling

"MRI of 11-yr distal clavicle fracture shows?"intact inferior periosteal sleeve
✗ Wrong options: CC disruption · AC dislocation

"Last physis to close?"medial clavicle (20–25 yr)

Distal Femoral Physeal Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 35 / 112

1Basics

Whoopen physes · often misdiagnosed as collateral ligament sprain · 2–5% of physeal injuries (<2% OB)

Most common typeSalter-Harris II (physis fails on tension side, metaphysis on compression side → Thurston-Holland)

Anatomy

Ossificationsingle nucleus present at birth — first epiphysis to ossify

Physisundulating (mammillary processes) → fracture crosses multiple layers → high arrest rate

Musclesgastrocnemius + plantaris arise just proximal → flex distal fragment

Ligamentscollaterals + cruciates attach to epiphysis → stress transmitted to physis (ligament injury uncommon)

Vesselspopliteal artery directly posterior, trifurcates here, poor collaterals → limb-threatening

Growth

Physis Growth / yr
Proximal femur 3 mm
Distal femur 9 mm (Orthobullets) · 10 mm (TO) · 10–12 mm at peak
Proximal tibia 6 mm
Distal tibia 5 mm

Distal femur70% of femoral growth, 37% of limb (TO) · most lower-limb growth at the knee

Growth stops14 yr girls, 16 yr boys (Orthobullets) · fuses 14–16 ♀ / 16–18 ♂ (TO)

Physeal histology – hypertrophic zone

Fracture planehypertrophic zone (chondrocytes enlarge, then apoptosis + matrix calcification in zone of provisional calcification)
✗ Wrong options: proliferative (cells ↑ in number, max matrix) · reserve (precursors) · primary spongiosa (woven bone) · secondary spongiosa (lamellar)

Distal femur SH Ipropagates through multiple layers (undulating physis) (OB)

2Mechanism

Mechanismdirect trauma + rotation · valgus or hyperextension force · sports, vehicle

Displacement directionanterior = hyperextension · posterior = hyperflexion · medial = valgus · lateral = varus

3Presentation

Exampain, can't bear weight · knee held flexed (hamstring spasm) · tenderness over physis (medial epicondyle region) · effusion · varus/valgus "instability" · popliteal swelling → vascular injury

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis – occult Salter-Harris I, MRI & imaging

InitialAP, lateral, oblique knee
✗ Wrong options: MRI first · stress views · CT · notch view

Physeal wideningnormal 3–5 mm · compare contralateral

Stress radiographsfallen out of favour (pain, sedation, physeal damage) → MRI (or US) replaced them

MRImodality of choice to confirm occult physeal fracture
✗ Wrong options: CT · weight-bearing views · aspiration/NSAID trial

CTintra-articular extension, fixation planning

AngiographyABI <0.9 · wide displacement, posterior spike

Alternativesuspected SH I → long-leg cast + repeat X-ray 2–3 wk

Key radiology findings

Peterson classification (TO)I metaphyseal transverse into physis · II SH II equivalent · III through physis · IV epiphyseal along physis · V traverses all · VI part of physis missing

5Management

Operative criteria

Fracture Treatment
Nondisplaced (incl. occult SH I) Long-leg cast 4–6 wk, crutches, close follow-up (✗ Wrong options: hinged brace WBAT · immobiliser)
Displaced SH I / II (majority) Closed reduction + percutaneous fixation + cast (unstable even if reduced) (✗ Wrong options: cast alone · traction · plate)
SH III / IV with anatomic closed reduction CRPP
SH III / IV with articular displacement ORIF (avoid physis)
Irreducible SH I / II Open reduction — remove periosteum on tension side
Distal femoral physeal fracture
  • Nondisplaced→long-leg cast 4–6 wk, close follow-up
  • Displaced→gentle reduction under GA (90% traction, 10% manipulation)
    • SH I / SH II with small T-H fragment→smooth K-wires across physis (remove 3–6 wk)
    • SH II with large T-H fragment→metaphyseal lag screws (avoid physis)
    • SH III / IV→epiphyseal lag screws (open if needed)

Fixation – smooth pins vs screws (Thurston-Holland fragment)

Pins vs screwsdecided by size of Thurston-Holland fragment · large → metaphyseal lag screws · small / SH I → smooth K-wires across physis + supplemental cast

SH Ivery unstable → anatomic reduction + smooth pins + cast
✗ Wrong options: screws (↑ physeal injury) · blade plate · flexible nails

Avoidthreaded wires, screws, plates across physis (rigid tether)

Pin directionretrograde (through joint) theoretical ↑ septic arthritis (no proven difference)

Screwsfully vs partially threaded: no difference with lag technique

Vascular injury

Pulses only on Doppler / ABI 0.8 → urgent reduction + (percutaneous) fixation, then reassess vascular status
✗ Wrong options: arteriogram/CT/MRI first · cast · fasciotomy first · vascular exploration before reduction · plate across physis

Highest riskanterior epiphyseal displacement (hyperextension) / posterior metaphyseal spike → treat like knee dislocation · arterial injury up to 20% in some series · compartment syndrome <1–3%

6Complications

Growth arrest risk – LLD & angular deformity

Most common complicationphyseal arrest → LLD / angular deformity
✗ Wrong options: nonunion (rare) · ligament injury · stiffness (transient) · AVN

Physeal arrest rate30–50% (Orthobullets, OB "~40%") · **~60%** (OB) · 50–55% / 50–80% (OB) — read the options

LLD >2 cmone-third of cases

SH type Growth disturbance
I 36%
II 58%
III 49%
IV 64% — highest (✗ Wrong options: "type III maximal" (TO false statement))

PatternSH I + V → LLD (non-angular) · SH II → angular deformity

Predictors of complicationsSH type · displacement · hardware crossing physis · articular incongruity · open fracture · surgical treatment · younger age / less skeletal maturity (tibial tuberosity ossification stage) · NOT direction of displacement

Rate of arrest ↑ with displacement; older age (OB)

LLD calculation

Complete arrest LLD = remaining years × ~9–10 mm · e.g. 11-yr girl (stops 14) → 3 cm · 13-yr boy with 2 cm LLD (stops 16) → 20 + 27 = ~4.7–5 cm, affected side short

Physeal bar – resection

Post-traumatic distal femoral bar / LLD
  • Predicted LLD <2 cm, no angulation→observe
  • Bar <50%, ≥2 yr (2–2.5 cm) growth left→bar resection + PMMA / fat
    (angulation >20° → add osteotomy)
  • LLD 2–6 cm→contralateral distal femur ± proximal tibia epiphysiodesis
    (>5 cm → ipsilateral lengthening)

11-yr, 5° varus, 25% bar, rest open → bar resection + PMMA · results 62–90% good
✗ Wrong options: observe · osteotomy · guided growth · epiphysiodesis

12-yr girl after fixation (~2 yr growth left) → physeal disturbance — close observation (predicted LLD <2 cm)
✗ Wrong options: contralateral epiphysiodesis · lengthening

Septic arthritisintra-articular pins

Smooth K-wires Lag screws
Use SH I, SH II with small T-H fragment SH II large T-H (metaphyseal), SH III/IV (epiphyseal)
Physis Cross it (smooth) Parallel, avoid physis
Removal 3–6 wk —

1Basics

Also calledtransphyseal distal humerus fracture

Age<3 years (physis weaker than bone–ligament interface → physeal fracture, not dislocation)

Mechanismbirth trauma (vaginal delivery, shoulder dystocia; C-section traction) · non-accidental trauma (rotational/twisting shear — up to 50% battered child) · FOOSH, fall from bed/couch

Displacementposteromedial (most) · rarely anterior

Age SH type
<3 yr SH I (pure physeal)
>3 yr SH II (metaphyseal fragment)
Rare SH III/IV — mimics lateral condyle fracture

3Presentation

Exampseudoparalysis / not using arm · swelling, ecchymosis · NV compromise rare

NAT red flagsunwitnessed, inconsistent history, multiple injuries, burns, bites, bruises (skin lesions most common NAT finding)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis & non-accidental trauma association (skeletal survey)

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral centred on elbow · stress views may help · skeletal survey if abuse suspected
✗ Wrong options: "babygram" (misses it)

Findingsradius + ulna displaced posteromedially relative to humerus (may be the only sign in infants) · forearm not aligned with humeral shaft · radiocapitellar alignment maintained (capitellum stays with radius — definitive if ossified) · effusion, swelling

Capitellum ossifies1–2 yr (first elbow centre)

Ultrasounduncertain dx, no sedation · static (cartilage absent on metaphysis) / dynamic instability

Arthrogramuncertain dx, in OR with CRPP · direct posterior portal (olecranon fossa) in young · shows pin start on capitellum + anterior humeral line

MRInot routine (sedation)

Missedup to 50% by radiologists · delayed up to 1 wk

5Management

Transphyseal distal humerus fracture (<3 yr)
  • Suspect NAT→skeletal survey + child protective services
  • Displaced (most)→arthrogram + closed reduction + percutaneous pinning
  • Nondisplaced / late presentation→long-arm splint/cast 2–3 wk
    (late: deformity → osteotomy later)

After immobilisation, 8-month-old → contact child protective services
✗ Wrong options: MRI · CT elbow/head · emergent fixation (not emergent without open/NV injury)

NAT team consultmost likely for distal humerus physeal separation in 16-month-old
✗ Wrong options: BBFF 5-yr · type II supracondylar 4-yr · femur 10-yr · Tillaux 13-yr

Treatment – closed reduction & pinning

Displaced (even if NAT ruled out) → CRPP under GA with arthrogram
✗ Wrong options: observe · sling · rigid immobilisation · compartment monitoring · ORIF / plate · hinged ex-fix

Reductiongentle traction (little force) → correct translation/rotation → flex

Acceptableno cubitus varus · anterior humeral line bisects capitellum · no malrotation

Pins2–3 × 0.062" lateral, divergent, bicortical, wide spread · test under live fluoro

Post-opsplint · X-ray 1 wk · remove pins at 3 wk · follow 2–4 yr (arrest, deformity, AVN)

Nonoplimited: nondisplaced · late-presenting (→ later osteotomy)

6Complications

Cubitus varusup to 70% — more common than supracondylar · from medial condyle AVN, malunion (missed/lost reduction), growth arrest → lateral closing-wedge osteotomy

Medial/lateral condyle AVNfishtail deformity

Growth disturbanceobserve, operate >5 yr (bigger limb, cooperative, one-stage)

Loss of motionrarely functional

NOT associatedtardy ulnar nerve palsy (→ lateral condyle nonunion + cubitus valgus)

Transphyseal separation Elbow dislocation
Age <3 yr Older (almost never <3)
Displacement Posteromedial Posterolateral
Radiocapitellar line Intact Disrupted
NAT Strong association —

Distal Radius Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 37 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology – most common paediatric fracture

Most common fracture <16 yrdistal radius (22.7%) > hand phalanges (18.9%) > carpal/MC (8.3%) > clavicle (8.1%) > supracondylar (3.3%) > distal femur (1.6%)

Forearm~40% of pediatric long-bone fractures (OB: distal radius = 40% of all pediatric fractures) · M 2–3× · peak 10–12 yr ♀, 12–14 yr ♂ (metaphyseal growth spurt)

Lifetime fracture risk <16 yrboys 42%, girls 27%

Anatomy & remodelling

Distal radial physis75% of radial growth, 40% of upper limb · ~5.25 mm/yr

Locationmetaphysis 62% > diaphysis 20% > physis

Remodellinggreatest near physis + in plane of joint motion (sagittal — flexion/extension) · ~1°/month · least for rotation (rotation doesn't remodel)

2Mechanism

FOOSH, wrist extended · rule out abuse (inconsistent history, multiple-age injuries, grip marks)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Type Feature
Torus / buckle Unicortical, nondisplaced, compression side
Greenstick Fails on tension (convex) side; plastic deformation on compression side
Plastic deformation Many microfractures, lower force over time
Complete metaphyseal Apex volar (Colles-type) / apex dorsal (Smith-type)
Physeal SH I–V (SH II most common)
Galeazzi Distal-third radius + DRUJ injury
Monteggia Ulna + radiocapitellar dislocation

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral wrist and forearm · elbow if tender or diaphyseal · check SL interval, DRUJ, ulnar styloid

CTintra-articular only (radiation)

5Management

Remodelling potential & acceptable angulation (buckle fractures need no follow-up)

Age Bayonet Shaft angulation Malrotation Distal radius dorsal angulation
<10 yr <1 cm 15–20° 45° 30°
>10 yr None 10° 30° 20°

Other cut-offsyoung child remodels sagittal deformity up to ~20°, older ~10° (OB) · operate <9 yr if post-reduction dorsal angulation >30° or malrotation · >10 yr: angulation >20°, rotation >30°

Diaphyseal 10° angulation → blocks 20–30° rotation

4-yr, 12° apex volar at 2 weeks → observe — remodels within ~1 year
✗ Wrong options: osteoclasis · re-reduction · 2 years

9-yr, 18° unreduced metaphyseal deformity → no long-term deformity or deficit

Buckle (torus) fracture → removable splint, no cast, no follow-up · same pain + refracture as cast
✗ Wrong options: physeal-arrest monitoring · close follow-up

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Unicortical/bicortical, <10°, buckle SAC 2–3 wk / removable splint
>10–20° angulation, SH I/II unacceptable Closed reduction + cast
Unstable / lost reduction in cast / reduced only in OR / SH I–II with NV compromise CRPP
Displaced SH III/IV · irreducible (periosteum, pronator quadratus) ORIF
Near-mature, redisplaced shaft / bayonet (15-yr) ORIF (✗ Wrong options: accept · remanipulate)
Pediatric distal radius fracture
  • Buckle→removable splint, no follow-up
  • Angulated beyond limits→closed reduction + well-moulded cast (index ≤0.7–0.8)
    • Redisplaced (unacceptable)→re-reduce + percutaneous pins
  • Irreducible / SH III–IV displaced→open reduction

Cast index & loss of reduction – management of redisplacement

Cast indexsagittal (lateral) ÷ coronal (AP) inner width · best predictor of failure · good ≈ 0.7 · loss of reduction >0.8 (mean 0.79 in failures) · OB answer >0.85
✗ Wrong options: padding, gap, three-point, 2nd MC–radius indices

Short vs long arm castwell-moulded SAC = LAC (no ↑ displacement, fewer missed school days)
✗ Wrong options: LAC/SAC/plaster/sedation as risks

Redisplacement20–25% early · risks: poor cast index, ↑ initial displacement, incomplete reduction

11-yr, redisplaced to 22° at 1 week despite good mould → closed reduction + percutaneous fixation
✗ Wrong options: accept · recast · flexible nail (too distal) · plate

Physeal reductiongentle, one attempt, not >1 week after injury (late reduction → arrest)

Techniquemetaphyseal: recreate deformity, use periosteal hinge (traction counterproductive) · intact ulna: ulnar-deviate wrist

Reduction manoeuvre – greenstick fractures

Rotate the palm toward the apexapex-volar (supination injury) → pronate · apex-dorsal (pronation injury) → supinate

CRPP technique

Radial styloid pinsentry just proximal to physis (smooth if transphyseal) · avoid dorsal sensory radial nerve · dorsal pin for volar tilt · DRUJ pin → long-arm cast

6Complications

Cast thermal injury

Risk factor
Dip water >24 °C (75 °F) Yes
>8 plaster layers / thick cast Yes
Resting on pillow while curing (most significant) Yes
Fibreglass over plaster Yes
Excess moulding pressure Yes
Fracture pattern not a risk
22 °C water, thin fibreglass, single padding layer No

Physeal growth arrest (radius/ulna) – CT & epiphysiodesis

Distal ulnar physismost likely to arrest (30–40%) vs distal radius <5%

Radial arrest → ulnar-positive variance → ulnocarpal impaction, TFCC + DRUJ injury, radial deviation · variance changes visible 3–4 months

Risk factorsrepeated injury, late presentation/late reduction, multiple attempts, SH III/IV

Distal radial physeal arrest
  • First→CT (physeal map) to size the bar
  • Bar <50% + growth left→bar resection
  • Bar >50% / little growth→complete radial + ulnar epiphysiodesis
    (± radial lengthening for established discrepancy)
  • Skeletally mature, ulnar-positive→ulnar shortening osteotomy

10-yr, painful radial deviation after SH II → CT to assess bar first
✗ Wrong options: osteotomy · bilateral epiphysiodesis

14-yr asymptomatic, radial arrest, small discrepancy → ulnar epiphysiodesis
✗ Wrong options: bar resection · lengthening · styloid repair

>50% radial bar, ulnar-positive, immature → distal ulna epiphysiodesis
✗ Wrong options: mature (ulnar shortening) · Kienböck · Madelung (Vickers ligament release)

Othermalunion (most common complication) · median neuropathy / acute carpal tunnel · cast-saw burns (cool blade)

"9-yr, 18° unreduced?"no long-term deformity or deficit

"2-yr buckle fracture — true?"no cast or follow-up needed

"Risk of displacement after reduction?"cast index >0.85
✗ Wrong options: long/short arm cast · plaster · sedation

"11-yr redisplaced 22° at 1 week?"closed reduction + percutaneous fixation

"15-yr redisplaced distal radial shaft, physis closing?"ORIF

"Best predictor of failure of closed treatment?"cast index

"Isolated pronation reduces?"apex-volar greenstick (supination injury)

"Thermal injury risk — EXCEPT?"fracture pattern

"Most significant cast-burn risk?"resting wet cast on pillow

"14-yr, radial arrest, asymptomatic?"ulnar epiphysiodesis

"Most common fracture <16 yr?"distal radius

Down Syndrome

Pediatrics · 38 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Most common chromosomal abnormality (US) · 1:700 live births

Riskadvanced maternal age: 1 in 250 if >35 yr · 1 in 5000 if <30 yr

Genes & lab markers

Geneticstrisomy 21 (maternal duplication)

Collagenchr 21 codes type VI collagen (COL6A1, COL6A2) → generalised laxity

Labs / medicalhypothyroidism (check with SCFE) · cardiac disease 50% (ASD, PDA) · duodenal atresia · premature aging · Alzheimer's · intellectual disability

Orthopaedic manifestations

Ligamentous laxity + hypotonia · short stature · delayed walking (2–3 yr) · C1–2 instability · occipitocervical instability · hip instability · patellofemoral instability · scoliosis, spondylolisthesis (6%) · pes planus (50%) · metatarsus primus varus · hallux valgus (25%) · SCFE

3Presentation

Examflattened facies · upward-slanting eyes · epicanthal folds · single palmar (simian) crease · laxity · hearing loss

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosischromosomal testing (trisomy 21)

Key radiology findings

C-spineflexion-extension lateral — ADI normal <5 mm (Orthobullets) / up to 4 mm (OB) · 5–10 mm tolerated in Down · space available for cord (SAC) threshold 14 mm

OccipitocervicalPowers ratio

Hipacetabular retroversion (crossover + ischial spine signs) · coxa valga

Kneelong-leg film (genu valgum) · sunrise/Merchant (patellar subluxation)

5Management

Atlantoaxial instability – ADI & sports clearance

Prevalence17.5% (Orthobullets) · ~15% (OB)

Presentationsubtle: change in gait, bowel/bladder

Flexion-extension filmsbefore intubation · Special Olympics requires C-spine imaging before gymnastics, swimming, high jump etc.
✗ Wrong options: AP pelvis · knee/elbow films · neurology referral · clear without work-up

Atlantoaxial instability in Down syndrome
  • ADI 5–10 mm, asymptomatic, SAC >14 mm→surveillance (neuro exam + repeat imaging); avoid contact sports
  • ADI >5 mm + myelopathy, or ADI >10 mm, or SAC <14 mm→C1–2 posterior fusion
    (complications up to 50%)

Asymptomatic, ADI 6 mm → avoid contact sports, high jump, diving, gymnastics, butterfly
✗ Wrong options: clear all · collar · halo · fusion

Asymptomatic, ADI 5 mm → surveillance: symptoms, neuro exam, repeat imaging
✗ Wrong options: O–C2 fusion · anterior fusion · soft collar · traction

Operative criteria

Problem Surgery when
C1–2 instability ADI >5 mm + symptoms/myelopathy · ADI >10 mm · SAC ≤14 mm · cord compression on MRI/CT
Occipitocervical Progressive neuro deficit / myelopathy → occipitocervical fusion (most observed)
Scoliosis Brace 25–30° · fuse >50° (more complications than idiopathic)
Hip instability Older symptomatic → capsulorrhaphy + pelvic (triple / PAO for retroversion) + femoral varus osteotomy (high complications)
Patellar instability Symptomatic → lateral release, medial reefing, semitendinosus tenodesis, TTO if mature
SCFE Pin both hips
Pes planus Orthotics if symptomatic; surgery if refractory

Lower-limb problems – hip instability, patellar instability & genu valgum

Hip instability5%, age 2–10 yr · laxity + acetabular retroversion, coxa valga · young, mild subluxation, no bony change → abduction brace
✗ Wrong options: observe · NSAIDs · shoe lift · osteotomy

Patellofemoral instabilitymature, painless, knock-knees → observation · symptomatic → patellar stabilising brace → surgery (TTO in mature)
✗ Wrong options: lateral release alone · trochleoplasty first

10-yr with Down facies, laxity, new limp → associated image = acetabular retroversion
✗ Wrong options: foramen magnum stenosis (achondroplasia) · absent cruciates (fibular/femoral deficiency) · iliac horns (nail-patella) · absent clavicles (CCD)

How it's asked

"10-yr Down, high jump, ADI 6 mm, asymptomatic?"avoid contact sports, high jump, diving

"7-yr Down, ADI 5 mm, asymptomatic?"surveillance with neuro exam + repeat imaging

"15-yr gymnast with trisomy 21 — before participation?"cervical spine imaging

"17-yr Down, painless knock-knees, dislocated patellae?"observation

"3-yr Down, mild hip subluxation, no bony change?"abduction brace

"Hip image associated with Down syndrome?"acetabular retroversion

"Indication for C1–2 fusion?"myelopathy with ADI >5 mm, ADI >10 mm, or SAC <14 mm

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

Pediatrics · 39 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease (most common MD) · prevalence 2–3/10,000 (Orthobullets) · ~1 in 3500 male births (OB)

Whoboys only · onset 2–6 yr

Genetics – dystrophin, X-linked recessive, carrier mother & offspring risk

InheritanceX-linked recessive
✗ Wrong options: AD · AR · X-linked dominant · mitochondrial · Y-linked

Genedystrophin, Xp21(.2) · point deletion / nonsense (out-of-frame) → absent dystrophin (<5%)

Spontaneousone-third new mutations

Carriersmother carries · sons 50% affected, daughters 50% carriers · affected male → 0% sons affected (gives Y), all daughters carriers · 2.5–20% of carrier females symptomatic (Lyon hypothesis) · CK ↑ in 80% of carriers (peak 8–12 yr)

Confirm DMD via familytest mother's CK
✗ Wrong options: father (always normal) · unaffected brother

Pathophysiologydystrophin–glycoprotein complex lost → membrane fragility, Ca²⁺ dysregulation, oxidative damage → necrosis/regeneration cycles → fibrofatty replacement

Genes & lab markers

Disorder Gene / inheritance
Duchenne Dystrophin, Xp21 (XLR)
Becker Dystrophin (in-frame, ↓ amount) (XLR)
Emery-Dreifuss Emerin (X-linked)
FSH dystrophy D4Z4 deletion, 4q35 · AD
Myotonic dystrophy DMPK / CNBP, chromosome 19
Limb-girdle AR and AD (LGMD2 / LGMD1) · chr 2p (TO)
Marfan FBN1
CMT PMP22 (AD)
Turner 45,XO

CKmarkedly ↑ — 10–200× (Orthobullets) · 50–100× (TO) · often >25,000 IU/L (e.g. 43,000) · peaks by age 2, falls with fibrofatty replacement

EMGmyopathic (low amplitude, short, polyphasic), normal NCV

Biopsynecrosis, fibrofatty infiltration, absent dystrophin stain · DNA confirms ~two-thirds · dystrophin testing of biopsy NOT 100% confirmatory (TO)

3Presentation

Historydelayed walking (e.g. 30 mo) · toe walking, clumsy, waddling · difficulty climbing stairs, hopping · falls

Weaknessproximal first, starting with gluteals · lumbar lordosis (gluteal weakness) · wide-based stance

Gowers signrises by walking hands up thighs (gluteus maximus + quadriceps weakness)

Meryon signchild slips through examiner's hands when lifted under arms (shoulder girdle weakness)

Calf pseudohypertrophyfat + fibrous infiltration

Reflexespresent
✗ Wrong options: SMA · GBS

Trendelenburg · contractures (elbow, hip, knee, ankle) · equinovarus (tibialis posterior retains strength longest) · scoliosis · fractures (falls)

Othercardiomyopathy · mild intellectual impairment · pharyngeal weakness · malignant hyperthermia risk

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis – Gowers sign, CK & Becker variant

First testserum CK (✗ Wrong options: leg X-rays · NCS · brain/spine MRI) · screen asymptomatic at-risk boy with CK (✗ Wrong options: DNA, biopsy, Western blot first)

ConfirmDNA testing (± biopsy)

Key radiology findings

MRI muscle patterngastrocnemius early → gluteus max/med, adductor magnus → quads etc. · spared: sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus, semimembranosus, tibialis posterior · upper limb: triceps, biceps, rotator cuff; deltoid spared

Echodilated cardiomyopathy in all by late teens/20s

X-raylucent fatty soft tissue, scoliosis, cardiomegaly

Differential

Duchenne Becker SMA Emery-Dreifuss Limb-girdle GBS
Dystrophin Absent Decreased/abnormal Normal Normal (emerin absent) Normal —
CK Very high Very high Normal Near normal Mildly ↑ Normal
Pseudohypertrophy Yes Yes No No No No
Reflexes Present Present Absent + fasciculations — — Absent
Onset 2–6 yr ~8 yr, slower, lives to 40s Earlier Teens; early elbow + ankle contractures, heart block (pacemaker) 1st–4th decade Acute, post-infectious
Key test DNA DNA — ECG — CSF (lumbar puncture)

Differential – Guillain-Barré syndrome

GBSacute ascending flaccid weakness 1–6 wk after (GI) infection · areflexia · autonomic + diaphragm involvement · lumbar puncture (CSF) best test · IVIG / plasma exchange · 80% walk at 6 mo
✗ Wrong options: C-spine MRI/CT · M-spike · stool

5Management

Corticosteroids (prednisone / deflazacort)age 5–7 yr with progression · prolong ambulation (3–4 yr), ↓ scoliosis needing fusion 92% → 20%, delay pulmonary + cardiac decline, ↓ mortality 76% · side effects: osteonecrosis, osteoporosis, weight gain, cataracts, short stature · deflazacort — fewer glucose/bone effects, far costlier

Exon-skipping (eteplirsen, golodirsen, viltolarsen, casimersen)convert out-of-frame to in-frame (DMD → BMD-like) · hot-spot exons 45–53 (~50%) · costly

CardiacACE inhibitor + β-blocker · echo/ECG every 2 yr to age 10, then yearly (6-monthly with cardiomyopathy)

Othernocturnal ventilation · PT, power chair · nutrition

Soft-tissue releases (ambulatory)ITB (abduction contracture) · sartorius, rectus, TFL (flexion) · hamstrings · TAL + tibialis posterior lengthening/transfer · mobilise early

Equinovarusstretching, night AFO → TAL + PTT transfer + toe flexor tenotomies

Scoliosis – early fusion (20–30°, FVC), T2-pelvis & preoperative cardiopulmonary work-up

Natural history90–95% develop scoliosis · starts when full-time sitting (11–13 yr) · progresses rapidly (1–2°/month), small curves always progress · kyphoscoliosis + pelvic obliquity · restrictive lung disease
✗ Wrong options: 50%

Bracingineffective / contraindicated (impairs respiration)
✗ Wrong options: TLSO · PT · observe a 25° curve

Operative criteria

Criterion Value
Cobb angle 20–30° in non-ambulator (up to ~40° if responding to steroids)
FVC Operate before FVC ≤35% (≤35% = indication / threshold) · >50% = good outcomes · <10% contraindication (some)
Other Non-ambulatory · rapid progression · poor steroid response (✗ Wrong options: decreased muscle mass)
Fuse to pelvis Curve ≥40° · pelvic obliquity ≥10° · lumbar apex below L1
Construct T2–pelvis posterior instrumented fusion (pedicle screws) (✗ Wrong options: T10–pelvis · growing rods · T2–L5 with obliquity · delay for steroids)
Anterior approach Avoid (lung deflation, ↑ pulmonary complications)

Timingdriven by cardiopulmonary status, not Cobb angle · 12-yr, 38°, FVC 50% → as soon as possible
✗ Wrong options: wait for FVC 35% · cardiac decline · 50°

Pre-opechocardiogram + PFTs, cardiology consult · stop ACE-I 2–3 d, taper β-blocker over weeks · TXA · beware anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis, hypotensive anaesthesia may not be tolerated
✗ Wrong options: hematology · neurology · rheumatology/biopsy · MRI for ectasia · baclofen trial · bracing trial

DMD scoliosis
  • Ambulatory→steroids, keep walking (no brace)
  • Non-ambulatory, curve ≥20–30° or FVC falling toward 35%→early PSF (echo + PFT first)
    • Curve <40°, obliquity <10°, apex ≥L1→T2–L5 possible
    • Curve ≥40° / obliquity ≥10° / apex below L1→T2–pelvis

Other muscular dystrophies (FSH, myotonic)

FSH dystrophyAD, 4q35 · facial weakness (can't whistle, purse lips, wrinkle brow) · scapular winging — scapular stabilisers weak while deltoid (abductors) stay strong → can't flex/abduct arm · scapulothoracic arthrodesis · foot drop (AFO) · open-eyed sleeping
✗ Wrong options: "due to weak abductors"

Myotonic dystrophychromosome 19 (DMPK) · can't relax muscle · most common adult-onset MD · baldness, gonadal atrophy, cardiac, clubfoot, hip dysplasia, scoliosis

Limb-girdleAD (LGMD1) and AR (LGMD2) · pelvic/shoulder girdle · CK mildly ↑

Oculopharyngeal40–70 yr, eyelids + throat

6Complications & prognosis

Untreatedwalking lost by ~10 yr (10–12) · wheelchair by 15 · death from respiratory/cardiac failure ~20 (Orthobullets) / ~25 (OB) / early 30s (TO) · 15-yr survival 27.9% → 78.6% with steroids

Pediatrics · 42 / 112

1Basics

Incidence3–6% of pediatric elbow injuries · M:F 3:1 · peak 10–15 yr · very rare <3 yr (→ think transphyseal fracture + NAT)

MechanismFOOSH · posterior = hyperextension + valgus + supination · anterior = posterior-to-anterior blow on flexed elbow

Small coronoid in children → can't resist posterior ulnar displacement

Associatedmedial epicondyle avulsion = most common (may incarcerate in joint) · radial head/neck, olecranon, coronoid fractures

Nervesulnar (with medial epicondyle) = most common neuropraxia · median + brachial artery stretched / entrapped

Classification

By proximal radioulnar joint positionposterolateral (most common) · posteromedial · anterior (rare) · divergent

Examswollen, painful · held flexed · forearm looks short · distal humerus fullness in antecubital fossa · NV exam (brachial artery, median, ulnar)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral (± contralateral) · loss of radiocapitellar + ulnohumeral relationship, radius–ulna relationship maintained

Post-reductionlocate the medial epicondyle — if not seen in normal position, assume intra-articular

5Management

Reduce promptlyby the most available provider (ED) under sedation · don't delay for orthopaedics

Techniquesupine: elbow flexed, forearm supinated, gradual traction · prone: forearm hanging, anterior push on olecranon · anterior dislocation: inline traction, posterior push on forearm

Management & surgical indications

Stable after reduction (most) → brief immobilisation 1–2 wk (posterior splint ~8–12 days) → early active ROM
✗ Wrong options: cast 6 wk · hinged ex-fix · MRI

Absolute Relative
Open dislocation Significant instability (rare)
Incarcerated medial epicondyle (or coronoid) —
Failure to obtain/maintain closed reduction —

Medial epicondyle fracture — when to fixabsolute: incarcerated fragment, open, articular extension · relative: elbow dislocation / instability, ulnar nerve palsy, throwing/upper-limb athlete · nonunion common nonoperatively (often asymptomatic) · fuses 16–18 yr (last)
✗ Wrong options: buckle radius fracture · <2 mm displacement · radial nerve symptoms · video games

Entrapped medial epicondyle fragment

Incongruous joint after reduction / fragment in joint → open reduction (medial approach) + ORIF of medial epicondyle
✗ Wrong options: re-reduction attempt · lateral epicondyle · coronoid

6Complications

Loss of motion after immobilisation

Stiffness — loss of terminal extensionfrom immobilisation >2 weeks
✗ Wrong options: sex · age >9 · ED reduction · no ORIF

Othersheterotopic ossification (vigorous reduction) · transient nerve injury (median entrapment, ulnar with medial epicondyle) · brachial artery (rare) · compartment syndrome (hyperflexion splint) · recurrent instability (coronoid / radial head fractures)

X vs Y

Elbow dislocation Transphyseal distal humerus fracture
Age 10–15 yr <3 yr
Displacement Posterolateral Posteromedial
Radiocapitellar Disrupted Maintained
NAT Rare Strong association

Stage Feature
1 Delta-shaped diaphysis, radiolucent cartilaginous epiphysis

Longitudinal epiphyseal bracket
  • Young child, open bracket→early excision (physiolysis) + fat / PMMA interposition
  • Older, bracket closed→opening/closing wedge osteotomy ± lengthening

Treatment - bracket excision

Early open bracket excision + fat graft (or PMMA) interpositionbest; restores near-normal longitudinal growth, ↓ deformity

Osteotomyafter bracket epiphysis closes (older) · secondary realignment/lengthening if growth insufficient

Untreatedforefoot deformity, short bone, clinodactyly

1Basics

Definitionabnormal external rotation of the tibia → out-toeing · usually right-sided if unilateral

Key radiology findings

Thigh–foot axis (TFA)best clinical measure · prone, knee 90° · infancy ~5° internal · age 8: ~10° external (−5 to +30°) · >20° external = ETT

Transmalleolar axissupine · infancy 4–5° internal · adult 23° external (0–40°)

Foot progression angle~5° external in late childhood

CT torsional studytibial version = distal minus proximal axis; femoral version neck minus condyles

First linerest, rehab, activity modification (bracing ineffective)

Operative criteria

Source Indication
Orthobullets >8 yr + ETT >3 SD (>40° external)
OB ≥9 yr + TFA >30° (or < −15°) · normal TFA −5° to 20°

Proceduresupramalleolar (distal tibial) derotation osteotomy (most common) ± oblique fibular osteotomy · pins or plate · IM nail only if mature

Distal vs proximaldistal: easier, safer (↓ NV injury, ↓ compartment syndrome) · proximal: more contact/soft tissue but peroneal nerve risk → anterior fasciotomy

12-yr, right ETT 45° (left 32°), normal femoral version → right supramalleolar osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: observe · KAFO · distal tibial guided growth (causes coronal deformity) · femoral osteotomy

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence1.6–2% of pediatric fractures · most common orthopaedic cause of pediatric hospitalisation · bimodal: toddlers 2–4 yr + adolescents · M 2.6:1

Mechanism by age0–2 yr: NAT · <10 yr: falls · >10 yr: MVA (cortex thickens with age)

AssociatedOI · neuromuscular osteopenia · tumours

Deforming forces

Proximal fragmentiliopsoas (flexion) + abductors (gluteus medius/minimus → abduction) + short external rotators (piriformis → ER)
✗ Wrong options: adductors · hamstrings · rectus (insert distally)

Distal fragmentadductors → shortening + varus

Typical malunionvarus + flexion (procurvatum) of distal fragment

Stability

Length-stabletransverse, short oblique

Length-unstablelong spiral (length >2× diameter), comminuted

3Presentation

Examthigh pain, can't walk, deformity, shortening, swelling

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral femur + ipsilateral hip and knee

Non-accidental trauma

Suspect<3 yr (AAOS: evaluate <36 months), especially non-walkers

Patterns most predictivetransverse femoral shaft · metaphyseal corner fracture (pathognomonic) · posterior rib fractures, scapula, sternum, spinous process · injury inconsistent with history (9-month-old "running")
✗ Wrong options: spiral, long oblique, toddler's

Infant with metaphyseal corner fracture → admit + social services
✗ Wrong options: Pavlik and discharge · spondylometaphyseal dysplasia/syphilis work-up first · infection work-up

Distractorslytic lesion = pathologic · blue sclera = OI · low vitamin D / metaphyseal fraying = rickets

Treatment selection by age & weight

Age Pattern / factor Treatment
<6 months Any Pavlik harness (or spica)
6 mo – 5 yr Stable, shortening <2 cm Immediate spica
6 mo – 5 yr Unstable, >2–3 cm short, polytrauma, open Traction → delayed spica · ex-fix
5–11 yr Length-stable + <49 kg (100 lb) Flexible (titanium elastic) nails
5–11 yr Length-unstable (comminuted, long spiral), very proximal/distal, any weight Submuscular bridge plate · stainless Ender nails · ex-fix
>11 yr / >49 kg / near maturity Diaphyseal Antegrade rigid nail — trochanteric or lateral entry (✗ Wrong options: piriformis)
>11 yr Proximal/distal, severe comminution Submuscular plate
Polytrauma, open, vascular repair, damage control — External fixation

Age ranges varyspica 6 mo–5 yr (Orthobullets) · 6 mo–6 yr / 1–6 yr (OB) · Pavlik <6 mo (Orthobullets) / <1 yr (OB) · trochanteric rigid nail from ~9 yr (trochanteric apophysis no longer key; earlier → coxa valga) (OB)

Pediatric femoral shaft fracture
  • <6 mo→Pavlik harness
  • 6 mo–5 yr, <2 cm short→immediate spica
  • 5–11 yr
    • Length-stable, <49 kg→flexible nails
    • Length-unstable / heavy / proximal-distal→submuscular plate
  • >11 yr or >49 kg→trochanteric/lateral-entry rigid IM nail

Operative criteria

Device Key criterion
Flexible nails 5–11 yr · <49 kg / 100–108 lb · length-stable · open or closed OK · not comminuted
Contraindication to flexible nails Weight (e.g. 146 lb) — not age, height, multiple fractures, open fracture
Submuscular plate Length-unstable · >49 kg · proximal/distal · comminuted (incl. open comminuted in 4-yr)
Rigid IM nail >11 yr / near maturity · >49 kg · unstable · trochanteric/lateral entry
Spica Shortening <2 cm (loss of reduction doubles per cm: 12% → 24% → 50%) · not polytrauma, open, >2–3 cm
Ex-fix Polytrauma (damage control), open, vascular injury, segmental

Ipsilateral femur + tibia (floating knee) in 7-yr → flexible nails both
✗ Wrong options: spica · reamed nails (physeal/AVN risk)

Infant fractures - Pavlik harness

<6 months → Pavlik (no anaesthesia, easy diapering, fewer skin problems than spica) · not in neuromuscular spasticity or polytrauma · 9-month-old → spica
✗ Wrong options: flexible nails, ex-fix, growing rods, traction, plate

Pavlik riskfemoral nerve compression with excessive flexion + swollen thigh (↓ quads)

Spica technique

Positionhips 60–90° flexion, ~30° abduction, external rotation to correct rotation · mould into recurvatum + valgus · single-leg or 1½ spica (special car seat sometimes)

Acceptable<10° coronal, <20° sagittal, ≤2 cm shortening, ≤10° rotation

Union4–8 wk · check at 7–10 d

Spica cast complications

Most common needing revisionloss of reduction (11%)
✗ Wrong options: delayed/nonunion · cosmetic · LLD

Compartment syndrome risk"90/90" technique: short-leg portion first then traction · knee flexion >90° (e.g. 105°) · firm popliteal mould · high energy · NOT immediate ED casting under sedation, single-leg spica, casting within 24 h → apply body + thigh first, lower leg last

Traction

Distal femoral pin (proximal to physis) · avoid proximal tibial pin → tibial tubercle damage → genu recurvatum (also from SH V physeal injury) · 2–3 wk then spica · more complications than immediate spica

Flexible nailing technique & complications

Entryretrograde, medial + lateral, ~2–2.5 cm proximal to distal physis

Nail sizeeach = 0.4 × isthmus, two equal nails, 80% canal fill (e.g. 8-yr, 35 kg → two 4.0 mm) · largest equal nails → best stability
✗ Wrong options: asymmetric · impacted ends · open reduction routinely · hinged brace

Most common complicationpain/irritation at insertion site near knee (up to 40%) → keep protrusion <25 mm
✗ Wrong options: shortening · AVN · malunion · rotation

↑ Complications≥11 yr or >49–50 kg (>108 lb) → ↑ nonunion, malunion, complications, reoperation · comminuted/proximal/distal → malunion · ~50% have 15° malalignment

Union 10–12 wk · remove ~1 yr

Rigid nail entry point & femoral head AVN

Piriformis entrycontraindicated with open physes → injures deep branch of MFCA (lateral epiphyseal / superior retinacular vessels) → femoral head AVN (groin/hip pain months later) · AVN 1–2% (Orthobullets) · ≥4% (OB)

MFCAmain head supply after age 4

Safestlateral entry (lateral GT) > GT tip · GT entry risks GT apophyseal arrest → coxa valga, neck narrowing, hip subluxation

Rigid vs flexiblerigid: higher AVN (with open physes), less angular malunion, better in >11 yr / >49 kg · flexible: more knee pain, more malunion in older/heavier

Polytrauma, head injury & timing

Polytrauma + emergent laparotomy (13-yr, GCS 6) → external fixation (damage control)
✗ Wrong options: traction · nailing · plate

Early fixation with head injuryno ↑ pulmonary or CNS complications, ↓ length of stay
✗ Wrong options: ↑ ARDS/pneumonia · worse mental function

6Complications

Overgrowthmost common in young · 0.7–2 cm <10 yr (avg 0.9 cm 2–10 yr) · within 2 yr → accept shortening ≤2–3 cm

Shortening >2–3 cmsymptomatic → traction/fixation

Malunionvarus + flexion · remodels best in sagittal plane · rotation doesn't remodel

Refractureafter ex-fix removal, esp. varus (1.5–21%) · ex-fix: pin-tract infection (~50% of its complications), delayed/nonunion

Platerefracture after hardware removal

Genu recurvatumtibial tubercle arrest (traction pin / SH V)

X vs Y

Flexible nails Submuscular plate Rigid trochanteric nail
Age 5–11 5–11+ >11 (≥9 OB)
Weight <49 kg Any >49 kg

Main complication Knee pain Refracture on removal AVN (piriformis), coxa valga (GT)

Type Features Prognosis
1 (adult) — most common Bruising, anaemia, fractures, no CNS Enzyme replacement works

Erlenmeyer flaskdistal femur / proximal tibia in ~80% · most common radiological finding, asymptomatic abnormal remodelling, needs no treatment

Osteomyelitis↑ prevalence

Observation / supportive Unaffected (normal bloods, minimal organomegaly, no MRI bone lesions)
Enzyme replacement (imiglucerase, velaglucerase, taliglucerase) All children + symptomatic · not type 2
Substrate reduction (miglustat) Milder, can't tolerate IV ERT

Fracture surgery

Pre-opoptimise with ERT · blood, clotting factors, platelets available (bleeding) · maintain oxygenation (avoid bone crisis) · ↑ infection risk

Situation Treatment
