Hip Septic Arthritis - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 52 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence4–5 / 100,000 children/yr · 50% <2 yr · M:F 2:1 · hip and knee each 35% of septic joints

Risk factorsprematurity · C-section · NICU · umbilical/venous catheters, heel puncture (transient bacteremia)

Mechanism & pathophysiology

Routeshaematogenous (URI precedes ~80%) · direct inoculation · contiguous metaphyseal osteomyelitis — intra-articular metaphysis: hip, shoulder, elbow, ankle (NOT knee) · neonates: transphyseal vessels

Cartilage destructionmatrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) from bacteria, synovium, PMNs, cartilage → damage within 8 hours (6 h in animal studies) · TLR → NF-κB → MMP production
✗ Wrong options: MMPs anabolic · TLRs inhibit · activated by chelators (chelators inactivate; stromelysin is an MMP)

↑ Intra-articular pressure → femoral head osteonecrosis

Causative organisms by age (S aureus, GBS, Kingella, gonococcus)

Age / setting Organism Gram stain
Neonate, community (vaginal birth) Group B streptococcus GP cocci in chains
Neonate, nosocomial S. aureus —
<4 yr, subacute, mild labs, negative cultures Kingella kingae — grows in blood-culture bottles (BACTEC); PCR (rtxA) · resistant to vancomycin + clindamycin GN coccobacillus (facultative anaerobe)
>2 yr / overall S. aureus — most common (catalase + coagulase +) · also causes impetigo GP cocci in clusters
Adolescent, sexually active N. gonorrhoeae — migratory polyarthralgia, maculopapular rash, tenosynovitis · F:M 3:1 · cultures negative ~50% GN intracellular diplococci
Post-varicella Group A β-haemolytic strep —
Unvaccinated H. influenzae (↓ with vaccine) — LP if meningitis signs GN coccobacillus
MRSA osteomyelitis + DVT Panton-Valentine leukocidin · CRP very high —

Kingella"most common in children of all ages" (Orthobullets) · S. aureus most common overall (OB) · no organism in up to 55%

3Presentation

Symptomsacute pain (faster than osteomyelitis) · fever, toxic · limp / refusal to bear weight · antibiotics may mask

Examhip held in flexion, abduction, external rotation (max capsular volume) · pain with passive motion / log-roll · pseudoparalysis · check adjacent joints + spine

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnostic criteria — Kocher

Original Kocher criterion Threshold
Fever >38.5 °C (101.3 °F)
Non-weight-bearing ✓
ESR >40 mm/h
Serum WBC >12,000/mm³
Modified (Caird) — CRP >2.0 mg/dL (20 mg/L)
Criteria met Probability of septic hip
0 <0.2%
1 3%
2 40%
3 93%
4 99.6%

Most predictive orderfever > CRP > ESR > refusal to bear weight > WBC (CRP 2nd-best after fever)

CRP >2 mg/dL + refusal to bear weight → 74% · CRP <2 mg/dL (<20 mg/L) → favours transient synovitis · both absent <1%

Kocher criteria apply to the HIP onlynot the knee → knee: aspirate

LabsWBC ↑ in only 30–60% (neonates may be leukopenic) · ESR may be normal early · CRP rises in 6–8 h · blood cultures if febrile (often positive when joint culture negative)

Synovial fluid

Diagnosis Synovial WBC PMN
Traumatic effusion <5,000 —
Transient (toxic) synovitis 5,000–15,000 <25%
Rheumatic fever 10,000–15,000 ~50%
JRA 15,000–80,000 ~75% (gradual onset, keeps walking)
Septic arthritis >50,000 >75%

PMN % more sensitive than total WBC (85% PMN → 88% sensitivity) · glucose ≥50 mg/dL below serum · Gram stain + culture (± synovial tissue)

Key radiology findings

X-ray (AP + frog)often normal early · joint-space widening (infant: lateral displacement of proximal femur) · subluxation/dislocation · bone lesions

Ultrasoundeffusion (can't tell septic vs sterile) · guides aspiration · neonate: scan both hips if any septic joint

MRIeffusion + adjacent osteomyelitis · don't let it delay surgery

5Management

Workup & next step (US, aspiration, arthrotomy)

Irritable hip in a child
  • Non-toxic, equivocal→ultrasound for effusion
  • Effusion / high suspicion (≥2–3 Kocher, CRP ↑)→aspiration (before antibiotics)
    • WBC >50,000, PMN >75%, +Gram→urgent I&D + IV antibiotics
  • 3–4 criteria + effusion on US→emergent arthrotomy

6-week-old (preterm, C-section), afebrile, widened joint space, painful motion → aspiration
✗ Wrong options: MRI (delays) · CT · observe · Pavlik

Non-toxic 3-yr, normal X-ray, fever, ESR 50, CRP 5 → ultrasound next
✗ Wrong options: NSAID trial · CT · IV antibiotics first · discharge

Fever + refusal + ↑ CRP/ESR → hip aspiration
✗ Wrong options: IV abx · oral abx · ibuprofen · MRI · Lyme Western blot · rheumatology

3-yr, 3/4 criteria + US effusion → emergent arthrotomy + I&D
✗ Wrong options: observe · repeat US · MRI · antibiotics before cultures in a non-septic child

Lyme-endemic hiker, fever 38.2, WBC 14, CRP 5.5 → aspirate (septic more likely than Lyme)

Operative criteria

Urgent I&D = standard of caresurgical emergency (removes chondrolytic enzymes, ↓ pressure / epiphyseal ischaemia) · err toward drainage

Antibiotics aloneadolescent gonococcal arthritis (high-dose penicillin ± aspiration)

Techniqueanterolateral or anterior (Smith-Petersen) arthrotomy · remove pus, irrigate · ± 1 × 1 cm capsular window · drain · other joints open/arthroscopic

Antibioticsaspirate first, then empiric IV · 2–7 d culture-specific IV → 2–3 wk oral · stop when CRP/ESR + clinical picture normal

Age Empiric
<3 mo 1st-gen cephalosporin (GBS, S. aureus, gram-neg)
3 mo–5 yr 2nd/3rd-gen cephalosporin (Kingella, S. aureus, pneumococcus, GAS, H. flu)
5–12 yr 1st-gen cephalosporin
12–18 yr 2nd/3rd-gen cephalosporin (gonococcus)

6Complications

Sequelae, prognosis & cartilage destruction

Poor prognosisage <6 months · associated osteomyelitis · delay >4 days (strongest) · hip (vs knee)

Sequelaecomplete femoral head/neck destruction (neglected neonatal sepsis) · osteonecrosis, articular destruction · physeal arrest → LLD, angular deformity · chronic osteomyelitis · persistent limp · contracture · follow 1–2 yr

NOT a typical sequelchronic posterior instability/dislocation (esp. after anterior approach)

Salvagevarus/valgus proximal femoral osteotomy · trochanteric osteotomy · modified Albee arthroplasty

  • ≥3–4 yr, stage III–VI or MDA >20°→osteotomy
    • physeal bar (V–VI)→add bar resection / hemiepiphysiodesis

Bracing (knee-ankle-foot orthosis, KAFO)

Indicationstage I–II in children <3 yr (Orthobullets) · <3 yr and unilateral stage I–II (TO) · TO calls it "mermaid splints"

Duration~2 yr for bony resolution · improvement should show within 1 yr · fails after 12 months in 2–3 yr old → osteotomy (OB)

Poor results / failure riskobesity (>90th percentile) · bilateral · varus thrust · age ≥3 yr at start · Langenskiöld III · progressive deformity · age >4 (TO)

Evidenceno strong consensus on bracing efficacy (OB) · night KAFO poorly tolerated · (✗ Wrong options: AFO (doesn't address knee) · serial casting)
✗ Wrong options: "effective" · "ineffective" · needs PT

Proximal tibial osteotomy

Operative criteria

Indication for proximal tibia/fibula valgus osteotomy
Stage I–II in child >3 yr
Stage III, IV, V, VI
Age ≥4 yr (all stages)
Failed brace / progressive deformity
MDA >20°
Morbidly obese (OB)

Timingbefore age 4 → recurrence significantly ↓ · early osteotomy (2–4 yr) = best results, least recurrence (TO) · best results <4 yr (OB)

Techniquebelow the tibial tubercle · acute correction · distal fragment into valgus + external rotation + lateral translation · staged for IV–VI · epiphysiolysis in V–VI · medial plateau elevation if depressed · prophylactic anterior compartment fasciotomy

Overcorrection10–15° valgus (Orthobullets, TO) · ~10° valgus (OB) · at least 5° valgus (OB60) · ✓ medial physeal abnormality persists
✗ Wrong options: correction to neutral · undercorrection

✗ Wrong options: distal femur osteotomy

Renal osteodystrophypostpone until renal status stable (osteotomy short-lived otherwise)

Late-onset with distal femoral varusLDFA >92° → distal femoral osteotomy or guided growth (OB)

Guided growth & Hueter-Volkmann

Principle↑ compression → slows longitudinal growth · ↑ tension → stimulates growth

Lateral proximal tibial hemiepiphysiodesistension band plate / staples (extraperiosteal plates) · prevents worsening, does NOT fully correct (OB) · less morbid than osteotomy · not medial hemiepiphysiodesis (worsens varus)

Cautionyoung child, severe stage III → relies on injured medial physis → severe shortening → prefer osteotomy (OB) · lateral tibial epiphysiodesis after age 9 (TO)

Unilateral LLDepiphysiodesis of uninvolved leg (TO)

Physeal bar

Bar resectionneeds ≥4 yr growth remaining · with osteotomy · interposition fat or PMMA · hemiepiphysiodesis if bar >50%

Hemi-plateau elevationsevere uncorrected or relapsed disease

6Complications

Compartment syndromeafter high tibial/fibular osteotomy → prophylactic anterior compartment release

Recurrencemedial physeal bar → progressive varus after well-done osteotomy → lateral hemiepiphysiodesis or bar resection
✗ Wrong options: overcorrection · plate malposition · age 5 · vitamin D

Kohler's Disease

Pediatrics · 56 / 112

1Basics

Natural history & etiology

Definitionidiopathic avascular necrosis (osteochondrosis) of the tarsal navicular in young children

Demographicsage 4–7 yr (Orthobullets) · 2–9 yr (OB) · boys 4:1 (80%) · bilateral up to 25%

Blood supplyintraosseous flow centripetal → central one-third = watershed · primary supply = perforating branches of dorsalis pedis · revascularised from the perichondral ring → excellent prognosis

Theorynavicular is the LAST tarsal bone to ossify → compressed between the ossified talus and cuneiforms → central ischemia (✓ theorised etiology)
✗ Wrong options: first

Mimicoften misdiagnosed as infection

3Presentation

Symptomsdorsomedial midfoot pain + limp · may be asymptomatic · swelling, warmth, redness possible · point tenderness over navicular

Examantalgic gait, weight on lateral border of foot · no fever, no constitutional symptoms

Labs / biopsyunnecessary when no illness or constitutional symptoms
✗ Wrong options: ESR/CRP/cultures · biopsy

Classificationnone widely used

Kohler's disease
  • Mild / no severe pain→observation · NSAIDs · arch support orthotic
  • Pain with activity / failed orthotic→short-leg WALKING cast 4–6 wk
    (surgery never indicated)

Treatment - short leg cast

First lineNSAIDs short course · activity limitation · shoe modification / arch support

Castshort-leg walking (weight-bearing) cast for 4–6 wk → shortens duration of symptoms · 2 wk splint is insufficient (OB)

Weight bearingsafe, does not affect outcome · OB6130 accepts "restriction of weight bearing or short leg cast" · NWB 6 wk also relieves symptoms (OB211605)
✗ Wrong options: NWB cast (unnecessary, hard to enforce)

Long vs short castexcellent function regardless of casting technique
✗ Wrong options: long leg cast quicker

Surgerynot indicated
✗ Wrong options: core decompression · triple / subtalar fusion · curettage + graft · medial column lengthening · ORIF · I&D

PTdoes not aid recovery

Prognosis

Courseself-limiting · intermittent activity symptoms for 1–3 yr (✓ resolution in 1–3 yr; ✗ Wrong options: 6 months)

X-rayimproves 6–48 months from onset · navicular reconstitutes
✗ Wrong options: complete absorption

Long termno long-term disability · no midfoot collapse · no talonavicular arthritis · residual deformity almost always asymptomatic

Problem Treatment
Cervical kyphosis, no deficit Posterior cervical fusion in first 18 months

Knee dislocation Closed reduction + casting rarely works → open reduction + femoral shortening + collateral ligament excision

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence2nd most common pediatric elbow fracture (after supracondylar) · 17% of distal humerus fractures · 11% of elbow injuries · peak age 6 yr

Fracture linestarts posterior distal humeral metaphysis → distal + anterior across physis + epiphysis into joint · may extend into trochlear groove → unstable, prone to dislocation

Posteromedial dislocationrare association · FOOSH, slight flexion + adduction · LCL stays intact, attached to condylar fragment + radial neck
✗ Wrong options: LCL repair

Supplydistal humerus mainly from posterior anastomotic vessels · brachial artery anterior

ORIF ruleavoid posterior dissection → AVN of lateral condyle (and trochlea)

Centre Appears (yr) Fuses (yr)

External (lateral) epicondyle 11 12–14

5Management

Lateral condyle fracture
  • <2 mm all views, hinge intact→long arm cast 4–6 wk, weekly X-ray ×3 wk
  • 2–4 mm, cartilage intact→CRPP
  • >4 mm / incongruity→open reduction + fixation

Operative criteria

Castonly if <2 mm in ALL views + intact medial cartilaginous hinge · elbow ~90° · weekly X-rays (incl. internal oblique) for 3 wk · occasionally >6 wk

Surgery>2 mm on any view = unstable → fixation

Treatment (ORIF displaced)

Approachanterolateral (blood supply posterior) · dissection often done by injury · see joint reduction directly · metaphysis may not fit perfectly (plastic deformation)

Fixation2 smooth pins (3 if comminuted), parallel or divergent (most stable) · smooth pins because fixation crosses the physis · single cannulated screw for large fragment / nonunion → compression + early motion · no plate · 3–6 wk above-elbow cast

Closed reductionrarely succeeds for type 3 · CRPP can't inspect articular surface
✗ Wrong options: CRPP in widely displaced

With posteromedial dislocationopen reduction + percutaneous or internal fixation
✗ Wrong options: LCL repair · cast

Nonunion, cubitus valgus & tardy ulnar palsy

Stiffnessmost common · may be early sign of delayed/nonunion · 90% motion by 24 wk, full by 48 wk

Delayed unionnot healed after 6 wk · risk: seen >2 wk after injury

Nonunion causespull of wrist extensors (fragment rotates up to 180°, TO) · intra-articular synovial fluid · poor metaphyseal circulation / small metaphyseal fragment · instability in cast · risk ↑ nonoperative care

Nonunion scenario Treatment
Asymptomatic, isolated Observation
Painful / unstable / valgus + ulnar palsy ORIF of nonunion (minimal posterior stripping) ± bone graft (✗ Wrong options: fragment excision → valgus)
Painless nonunion (OB3302) In situ screw + bone graft
Untreated 4 months, painful ORIF (✗ Wrong options: late percutaneous pins · cast · MRI)
Well-established (TO) Osteotomy (varus) · avoid arthrotomy / articular realignment → stiffness, AVN

Nonunion goalunion of metaphyseal fragment, not joint surface

Cubitus valgusfrom nonunion (most common) or lateral physeal arrest · ~10% · less common than cubitus varus

Tardy ulnar nerve palsyslow stretch palsy from cubitus valgus · lateral condyle nonunion = most common cause (TO) · counsel ring + small finger numbness · also after cubitus varus (nerve dislocates anterior to medial epicondyle, FCU band, TO) · treat: supracondylar osteotomy after maturity + ulnar nerve transposition

AVN1–3 yr after fracture · from posterior dissection, most often in treatment of nonunion/delayed union

Fishtail deformitygap between medial + lateral ossification centres fails · usually no dysfunction · supracondylar osteotomy if needed

Lateral spur/overgrowth

Incidenceup to 50% regardless of treatment → counsel families in advance

Factssize correlates with initial displacement · independent of age · does NOT affect final ROM · gives pseudo-varus look, not true varus · no trimming asymptomatic spur · lateral periosteal realignment prevents it
✗ Wrong options: caused by surgery

Growth arrestrare · young → bar resection or osteotomy · older → complete epiphysiodesis + osteotomy

Prognosisworse than supracondylar (articular, missed diagnosis, nonunion) · with dislocation: slower ROM, same final ROM

Lateral CT scanogram Lateral scout Best with knee flexion contracture (others are coronal)

Epidemiology – age

Definitionidiopathic AVN of the proximal femoral epiphysis in children · self-limiting, heals + remodels

Medial Epicondylar Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 65 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequency3rd most common pediatric elbow fracture · up to 20% of elbow fractures (Orthobullets, OB) · 12% (OB5909) · 75% boys 9–14 yr · rising with youth sport

Mechanismavulsion: valgus stress + flexor-pronator contraction (throwers) · direct blow

Elbow dislocationpresent in 50–60% · most common fracture with pediatric elbow dislocation (33% of dislocations, Rasool) · fragment stays incarcerated in ~15%

Anatomy & ulnar nerve risk

Medial epicondyleapophysis (no longitudinal growth) · last distal humeral centre to fuse · origin of flexor-pronator mass + UCL · lies posteromedial, fragment displaces ANTERIORLY (flexor-pronator pull)

Flexor-pronator masspronator teres · FCR · palmaris longus · FDS · FCU
✗ Wrong options: pronator quadratus · brachioradialis · ECRL · brachialis

Blood supplyanterior: inferior ulnar collateral a. · posterior: superior + inferior ulnar collateral aa.

Ulnar nerveC8–T1, medial cord · splits two heads of FCU → runs between FDP and FCU · Guyon's canal, superficial to transverse carpal ligament · sensation palmar + dorsal ulnar 1½ digits · injury → ↓ wrist palmar flexion (FCU) + ring/small finger numbness

Centre Appears (Orthobullets) Fuses
Capitellum 1 12–14
Radial head 3 14–16
Medial epicondyle 5 16–18
Trochlea 7 12–14
Olecranon 9 15–17
Lateral epicondyle 11 12–14

CRITOE (OB214100 variant)1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9 yr · same text: medial side not ossified before ~5, trochlea complete ~9

3Presentation

Exammedial pain · valgus instability · ecchymosis · document ulnar nerve motor + sensory · generalised swelling → elbow probably dislocated

Classificationnone routine · acute (nondisplaced, minimally displaced, displaced, entrapped, through apophysis) vs chronic (tension stress)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Displacement assessment & imaging

ViewsAP + lateral + internal oblique · distal humeral axial view (beam 25° anterior to humeral axis) = most accurate X-ray for displacement

PitfallAP, lateral, IR views underestimate; fragment invisible on lateral if <10 mm

CTmost accurate, more radiation

Arthrogrambefore ossification · e.g. displaced medial condyle fracture in a 4-yr-old
✗ Wrong options: nondisplaced medial epicondyle at 6 · radial head at 5

Young child (<5 yr)unossified epicondyle → irreducible dislocation = incarcerated epicondyle until proven otherwise
✗ Wrong options: capitellum / radial head fracture (would be visible)

5Management

Medial epicondyle fracture
  • Incarcerated fragment / open / medial condyle extension→ORIF (absolute)
  • Thrower or gymnast >2–5 mm, ulnar nerve dysfunction, dislocation→consider ORIF (relative)
  • Others→long arm cast 1–3 wk at 90°, then early motion

Incarcerated fragment & post-reduction incongruity

Post-reduction incongruent ulnohumeral joint → interposed medial epicondyle
✗ Wrong options: annular ligament · brachialis · ulnar nerve

Roberts maneuverforearm supination + wrist/finger extension + valgus load → may pull fragment out
✗ Wrong options: Patterson (radial neck)

Persistent incarcerationabsolute indication for ORIF
✗ Wrong options: repeat closed reduction · CRPP · immobilization

With ulnar paresthesiaORIF
✗ Wrong options: observation · nerve transposition (not usually needed) · UCL reconstruction

Operative indications & union (displacement, throwers)

Absolute Relative
Incarcerated fragment Ulnar nerve dysfunction
Medial condyle / articular extension Displacement >2–15 mm (controversial) · 2–10 mm (OB)
Open fracture >2–5 mm in throwers / gymnasts (valgus stability)
— Associated dislocation · valgus instability

Non-oplong arm cast 1–3 wk, elbow 90° (AROM within ~1 wk) · historically <5 mm · RCTs: mean ~7 mm with equal outcomes · grip + ROM equal by 3 months

Non-op vs ORIFfunctional outcome equivalent (displacement <15 mm) · ↑ nonunion without surgery · union odds 9× with surgery
✗ Wrong options: cubitus varus · fishtail · ↑ ulnar neurapraxia

Throwing athlete, 7 mm or large displaced fragment → ORIF (highest union, valgus stability)
✗ Wrong options: excision (destabilises) · CRPP (ulnar nerve risk)

ORIF techniquemedial approach, supine, arm abducted 90° (or prone) · interval brachialis (musculocutaneous) / triceps (radial) · find + protect ulnar nerve proximal → distal · cannulated screw ± washer · K-wires for small fragments / young children · avoid comminution · bicortical screw risks radial nerve
✗ Wrong options: triceps/brachioradialis (lateral condyle) · brachialis/brachioradialis

6Complications

Asymptomatic fibrous union

Nonunioncommon after non-op · majority asymptomatic · poor correlation with function
✗ Wrong options: Tinel · valgus pain · malalignment

Ulnar nerve injury10–16% (~10% OB) · neurapraxia after dislocation usually resolves · delayed palsy from missed fracture recovers if treated promptly

Missed incarcerationesp. young child with unossified epicondyle

Stiffnessmost common: loss of a few degrees of extension · ↑ with prolonged immobilization

Prognosisgood to excellent with either treatment

Definitionradial head dislocation + proximal ulna fracture or plastic deformation of ulna

Ruleelbow X-rays for every forearm / ulna fracture · forearm X-rays for every radial head dislocation · orthogonal films of whole forearm, wrist + elbow

Radiocapitellar lineline along radial neck axis passes through centre of capitellum on every view · any deviation = Monteggia

Type Ulna apex Radial head Cast position
I Anterior Anterior (most common in children) 110° flexion + full supination
II Posterior Posterior Full extension

Pediatric Monteggia
  • Length-stable ulna (plastic / greenstick / buckle) + stable RC joint→closed reduction + long arm cast
  • Length-unstable ulna or RC unstable→fix ulna (IM nail or plate) + closed RC reduction
  • RC joint irreducible after anatomic ulna→open reduction (annular ligament block)
  • Bado IV · open · ≥10 yr unstable · closed physes→operative

Acute treatment - restore ulnar length

First considerationreduce + maintain ulnar length and alignment → radial head usually reduces itself
✗ Wrong options: open RC reduction first · annular ligament reconstruction · RC pin

Closed reduction firsttraction · Type I: flexion is main maneuver (+ supination) · prompt reduction → delay makes it difficult/impossible
✗ Wrong options: plate · pins · splint without reduction

✗ Wrong options: tightens biceps

Operative indication
Types I–III with unstable radial head after reduction Yes
Ulnar length not maintained (complete, comminuted, displaced) Yes
Acute Bado IV (even if head reduces) Yes
Open fracture · ≥10 yr unstable · closed physes (adult ORIF) Yes
Loss of RC reduction on follow-up Yes
Incomplete ulna fracture + reduced radial head No (cast)

Ulna fixation choicetransverse / short oblique → IM flexible nail · long oblique / comminuted → open reduction + plate (nails won't prevent shortening)

✗ Wrong options: RC pin (breaks) · IM nail · repeat closed reduction

Key radiology findings

X-raymonitor scoliosis / kyphosis, hips, fractures · standing AP ankle → tibiotalar valgus / talar tilt

MRIany change in neuro exam or rapid curve progression → urgent MRI for tethered cord

5Management

Hip dislocation management & functional level

Causeparalytic: unopposed flexors + adductors · most common at L3 · can be teratologic

Rulefunction depends on neurologic level, NOT hip status · open reduction → high redislocation + complications, no functional gain · reduced hips may even hurt more

Scenario Treatment
Thoracic / L3 and above Leave dislocated · observation + ROM to prevent contractures (✗ Wrong options: Pavlik · spica (promote contractures) · open reduction)
L4 Most controversial · may consider if unilateral (OB) · L4 household ambulator with full ROM → no intervention
Contractures Contracture release (improves ROM → ambulation)

Hip abduction contracturepelvic obliquity, scoliosis → Ober-Yount (proximal fascia lata + distal ITB release) if limits sitting/bracing

Hip flexion contracturehigh lumbar / thoracic → anterior release (iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus, TFL) if >40°

Knee

Problem Treatment
Weak quads KAFO
Flexion contracture >20° Hamstring lengthening ± posterior capsulotomy · older / failed → supracondylar extension osteotomy
Extension contracture Serial casting to 90° flexion
Tibial torsion <5 yr observe + orthotics · >5 yr distal tibial derotation osteotomy

Foot & ankle deformity

Incidence60–90% (low nerve roots)

Clubfoot30%, most common · rigid + insensate · serial casting first (high complication rate) → posteromedial-lateral release at 12–18 months · rigid clubfoot, no muscles below knee → soft-tissue releases for plantigrade AFO foot · releases beat transfers
✗ Wrong options: tendon transfers (nothing to transfer) · Botox · triple

Calcaneus / dorsiflexion (L5, sacral)unopposed tibialis anterior · bulky heel pad · posterior transfer of tibialis anterior if bracing can't get neutral
✗ Wrong options: triple arthrodesis

Planovalgusdistal tibial valgus (mature) → supramalleolar osteotomy · hindfoot valgus → calcaneal lengthening + TAL · also calcaneal slide, subtalar arthrodesis, Grice · tibiotalar valgus missed pre-op → poor surgical result
✗ Wrong options: equinus · calcaneovalgus · forefoot abduction

Arthrodesisavoid (skin sores, Charcot) · triple only for severe deformity with sensate feet

Spinal deformity & kyphectomy

Scoliosisneurogenic or congenital · 100% with thoracic level · rapid progression → tethered cord · bracing ineffective → ASF + PSF with pelvic fixation (anterior needed — dysplastic posterior elements) · high pseudarthrosis · infection 15–25% (poor soft tissue)

Congenital kyphosis10–15% · progressive · gibbus → recurrent skin breakdown sitting · kyphectomy + fusion + posterior instrumentation · check shunt function first (shunt failure intra-op can kill)

Both curves progressive → ASF + PSF with pelvic fixation + kyphectomy
✗ Wrong options: kyphectomy alone · bracing

Multidisciplinary team↓ postoperative complications
✗ Wrong options: ↓ deformity progression · ↓ revision

6Complications

Pathologic fracture & neuropathic joints

Fracturesdisuse osteopenia · ↑ with higher level · hip + knee, age 3–7 · fever, warmth, erythema, swelling → mimics infection / cellulitis / osteomyelitis → get X-rays · not immunocompromised · treat with short well-padded splint/cast · avoid long casting (↑ osteopenia, refracture)

Prognosisuntreated infants 90–100% mortality · L3 and above mostly wheelchair · L5 good community ambulation

NIH 1987 — ≥2 of

Criterion Detail
Café-au-lait ≥6, >5 mm prepubertal / >15 mm postpubertal · smooth "coast of California" border

Orthopaedicanterolateral tibial bowing / pseudarthrosis (most common presentation, more than forearm) · forearm (radius/ulna) bowing + pseudarthrosis · hemihypertrophy / limb overgrowth · scoliosis, kyphosis · atlantoaxial instability · verrucous hyperplasia

Plexiform neurofibromapathognomonic · 4% (Orthobullets) · 25% (Crawford) · limb overgrowth · → neurofibrosarcoma / MPNST

Congenital pseudarthrosis of tibia

Association50% of anterolateral bowing have NF1 (55% OB) · 10% of NF1 have it · pseudarthrosis = NF1 (✗ Wrong options: NF2) · dysplastic constricted diaphysis (✗ Wrong options: abuse · OI II · osteopetrosis)

  • No fracture / pseudarthrosis→total contact (clamshell) orthosis
    (no remodeling expected; osteotomy contraindicated)
  • Fracture / pseudarthrosis→resect + bone graft + fixation (IM rod / free fibula / Ilizarov)

Amputationafter 3 failed surgeries · Syme (calf atrophic and scarred)

Ruleexclude fracture before manipulating

Klumpketraction on abducted arm / arm presentation (breech)

Obstetric brachial plexus palsy
  • All→observation + daily passive ROM by parents (first 3 months)
  • Antigravity biceps by 3 months→continue therapy, expect full recovery
  • No biceps by 3 months, postganglionic→neuroma excision + sural graft (3–9 months)
  • Preganglionic (Horner, phrenic, winging, rhomboids)→nerve transfer at ~3 months

Prognosis (biceps recovery by 3 months, Horner)

Overall90% recover without surgery · recovery up to 2 yr · most with elbow flexion by 3 months normal by 18 months

GoodErb palsy (absent shoulder abduction + ER, intact wrist/hand = best) · antigravity biceps + deltoid by 3 months · early biceps twitch · elbow flexion by 3 months → recovery up to 100% · partial antigravity strength in first 2 months

✗ Wrong options: shoulder abduction · ER · elbow extension · axillary at 1 yr

No prognostic valueclavicle fracture · age at diagnosis · head circumference

Lesion Surgery Timing
Postganglionic (rupture, neuroma-in-continuity) Neuroma excision + sural nerve grafting (shorter grafts <10 cm better · no direct repair) 3–9 months (Gilbert: biceps < MRC 3 at 3 months → surgery at 4–6 months, TO)
Preganglionic (avulsion) Nerve transfer / neurotization (grafting impossible) ~3 months (or less)
Global palsy + Horner Microsurgery ~3 months (TO) · flail + Horner at 1 month (OB)

Nerve transferfascicles from one nerve into another nerve's motor branch · neurotization = fascicles directly into neuromuscular junction

Transfersulnar fascicle → biceps branch (Oberlin) + median fascicle → brachialis branch · accessory → suprascapular (abduction) · intercostals → musculocutaneous (elbow flexion) · triceps (long head) / thoracodorsal → axillary · contralateral C7 in total avulsion

Olecranon Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 74 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiologyuncommon · <5% of pediatric fractures (US) · peak 5–10 yr

Mechanism

Mechanism Result
FOOSH, elbow FLEXED (most common) Triceps + brachialis tension → transverse fracture
FOOSH, elbow extended Varus/valgus → longitudinal lines · varus → radial head dislocation · valgus → radial neck fracture
Direct blow (least common) Shear → anterior tension failure, distal fragment anterior, posterior periosteum intact

Locationmetaphyseal (most common) · physeal · apophyseal (intra- or extra-articular)

Association with osteogenesis imperfecta

OIolecranon (avulsion) fracture after trivial trauma = highly suspicious ("pathognomonic" per OB) for OI
✗ Wrong options: NF · abuse · ABC

Ossification

Olecranon apophysisappears 9 yr · fuses 15–17 yr · fuses anterior → posterior · partial closure mimics fracture

Age 5 girlcapitellum, radial head, medial epicondyle ossifying · trochlea, olecranon, lateral epicondyle still cartilaginous → any olecranon disruption = fracture

3Presentation

Symptomsposterior swelling · pain · can't actively extend elbow

Exampalpable gap / crepitus · gapping → posterior periosteum torn → unstable · abrasion suggests direct blow

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral

Physis vs fracturephysis is oblique; fracture usually transverse · patella cubiti (secondary ossification centre) ≠ fracture

Look forradial neck, lateral condyle, distal radius injuries

5Management

Treatment - tension band

Fracture Treatment
Stress fracture / apophysitis (throwers) NSAIDs, rest, immobilise, avoid resisted extension
Minimally displaced, extensor mechanism intact Long arm splint/cast 3–4 wk · repeat X-ray at 7 days
Displaced · lost posterior periosteum · comminuted ORIF

Fixation

Option Note
Tension band wiring (AO, axial K-wires) ✓ standard for displaced · wires stronger for high loads · high hardware removal rate
Tension band suture (PDS / FiberWire) ± oblique lag screw Metaphyseal fractures
Plate + screws Comminuted with partly fused centres / near maturity
Axial screw ± wire Risk of physeal disruption with IM lag screw

Never in childrenESIN · CRPP · casting a displaced fracture · fragment excision + triceps advancement (elderly, low-demand only)

6Complications

Listnonunion · delayed union · compartment syndrome · ulnar neurapraxia (pseudarthrosis, poor fixation) · loss of reduction · stiffness

How it's asked

"Olecranon fracture after minimal trauma — suspect?"osteogenesis imperfecta
✗ Wrong options: abuse · NF

"5-yr, displaced olecranon fracture?"ORIF with tension band
✗ Wrong options: ESIN · cast · plate

"10-yr skateboard FOOSH, displaced?"tension band construct with wires
✗ Wrong options: IM lag screw (physis) · CRPP · excision + triceps advancement

Osteogenesis Imperfecta

Pediatrics · 75 / 112

1Basics

Genetics & type I collagen defect

Type I collagenmain structural protein of bone, skin, tendon, dentin, sclera · triple helix = 2 α1 chains (COL1A1) + 1 α2 chain (COL1A2) · glycine every 3rd residue allows helix

MutationCOL1A1 / COL1A2 in 90% (Orthobullets) · 85% (OB) · missense glycine substitution in procollagen → abnormal cross-linking · dominant-negative effect → severe phenotype
✗ Wrong options: nonsense

Pathophysiology↓ collagen secretion + abnormal collagen → insufficient osteoid by physeal + periosteal osteoblasts → bone can't remodel
✗ Wrong options: ↑ secretion · "uninterrupted remodeling"

Quantitative vs qualitativequantitative (half normal amount, haploinsufficiency) → mild (type I) · qualitative (glycine substitution) → severe (II, III, IV)

InheritanceAD most common · AR forms (VI, VII, CRTAP / LEPRE1 — severe/lethal, no primary collagen defect) · not X-linked recessive · AR forms more severe

Defect (distractors) Disease
Glycine substitution in procollagen OI
Gsα Fibrous dysplasia
Vitamin C (hydroxylation) Scurvy
Sulfate transporter Diastrophic dysplasia
Homogentisic acid oxidase Alkaptonuria
Osteoclast (carbonic anhydrase / M-CSF) Osteopetrosis
Activating FGFR3 Achondroplasia
Type V collagen (basement membrane) Ehlers-Danlos (OB)
N-Ac-Gal-6-sulfate sulfatase Morquio
EXT (prehypertrophic chondrocytes) MHE
COMP / type II collagen Pseudoachondroplasia / MED, SED

Sillence classification

Type Inheritance Collagen Sclera Features
I AD Quantitative Blue Mildest, most common · preschool (tarda) · hearing loss 50% · A (no DI) / B (DI)
II AD (Orthobullets, TO) · AR (OB) Qualitative Blue Perinatal lethal
III AD (Orthobullets, TO) · AR (OB) Qualitative Normal Most severe survivable · fractures at birth · progressive short stature
IV AD Qualitative Normal Moderate · bowing, vertebral fractures · hearing normal · A/B by teeth
V AD No collagen defect (IFITM5) — Congenital anterolateral radial head dislocation · hypertrophic callus · IOM ossification (forearm, leg)
VI AR No collagen defect (SERPINF1) — Like IV · ↑ ALP · fish-scale lamellae · responds poorly to bisphosphonates → denosumab (TO)
VII AR No collagen defect (CRTAP) — Rhizomelia, coxa vara · severe

90% fall into types I + IV · TO adds VIII (LEPRE1), IX (PPIB), X (SERPINH1), XI (FKBP10, Bruck), XV (WNT1)

Recurrent fractures + hearing loss in a child → type I (TO) · hearing loss 50–92%, rare in type IV

3Presentation

Orthopaedicfragility fractures (heal normally, don't remodel → bowing, saber shin) · ligamentous laxity · short stature · scoliosis · codfish vertebrae · basilar invagination · coxa vara (10%) · congenital radial head dislocation

Olecranon apophyseal avulsionmost common first presenting sign · minor trauma (e.g. pushing a sibling) · bilateral → work up OI · high contralateral risk · ORIF if displaced
✗ Wrong options: abuse · Noonan · vitamin D

Non-orthopaedicblue sclera · triangular facies · hearing loss (50% adults; conductive, sensorineural, mixed) · dentinogenesis imperfecta (brown/blue opalescent teeth, primary > secondary) · wormian bones · hypermetabolism → malignant hyperthermia risk · thin skin, bruising · MVP, aortic regurgitation

Fracture coursefewer with age, usually stop after puberty

4Diagnosis & Classification

Radiographic recognition

X-raythin cortices · generalized osteopenia · saber shins / bowing · wormian bones on skull · coxa vara

Bisphosphonate zebra linesdense parallel horizontal metaphyseal bands (growth arrest lines) after 8–10 wk of cyclical therapy · migrate to diaphysis, vanish after physeal closure
✗ Wrong options: from growth hormone (TO false statement)

Diagnosisfamily history + clinical + radiographic · no commercial test · labs normal (mildly ↑ ALP) · skin biopsy / fibroblast culture for collagen (diagnostic per TO; positive in 80% of type IV) · iliac crest biopsy · prenatal PCR on chorionic villi at 8–12 wk (TO)

Histology↑ Haversian canal + lacunar diameter · replicated cement lines · ↑ osteoblasts + osteoclasts · ↓ trabeculae · thin cortex · woven bone, crowded osteocytes (TO)

5Management

Bisphosphonates

Indicationmost OI · ↓ fracture rate, ↓ pain (1–6 wk), ↑ ambulation, ↑ lumbar BMD

Mechanisminhibit osteoclast resorption (N-bisphosphonate → FPP synthase → osteoclast apoptosis) · endosteal resorption ↓ while periosteal formation continues → cortex thickens
✗ Wrong options: ↑ mineralization · better collagen · ↑ turnover · RANKL antibody

Effectcortical diameter ↑88% · cancellous volume ↑46% · no effect on scoliosis

Pamidronate1 mg/kg/day × 3 days every 2–4 months · zoledronic acid every 6 months (TO)

IM roddingbisphosphonate-free period around surgery (impairs osteotomy healing >> fracture healing)

Othersgrowth hormone (adjunct) · BMT (some success) · denosumab (type VI, refractory) · teriparatide adults only (osteosarcoma risk) · early bracing to limit deformity

Fracture management - intramedullary rodding

Situation Treatment
<2 yr Treat as non-OI child (closed)
>2 yr Telescoping rods (Bailey-Dubow, Sheffield, Fassier-Duval) — grow with child · preferred (TO)
Deformity beyond tolerance after reduction Load-sharing IM device
Severe bowing Sofield-Miller (shish-kebab / "seekh kebab") multiple osteotomies + IM rod

IM rod over plateplates → stress shielding + periprosthetic fracture · OI not at higher nonunion risk

Teen forearm (14–15 yr)>10° won't remodel → open reduction + IM rod
✗ Wrong options: plate · cast · realignment osteotomy (that's for chronic deformity)

Non-telescopicRush, Williams rods

Spine (basilar invagination, scoliosis)

Scoliosiscurves early + progress · VC falls to 40% at 60°

Curve Treatment
<45° Observe
>45° mild OI PSF
>35° severe OI (thin bones) PSF early
Bracing Ineffective, not recommended (rib fragility)

PSFallograft (little autograft) · large blood loss · ASF only in very young (crankshaft) · no anterior approach (pulmonary) · not telescoping rods (long bones)

Basilar invaginationodontoid into foramen magnum · severe forms · 3rd–4th decade (teens possible) · apnea, altered consciousness, ataxia, myelopathy (finger escape, Hoffmann) · → brainstem compression, hydrocephalus, syrinx · transoral decompression + posterior fusion · also Klippel-Feil, achondroplasia, Morquio, SED
✗ Wrong options: AAI (Down)

X vs Y

OI Non-accidental trauma
Sclera / teeth Blue / DI Normal
Family history Fractures —
Signature fracture Olecranon apophysis Metaphyseal corner, posterior ribs
Bones Osteopenic, wormian Normal

Osteomyelitis - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 76 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence1 in 5,000 children <13 yr · mean age 6.6 yr · boys 2.5× · common in healthy children · first decade (rich metaphyseal supply, immature immunity) · mortality 50% → <1% with antibiotics

Routehematogenous seeding of the METAPHYSIS
✗ Wrong options: epiphysis · direct inoculation

Trauma history30% (Orthobullets) · 20–40% (OB) · bacteremia source: skin, otitis, pharyngitis, tooth brushing / dental care

Risk factorsdiabetes · hemoglobinopathy · JRA · chronic renal disease · immune compromise · varicella

Pathophysiology

Metaphysiscapillaries make sharp turns into venous sinusoids → sluggish, turbulent flow · low pH + low O2 near physis · spread via Haversian + Volkmann canals

Pus through metaphyseal cortex → subperiosteal abscess

Pus through INTRA-ARTICULAR metaphysis → septic arthritis · hip, shoulder, elbow, ankle ("SHEA") · not knee (extra-articular metaphysis)

Infantstransphyseal vessels → epiphyseal osteomyelitis + septic arthritis · <1 yr (Orthobullets) · <2 yr (TO)

Intra-articular metaphysis & septic arthritis spread

Bone (intra-articular metaphysis/physis) Joint
Proximal femur Hip
Proximal humerus Shoulder
Proximal radius / radial neck Elbow
Distal fibula / distal lateral tibia Ankle
✗ Wrong option: distal femur, proximal tibia Knee — least likely
✗ Wrong option: distal radius Wrist — not (TO)

Organisms & antibiotics (MRSA, PVL, GAS, Pseudomonas)

Setting Organism
All children S. aureus (90% Song & Sloboda · 70% Blyth)
Neonate Group B strep
Young child Kingella kingae (↑) · most common SA organism 3 months–5 yr · PCR-negative cases
Puncture wound of foot (through sneaker) Pseudomonas (100% in Puffinbarger)
After varicella Group A β-hemolytic strep
Sickle cell Salmonella
Unvaccinated H. influenzae (now rare)
TB Extrapulmonary in children · spine 50%, large joints 25%, long bones 11%

PVL (Panton-Valentine leukocidin)CA-MRSA (also some MSSA) cytotoxin · <5% of S. aureus · complex/multifocal infection, prolonged fever, abscess, DVT, sepsis, necrotizing pneumonia · lyses neutrophils (indirect)
✗ Wrong options: Strep · S. epidermidis · Klebsiella

CoagulaseS. aureus factor that activates prothrombin → thrombin → fibrin clot → DVT (✓ direct cause; PVL indirect)
✗ Wrong options: adhesins · eDNA (biofilm) · vWF binding protein

Other virulence (distractors)superantigens (toxic shock) · biofilm · protein A (binds IgG Fc)

MRSA predictorsT >38°C · WBC >12,000 · Hct <34% · CRP >13 mg/L → MRSA probability 4/4 = 92% · 3 = 45% · 2 = 10% · 1 = 1%

3Presentation

Symptomslimp / refusal to bear weight · usually not toxic · ± fever · prior antibiotics mask

Examwarm, swollen, point tenderness (check pelvis, spine) · motion limited by pain · pelvic compression pain (Gaenslen) → pelvic osteomyelitis

Neonatefailure to thrive, multifocal (shoulder + hips) → ultrasound of hip + shoulder
✗ Wrong options: MRI first · Pavlik

4Diagnosis & Classification

Workup - aspiration negative, MRI & US

Labs

Test Fact
CRP ↑ in 98% · rises in 6 h · best to monitor response · should fall by 48–72 h · normalises ~1 wk (Orthobullets) / 1 month (OB)
ESR ↑ in 90% · peaks 3–5 days · falls too slowly (normal ~3 wk) · unreliable in neonates + sickle cell
WBC ↑ in only ~25% (✓ "often normal")
Procalcitonin ↑ in 58% · falls with effective treatment
Blood culture + in 30–50% (✗ Wrong options: 75–80%)
Bone aspirate culture + in 50–70% (51–73%, 50–85% OB)

Most likely abnormal test → CRP

Imaging

Modality Fact
X-ray Early normal / soft-tissue edema · periosteal new bone 5–7 days · osteolysis 10–14 days · metaphyseal rarefaction 1–2 wk
MRI Gold standard · T1 ↓, T2 ↑, gadolinium ↑ · sensitivity 88–100% · shows abscess · plan surgery
Bone scan 92% sensitive · non-focal toddler, multifocal · cold scan = aggressive / osteonecrosis
CT Later bone changes (✗ Wrong options: study of choice)
US Neonate effusion, subperiosteal collection

Fever + ↑ CRP + negative joint aspirate (e.g. 1,000–9,000 cells) → MRI (osteomyelitis / subperiosteal abscess)
✗ Wrong options: arthrotomy · observe · oral antibiotics

Septic joint excludedsynovial WBC <50,000 essentially rules out (Kocher 2/4 ≈ 40%)

Suspected SA of shoulder/hip/elbow/anklepre-op MRI ↓ repeat surgery · don't delay unstable patient
✗ Wrong options: MRSA low risk · negative PCR rules out

Subacute osteomyelitis vs tumour - biopsy

Subacutebone pain + X-ray changes, no systemic signs · ↑ host resistance / ↓ virulence / prior antibiotics · afebrile, mild pain, normal WBC, ↑ ESR

ClassificationIA/IB lucency · II metaphyseal with cortical loss · III diaphyseal · IV onion skin · V epiphyseal · VI spinal

Biopsy + culturewhen diagnosis unclear / rule out tumour (Ewing, osteosarcoma, EG, lymphoma) · send tissue for pathology at every debridement

Brodie abscess – subacute osteomyelitis

Typesubacute (TO) · age 10–20 yr · proximal tibia most common · metaphysis (tibia, femur) · S. aureus

X-raysolitary well-circumscribed lucency with sclerotic rim at metaphyseal-epiphyseal junction

MRIpenumbra sign: rim of vascular granulation tissue, higher T1 signal than cavity (TO)
✗ Wrong options: hydatid · hemangioma

Labsnormal or mildly ↑
✗ Wrong options: "elevated blood counts" (TO false statement)

Treatmentsurgical debridement / curettage (± graft) + antibiotics
✗ Wrong options: wide resection + chemo · empiric antibiotics alone · cast

TB osteomyelitis

Featuresconstitutional symptoms, night sweats · normal WBC, ↑ ESR · PPD + · osteopenia + subchondral erosions · polyostotic

Diagnosisbiopsy: caseating granulomas, giant cells · Ziehl-Neelsen ("red snappers") · Löwenstein-Jensen culture

Treatmentmulti-agent antibiotics ≥1 yr · rarely debridement (sinus risk)

5Management

Pediatric acute hematogenous osteomyelitis
  • No abscess → aspirate / biopsy for culture→empiric IV antibiotics
    (improves within 48 h → no surgery; IV → oral)
  • Subperiosteal / intraosseous abscess, pus aspirated→I&D + antibiotics
  • No improvement 48–72 h or CRP not falling → repeat MRI→I&D

Surgical indications & subperiosteal abscess

Surgerysubperiosteal or deep abscess · pus on aspiration · failure of appropriate antibiotics (48–72 h) · chronic infection / sequestrum · adjacent septic arthritis

Not failureimproving at 24 h · on wrong drug (e.g. gentamicin for S. aureus) · no trial yet

Worsening at 2–3 days on antibiotics → subperiosteal abscess
✗ Wrong options: CRMO · atypical organism · Brodie

Subperiosteal abscess sitesfemur 23–29%, tibia 19–26%

Septic shock + MRSA + abscess → fluids + antibiotics + urgent I&D
✗ Wrong options: wait for cultures

Septic hip with adjacent osteomyelitisstraight to OR debridement (cultures intra-op) · complication rate 38% vs <1% isolated SA

Techniqueevacuate pus, debride, drill intraosseous collections, culture + pathology · drains or pack, re-look in 2–3 days · remove sequestrum in chronic

Antibiotics before culturesonly if septic / unstable

Antibiotic choice

Situation Drug
Low MRSA prevalence Nafcillin / oxacillin (PBP binders)
High MRSA prevalence Clindamycin (50S) or vancomycin
Sepsis / severe / MRSA Vancomycin — binds D-Ala-D-Ala
Gram-negative rods + 3rd-gen cephalosporin
<1 month (Copley) Ampicillin/sulbactam + gentamicin
1–3 months Vancomycin + ceftriaxone

DurationIV 4–6 wk (Orthobullets, controversial) · 3–4 wk (OB) · 20 days = 30 days for MSSA/strep · MRSA: 24–48 h IV → 4–6 wk oral (OB)

Oral vs PICC IVequal cure · PICC → more ED visits / rehospitalisation, ↑ cost

Monitoring response - CRP

Best early indicatorserial CRP · peaks ~day 2 post-op then falls
✗ Wrong options: ESR · WBC · MRI · X-ray · procalcitonin rise

6Complications

DVT with MRSA osteomyelitis

Risk factorsCRP >6 mg/dL · surgical treatment · age >8 yr · MRSA
✗ Wrong options: fever >38.5°C

OrganismMRSA · PVL endothelial injury + coagulase
✗ Wrong options: MSSA · Kingella · TB

Actioncalf pain / swelling → venous duplex US · therapeutic anticoagulation · MRSA often needs repeat I&D

Chronic osteomyelitis (sequestrum, involucrum)

Sequestrumnecrotic bone walled off from blood supply = nidus of chronic infection

Involucrumnew periosteal bone around sequestrum

Brodie abscesschronic abscess walled by sclerosis + fibrous tissue

Late growth disturbance

Physeal damage → LLD + angular deformity (∝ physeal destruction) · LLD apparent ~9 yr average · follow to maturity with standing full-length X-rays

Othersseptic arthritis (I&D) · meningitis · pathologic fracture · AVN · chronic / multifocal infection

X vs Y

Acute osteomyelitis Subacute (Brodie)
Systemic Fever, ↑ CRP Afebrile, normal WBC, ↑ ESR
Age Mean 6.6 10–20
X-ray Normal early Lucency + sclerotic rim
Treatment IV antibiotics ± I&D if abscess Curettage + antibiotics

Osteopetrosis

Pediatrics · 77 / 112

1Basics

Definition"marble bone disease" · defective osteoclastic resorption → dense but brittle bone, obliterated medullary canals

PrevalenceAD 1 in 20,000 · AR 1 in 200,000 · AD = most common · 75% penetrance, may skip generations

Pathophysiology (carbonic anhydrase II, osteoclast acidification)

Core defectosteoclast cannot acidify Howship's lacuna → no HCl → hydroxyapatite not dissolved → bone stays thick, disorganised
✗ Wrong options: ↑ remodeling · ↓ osteoblasts · ↓ hydroxyapatite

Carbonic anhydrase IICO2 + H2O → H+ + HCO3− · H+ pumped across ruffled border

Causescarbonic anhydrase II loss-of-function or chloride channel dysfunction (Orthobullets) · CA II "most common" (OB4418, OB219284) · proton pump 60%, CLCN7 12%, CA II <5% (OB4814) — read the options

Defect (distractors) Disease

Classification

Type Inheritance Defect Course
Malignant (infantile) AR (11q13) Proton pump / Cl channel Fatal early without BMT
Intermediate AR Carbonic anhydrase II / Cl channel —
Benign AD (most common) Cl channel Normal life · type II = Albers-Schönberg (anemia, fractures, early OA) · most seen by orthopaedists

ADO I vs III: diffuse sclerosis, esp. cranial vault · II: rugger jersey spine, bone-in-bone iliac wings, skull base

TOlists AD, AR and X-linked recessive forms

3Presentation

Clinical features & complications

AR (malignant)severe anemia from infancy (marrow encroachment) → bleeding, infections · hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary hematopoiesis) · macrocephaly · progressive blindness + deafness · dental abscess, mandibular osteomyelitis · death from bleeding / infection

AD (benign)often asymptomatic until low-energy (transverse) fracture · anemia · low back pain (↑ spondylolysis) · early hip OA · normal height · high risk of cranial nerve palsy

Cranial nerve palsiesforaminal overgrowth · optic > auditory > trigeminal > facial

Fractureslifelong 40–50% (40–60% OB) · LE > UE > axial · transverse · delayed union, malunion

Associatedcoxa vara (femoral neck nonunion / stress fractures) · osteomyelitis (poor marrow vascularity, ↓ WBC function) · carpal tunnel · Caffey disease (listed by Orthobullets) · seizures

NOT associatedvertebral compression fractures

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

General↑ cortical thickness · ↑ overall density · loss of medullary canal · bone-in-bone (endobones — pathognomonic, TO)

Signs"rugger jersey" / sandwich spine (dense endplate bands) · Erlenmeyer flask distal femur + proximal humerus · block femoral metaphysis · coxa vara · thick skull base, poor sinuses

Not osteopetrosisdripping candle wax (melorheostosis) · Paget pelvis · bone infarct

LabsAR: ↑ acid phosphatase, ± ↑ PTH, ± ↑ Ca · anemia ± thrombocytopenia · AD: normal

Histologyosteoclasts lack ruffled border + clear zone · islands of calcified cartilage in trabeculae · empty lacunae, plugged Haversian canals

Rugger jersey spine Osteopetrotic femur

Erlenmeyer flask deformity – differential

Definitionconstricted diaphysis + flared metaphysis (undertubulation)

Causesosteopetrosis · Gaucher, Niemann-Pick · thalassemia, sickle cell · Pyle (metaphyseal dysplasia) · craniotubular dysplasias · achondroplasia · fibrous dysplasia · Ollier · MHE · rickets · RA · lead toxicity

NOTLangerhans cell histiocytosis · Sprengel · melorheostosis · DEH (TO)

5Management

Medical

Form Treatment
AR malignant Bone marrow transplant (only durable cure, TO) · high-dose calcitriol
AD Interferon γ-1b
Supportive (TO) Erythropoietin (darbepoetin), vitamin D, corticosteroids
✗ Wrong option: alendronate Inappropriate — bisphosphonate further suppresses osteoclasts

Cranial nerve impingementneurosurgical decompression

Fracture management

Fracture Treatment
Diaphyseal long bone, upper extremity Non-op: prolonged casting, NWB · slow healing, limited remodeling → malunion, refracture
Proximal femur ORIF with plate + screws — avoid IM devices (can't pass reamer) · ↑ union, ↓ coxa vara

Techniqueslow steady drilling, constant cooling, frequent drill-bit changes · ↑ hardware failure

ArthroplastyTHA: cannulated reamers under fluoro, short-stem uncemented femur, small sharp acetabular reamers + screws · TKA: consider navigation

6Complications

Refracture (brittle bone, hardware failure) · infection (↓ vascularity) · malunion · nonunion

Osteopetrosis Melorheostosis
X-ray Diffuse density, bone-in-bone, rugger jersey Dripping candle wax cortical hyperostosis

Patella Sleeve Fracture

Pediatrics · 79 / 112

1Basics

Definitioncartilage "sleeve" pulled off the ossified patella ± small bone fleck · unique to skeletally immature

Epidemiology<1% of pediatric fractures but >50% of pediatric patella fractures · boys 5:1 · 8–12 yr (ossification nearly complete)

Mechanismindirect: powerful quadriceps contraction on a flexed knee (stumble, pop) · not a direct blow · superior pole: patella pushed down → intra-articular dislocation (OB)

Anatomylargest sesamoid · ossifies 3–5 yr · lateral facet larger · cartilage up to 1 cm · quadriceps 3 layers (rectus superficial, vasti middle, intermedius deep) · blood supply mainly inferior pole (geniculate ring)

Locationinferior pole most common · superior pole least common

3Presentation

Symptomssevere pain, can't bear weight, painful pop

Examhemarthrosis / tense effusion · high-riding patella or palpable gap = extensor mechanism disrupted · extensor lag / can't straight-leg raise

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP, lateral, tangential

Findingssmall bone flecks at superior or inferior pole (easily missed) · inferior sleeve → patella ALTA · superior sleeve → patella BAJA + slight anterior tilt of superior pole

Rulefragment is much larger than it looks (mostly cartilage)

MRI / ultrasoundwhen diagnosis unclear (soon after injury)

5Management

Treatment - ORIF

Situation Treatment
Nondisplaced, extensor mechanism intact (rare) · gap <2 mm Cylinder cast 6 wk
>2–3 mm displacement or step-off · disrupted extensor mechanism ORIF

ORIFmedial parapatellar approach · repair retinaculum / tendon · transosseous sutures through bone tunnels · modified tension band · suture anchors · screws · K-wires if fragment large · cylinder cast in extension 2–3 wk

Superior sleevesuture between bony fragments through tunnels in the larger distal fragment (fracture is distal to quadriceps insertion)
✗ Wrong options: quadriceps tendon repair · immobiliser

Neverexcision of the fragment (cartilage is large) · patellar tendon repair to tubercle · partial patellectomy · knee arthroscopy · PT alone · cast with extensor lag

6Complications

Listpatella alta · extensor lag · quadriceps atrophy · malunion · nonunion · painful hardware · worse with comminution + displacement

Pediatric Abuse

Pediatrics · 80 / 112

1Basics

Most common presentations & epidemiology

Burden>1 million substantiated victims/yr (US) · 15–42 per 1,000 children · >1,200 deaths/yr · ~⅓ of abused children see an orthopaedic surgeon

Mortality2nd most common cause of death in children >1 yr (after accidental injury) · after SIDS at 1–5 months (OB) · death usually from head trauma

Age90% of abuse fractures <5 yr · 50% of fractures <1 yr · 30% of fractures <3 yr (Orthobullets) · 10–15% <3 yr (Kempe, TO) · most common <3 yr

FemurNAT = most common cause of femur fracture in non-ambulatory infant · NAI up to 35% of femur fractures <3 yr, 40–90% <1 yr (OB)

Type (overlap) %
Neglect (✓ most common) 78%
Physical 18%
Sexual 9% (~10% TO)
Psychological 8%
Presentation Rank
Skin lesions (bruises in various stages, burns, cuts) Most common (✗ Wrong options: fractures)
Fractures 2nd
Head injury Most long-term morbidity (✗ Wrong options: burns)

Fracture locationhumerus > tibia > femur · diaphyseal 4× more common than metaphyseal · single transverse diaphyseal fracture classic (TO)
✗ Wrong options: metaphyseal 4×

Risk factors

Childfirst-born · unplanned · premature · disability (CP, neurocognitive syndromes, Down) · step-child · age <3 yr

Parent / socialsingle parent · recent stressor (job loss, move) · unemployment · drugs · abused as child · low SES · no support · age <20 · Medicaid (⅔)

NOT risk factorsfemale sex · no siblings

3Presentation

Red flagsinconsistent / no history · delay in seeking care · long-bone fracture in a non-ambulatory child (e.g. "fell running" at 6 months) · unwitnessed injury · multiple carers · bruises in various stages · pinna bruising, cigarette burns (highly specific)

Fracture patterns suggestive of abuse

Specificity Fractures
High Classic metaphyseal lesion (corner + bucket handle) · posteromedial rib · long bone in non-ambulatory child · transphyseal distal humerus (moderate per OB220897) · scapula · sternum · spinous process
Moderate Multiple fractures in various stages of healing · vertebral body · digital · complex skull
Low Toddler's fracture (non-displaced spiral tibia, ambulatory 9 months–3 yr) · clavicle · supracondylar humerus · SCFE

Classic metaphyseal lesionthrough primary spongiosa at metaphysis-physis junction · torsion / traction-shear (pull, twist, shake) · corner fracture = discrete metaphyseal avulsion · bucket handle = same seen en face · present in 40–50% of abused infants (TO) · "almost pathognomonic" (TO) · most suspicious femur pattern
✗ Wrong options: midshaft spiral/transverse

Femur NAI vs accidentmid-diaphyseal most common in both · NAI children younger
✗ Wrong options: corner fracture most common in NAI

Rib fracturesposteromedial · highest specificity (OB) · 70% chance of abuse · 51% of fractures in fatal abuse · anterior rib not pathognomonic

Transphyseal distal humerus separationrotatory shear · ≤3 yr · radiocapitellar line preserved (vs dislocation) · arthrogram/US/MRI if unossified · CRPP like supracondylar

Shaken baby syndromesubdural hematoma + retinal hemorrhage + posterior rib fractures (TO) · chest ecchymosis · seizures

No fracture is pathognomonicjudge age, ambulation, pattern, mechanism, psychosocial picture

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Skeletal surveystudy of choice / gold standard · AP appendicular + AP/lateral axial (skull, spine, ribs) · mandatory <2 yr with suspected abuse (AAP) · repeat at 2 wk for healing injuries
✗ Wrong options: SPECT · CT CAP · brain/spine MRI · isolated forearm film

Addlateral thoracolumbar <12 months · head CT <1 yr or neuro signs · ophthalmology if shaking suspected

Bone scanadjunct >1 yr · ↑ sensitivity for ribs, subtle shaft fractures, periosteal elevation · useless for metaphyseal + skull fractures · less efficient than survey

OI vs abuse (TO)DEXA 4–6 months apart (density rises without metabolic disease, not in OI) · fibroblast culture / collagen analysis if unclear

Differential

Listaccidental injury · OI · osteopenia of prematurity · scurvy · copper deficiency · Menkes · disuse osteopenia · chronic renal/liver disease · rickets

X-ray mimicsrickets (physeal widening, metaphyseal fraying) · wormian bones (OI, rickets; normal in 10% Caucasians, 80% Asians) · bisphosphonate zebra lines (vs Park-Harris arrest lines — persist, parallel to physis) · Caffey disease

Differential – Caffey disease (infantile cortical hyperostosis)

Featuresinfant · solid wavy periosteal new bone along long-bone shafts (ulna, femur), clavicles, mandible, ribs, scapulae · resolves spontaneously within ~a year

TO stemsinfant with forearm cortical hyperostosis (OI / congenital syphilis / Caffey / infantile osteomyelitis) · diffuse ulnar thickening + clavicle + femur, resolved in a year (scurvy / Ewing / Garré / Caffey) · answers not provided by the source

5Management

Management - skeletal survey & CPS

Rulereport reasonable suspicion → child protective services · admit for safety + multidisciplinary evaluation (pediatrics, social work, CPS, radiology) · document + photograph

OrderCPS/NAT work-up before definitive fracture plan or discharge
✗ Wrong options: cast and send home · next-week clinic · metabolic labs first · genetic testing first · talk home safety · restrain father / police

Fracture careusually splint/cast until callus (Pavlik / spica for infant femur) · surgery rarely needed · still treat appropriately (e.g. forearm: closed reduction + cast + skeletal survey + CPS)

Toddler's fracture alonenot abuse · plus corner fracture or suspicious skin lesions → admit / report to CPS

If missed30–50% repeat abuse, 5–10% death

Legal duty to report

Physicians = mandated reporters · need only reasonable suspicion · immune from civil + criminal liability in good faith · failure to report can be a crime
✗ Wrong options: prove cause · call daycare first

Sexual abuse disclosure (minor) → child protective services
✗ Wrong options: parents · school board · athletic director · counselor

Medical child abuse - multidisciplinary evaluation

Munchausen by proxy (caregiver-fabricated illness)usually biologic mother with medical knowledge · repeated doctor shopping, unwarranted tests/surgery · normal exam + X-rays → early multidisciplinary evaluation (medical, psychosocial, CPS, legal)
✗ Wrong options: CT · casting · coalition excision · another opinion

Developmental milestones

Milestone Age
Sits 9 months (not sitting at 15 months → work up)
Walks Up to 15 months still normal
Hand dominance 3rd year (~30 months) · strong preference <2 yr → neuro deficit
Shoes on correct feet, buttons 4 yr
Hops on one foot, heel-to-toe walk 5 yr

Cast saw burns

Reduce burnsvacuum · thinner cast · "up and down" technique · check blade often · avoid fiberglass (more heat than plaster)

Pediatric Trauma Evaluation & Management

Pediatrics · 81 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiologytrauma = most common cause of death in children >1 yr · polytrauma mortality ~20% · falls + MVAs most common

MorbidityCNS injury = highest overall morbidity + mortality · spine fractures = highest among MSK injuries · C-spine injury more common <8 yr (restraints don't fit)

Anatomy & physiology vs adults

System Child
Airway Smaller (obstructs easily) · large tongue, floppy epiglottis · large occiput flexes neck supine · larynx higher + anterior (C2–C3 vs C6–C7)
Breathing Hypoventilation = most common cause of arrest · horizontal ribs · diaphragmatic · fewer type I fibres → tire fast · RR varies with age
Circulation Relatively larger but absolutely small blood volume · lower SVR · hypotension is LATE (25–30% loss) · small veins → IO access
Disability Open sutures/fontanelle · thin skull · large head → head/neck injury
Exposure High BMR + surface area → heat loss · ↑ glucose need, small glycogen stores

5Management

Resuscitation (airway, IO access, blood volume, transport)

Transport<8 yr: spine board with occipital cut-out or raised chest (✓ modified board for suspected spine injury)
✗ Wrong options: routine pelvic binder · routine IO · nasal airway in head injury

ATLSAirway → Breathing → Circulation → Disability → Exposure · fix each before moving on

IntubateGCS <8 / can't protect airway (✗ Wrong options: GCS <12) · e.g. GCS 6 + SpO2 83% → intubation first (✗ Wrong options: splint ankle · CT · close laceration)

Formula Value
Broselow tape Drug doses, equipment size, defibrillation energy
ETT (uncuffed) (age/4) + 4 or (age + 16)/4
Systolic BP 80 + (2 × age)
Chest tube 4 × ETT
Blood volume 75 mL/kg (Orthobullets) · 75–80 mL/kg (OB)
First bolus 20 mL/kg NS
After 2 boluses 10 mL/kg PRBC

Shock signsnarrowed pulse pressure at ~15% loss · hypotension after 25–30% · 100 mL in 5 kg child ≈ 26.7% of volume

IV access fails (even normotensive) → intraosseous line
✗ Wrong options: PICC · cutdown · subclavian · keep trying

Triad of deathacidosis + hypothermia + coagulopathy (inadequate resuscitation)

Pediatric scoring systems

PTS Mortality
<0 100%
1–4 40%
5–8 7%
≤8 Send to pediatric trauma centre

Pediatric GCS <8 → ↑ mortality · SpO2 at presentation + GCS at 72 h predict long-term neuro recovery

Injury patterns & outcomes (TBI, multiorgan failure)

TBImost common ATV injury (✗ Wrong options: open fractures · pneumothorax) · greatest long-term morbidity (✗ Wrong options: spine · abdomen · open fracture) · pain ↑ ICP → fracture fixation ↓ ICP · HO more common → ↑ serum ALP heralds HO → NSAID prophylaxis

Peripheral nerve injurymostly with closed fractures · EMG if no return by 2–3 months

Multiorgan failureearly after admission, all organs simultaneously · adults: from 48 h, sequential starting with lungs · acute lung injury ~6× lower in children
✗ Wrong options: 48 h · sequential

Femur fixation in polytrauma with head injury

Timingfix once cerebral perfusion pressure stable · early fixation eases transport, ↓ malunion/shortening, ↓ ICP

9-yr TBI + transverse femoral shaft → retrograde flexible IM nails
✗ Wrong options: spica · 90-90 traction (spasticity) · piriformis reamed nail (AVN risk)

Prognosischildren recover from TBI better than adults

Pelvis Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 82 / 112

1Basics

Incidence1–2% of pediatric fractures · acetabulum 1–15% of these · avulsions almost only in adolescents

Mechanismring: high energy (MVA, pedestrian struck) · avulsion: low energy, explosive activity (sprint, jump, kick)

AssociatedCNS + abdominal visceral injury >50% (energy needed to break elastic pelvis) · chest injury ~63%, long bones ~50%, spine ~25% · femoral head fracture/dislocation with acetabular fracture · GU injury with Torode IV

Child vs adult pelvis

Child Reason
More lateral compression (adult: APC) —
More single-bone ring fractures Elastic bone, cartilage absorbs energy, elastic SI + symphysis, thick periosteum
"Dislocations" heal like fractures Periosteal tube
Less hemorrhage Small vessels vasoconstrict · pelvic volume rarely ↑
Acetabulum: transverse > both column Triradiate injury with less force → growth arrest

Anatomy

Primary centres (endochondral) — ilium 9 wk · ischium 16 wk · pubis 20 wk · fuse at triradiate 12 (girls) / 14 (boys)

Acetabulumenlarges by interstitial growth of triradiate cartilage · concavity from femoral head pressure · secondary centres appear 8–9, fuse 17–18: os acetabuli (anterior wall), acetabular epiphysis (superior), ischial secondary centre (posterior wall)

Apophysis Appears Fuses
Iliac crest (Risser) 13–15 15–17
Ischial 15–17 19–25
AIIS 14 16

Apophyseal avulsion fractures

Site Muscle %
Ischial tuberosity Hamstrings + adductors 54%
AIIS Rectus femoris 22%
ASIS Sartorius 19%
Pubic symphysis Abdominals 3%
Iliac crest Abdominals (external oblique) 1%
Lesser trochanter Iliopsoas —

Ischial avulsionage 13–17 as tuberosity ossifies (apophysis 2–5× weaker than tendon) · hip extension + knee flexion weakness · X-rays negative → MRI
✗ Wrong options: CT (for displacement) · EMG · bone scan · steroid

AIISgroin pain, snap, pain on resisted knee extension · ASIS — hockey check / eccentric sartorius

3Presentation

ExamATLS · rectal + GU exam (open fracture) · log-roll for ecchymosis · palpate ASIS, crests, SI, symphysis · iliac crest compression / posterior pressure pain · excess mobility = serious injury

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP pelvis · Judet (45° obliques — acetabulum) · inlet/outlet (35° caudal/cranial — ring)

CTX-rays miss ~50% of pediatric pelvic fractures · SI tenderness, negative films with suspicion, planning, spine injury

MRIoccasionally for apophyseal avulsions

Torode/Zieg classification (pediatric ring)

Type Injury Treatment
I Avulsion Protected WB if <2 cm · ORIF >2–3 cm (historically >3 cm)
II Iliac wing Protected WB if <2 cm · ORIF >2–3 cm
III Ring, no segmental instability WBAT 6 wk · ORIF if acetabulum displaced >2 mm
IV Ring with segmental instability <2 cm → bed rest · unstable / >2 cm → ORIF

TileA stable · B rotationally unstable, vertically stable · C unstable both

Bucholz classification (acetabulum / triradiate)

Type Physeal Features
Shearing SH I / II Blow to pubis/ischium/femur · triangular medial Thurston-Holland fragment (SH II)
Crushing / impaction SH V Hard to see · narrowed triradiate · premature closure · earlier = worse deformity

5Management

Pelvic ring injury management

Non-opsymphysis/SI "dislocations" heal by periosteum · types I–II <2 cm: protected WB 2–4 wk → stretch/strengthen 4–8 wk → sport after 8 wk · type III WBAT 6 wk

Stable type IV open book (symphysis 1.2 cm, SI 0.7 cm, stable) → bed rest + progressive mobilisation
✗ Wrong options: ex-fix · binder · fixation

Hemodynamically unstable + rotationally unstable (APC) ring → pelvic binder · ex-fix for instability / ↑ volume · angiography if still bleeding
✗ Wrong options: iliac wing · rami · avulsions

Adolescent with displaced symphysis + SI widening → anterior symphyseal plate + percutaneous SI screw
✗ Wrong options: non-op · anterior only · ex-fix

Operative indicationsdisplaced posterior SI · iliac fracture >2 cm · anterior disruption with vertical/rotational instability · older children/adolescents do better with fixation

Acetabulum ORIFdisplacement >2 mm · incongruity · intra-articular fragments · instability (medial/posterior subluxation) · central fracture-dislocation · open · comminution not improved by traction

Techniqueilioinguinal / Stoppa · physeal-sparing · if needed smooth pins across triradiate 4–6 wk, removed early

Apophyseal avulsion management

First linecrutches, protected WB, surveillance X-rays (e.g. minimally displaced lesser trochanter avulsion in hurdler)

Differential on hip filmsSCFE → in situ screw · FAI → PT · compression femoral neck stress fracture → NWB (screw if >50% width) · tension-sided → cannulated screws

6Complications

Triradiate premature closure<5% · risk: age <10 yr, Bucholz crush (SH V) · thick medial wall → shallow acetabulum, lateral subluxation, hypoplastic hemipelvis · bar excision (may still close) · late pelvic osteotomy (Chiari) · follow to maturity

OthersLLD (vertical displacement >2 cm) · malunion (well tolerated) · nonunion (rare) · NV injury · HO · femoral head AVN (acetabular fracture + dislocation) · hip OA (displaced acetabular) · death (head/visceral)

Prognosiscomplications rare · surgery more often needed after triradiate closure

Physeal Considerations

Pediatrics · 83 / 112

1Basics

Pediatric boneelastic → buckle + greenstick fractures · remodeling: faster in plane of joint motion (sagittal at wrist) and at most active physes · intra-articular fractures still need reduction

Most active physesUE: proximal humerus, distal radius ("away from the elbow") · LE: distal femur, proximal tibia, distal tibia ("at the knee")

Skeletal agediffers from chronologic age by >1 yr in 26% · maturity ~14 girls / 16 boys

Laws of the physis

Law Statement
Hueter–Volkmann ↑ compression slows longitudinal growth
Delpech ↑ tension speeds growth
Wolff Bone adapts to the loads placed on it
✗ Wrong option: Maxwell Not a physeal law (TO)

Physeal zones & fracture plane (hypertrophic zone)

Zone Function Disease
Reserve Stores lipid, glycogen, proteoglycan · low O2 Gaucher · Kniest · pseudoachondroplasia
Proliferative Chondrocyte stacking → longitudinal growth · most matrix production · ↑ O2 inhibits calcification Achondroplasia · gigantism
Hypertrophic — maturation, degeneration (cells ×5), provisional calcification Chondrocyte death → calcium release → matrix calcifies · type X collagen · PTHrP / Indian hedgehog SCFE (non-renal) · rickets (provisional calcification) · enchondroma · MPS · Schmid · physeal fractures
Primary spongiosa Vascular invasion, osteoblasts on cartilage bars → woven bone Metaphyseal corner fracture (abuse)
Secondary spongiosa Internal remodeling (lamellar bone) + funnelization Renal SCFE

Fracture planephyseal fractures run through the hypertrophic zone, specifically the zone of provisional calcification (weakest in tension; calcified/uncalcified transition) · applies to SH I, II and III (OB) · chronic gymnast wrist injury → same zone

Reserve + proliferative zones stay with epiphysis, blood supply preserved → good prognosis in SH I–II · TO: SH III + IV involve the reserve zone (germinal cells) → ↑ arrest risk · SH V crush of germinal layer

Perichondral ring (Ranvier, LaCroix)

Structure Role
Groove (zone) of Ranvier Fibrous ring in 1st year · ↑ mechanical strength · appositional growth · source of osteochondroma
Perichondral ring of LaCroix Dense fibrous limiting membrane · peripheral stability · up to 50% of shear resistance · injured in SH VI
Perichondral artery Major nutrition of physis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Salter-Harris classification

Type Path
I Through physis (separation)
II Physis → exits metaphysis · Thurston-Holland fragment · most common (>50%) · periosteum torn on convex (tension) side, intact on concave
III Physis → exits epiphysis (intra-articular)
IV Epiphysis → physis → metaphysis
V Crush of physis · diagnosed late

Physeal vs ligamentous ankle injury

Pediatric inversion injury, normal X-ray → lateral ligament sprain on MRI (more common than SH I)
✗ Wrong options: physeal widening · bone bruise · peroneal tear

Bone age estimation

Method Film / basis
Greulich-Pyle / Tanner-Whitehouse Left hand + wrist (right more often injured; anthropology convention) (TO)
TW-III RUS Distal radius, ulna, short bones · correlates with PHV
Sauvegrain Left elbow · 27 points: lateral condyle, trochlea, olecranon apophysis, proximal radial epiphysis
Olecranon method 6-monthly age: girls 11–13, boys 13–15
Risser Iliac apophysis 0–4 ossification, 5 fused · variable
Peak height velocity Better than Risser/age · 8 cm/yr girls, 9.5 cm/yr boys
Sanders Phalanx, metacarpal, distal radius epiphyses · predicts scoliosis progression

Hand dominance2–3 yr (third year) · strong preference <2 yr → neuro deficit · persistent ambidexterity normal

5Management

Treatmentclosed reduction vs CRPP vs ORIF by pattern · intra-articular must be anatomic

Displaced SH III/IV distal tibia (11-yr) → ORIF with fixation PARALLEL to physis (epiphyseal or metaphyseal screw) + NWB cast · ankle physeal arrest up to 50% → long follow-up
✗ Wrong options: transphyseal lag screw · closed manipulation

Growth contribution by physis

Physis Growth
Distal femur 9–10 mm/yr (✓ greatest LLD if arrested)
Proximal tibia 6 mm/yr
Distal radius 5–6 mm/yr
Proximal femur 3 mm/yr
Distal humerus 2–3 mm/yr
Humerus Proximal 80% · distal 20%

12-yr boy distal femoral arrest → 4 yr × 10 mm = 40 mm

6Complications

Growth arrest - location, mechanism & follow-up

Mechanismfracture through all zones (SH III/IV) → vascular invasion across physis → osteoblasts → bony bar
✗ Wrong options: LaCroix proliferation · Wolff · Hueter-Volkmann

Patterncomplete arrest → shortening · partial → angulation

Most common site of post-traumatic arrestdistal (medial) tibia · also high: distal femur, distal ulna · rare: distal radius, proximal humerus

Implant violation<7% of physeal area unlikely to arrest (Mäkelä: 7% arrested, 3% didn't) · retrograde nail through 5% central physis, screws above physis → injury unlikely

Follow-up≥2 yr after physeal injury · multiple X-rays needed
✗ Wrong options: one film · stop at 14/16

Bar Treatment
<50% of physis + >2 yr or 2 cm growth left Bar resection + interposition (fat / wax)
>50% Complete ipsilateral arrest ± contralateral epiphysiodesis / ipsilateral lengthening

Little League elbow outcome — Panner disease

Panner (osteochondrosis of capitellum)age 5–10 · repetitive valgus → ischemia of whole capitellar epiphysis → flattening, fragmentation, reossification (like Perthes) · symptomatic (pain, swelling, ↓ motion)

Outcomenon-op succeeds · full motion returns · X-ray irregularity / sclerosis often persists
✗ Wrong options: anatomic restoration · incidental · spontaneous · high failure

vs capitellar OCDfocal lesion, >10 yr

PFFD
  • Hip unstable (Aitken C/D)→femoral-pelvic fusion (Brown)

Procedure Indication
Lengthening ± contralateral epiphysiodesis Predicted LLD <20 cm · stable hip + functional foot · femur >50% of other side · head present (Aitken A/B) · not with unaddressed coxa vara, neck pseudarthrosis, acetabular dysplasia
Knee arthrodesis + foot ablation (Syme) Foot proximal to opposite knee · prosthetic knee won't sit below opposite knee · Syme at 10–14 months, knee fusion 3–4 yr (OB)
Femoral-pelvic fusion (Brown) Femoral head absent (Aitken C/D)
Van Ness rotationplasty Foot at level of opposite knee · ankle >60% motion · absent head (C/D) · 180° rotation → ankle DF becomes knee flexion → BK prosthesis
Amputation Femur <50% · keep length · through joint (avoid overgrowth) · prosthesis after 1 yr
Observation / extension prosthesis Bilateral PFFD

11-week-old, ankle will reach normal knee level → delayed Van Ness rotationplasty + hip stabilisation at 1 yr if head deficient
✗ Wrong options: immediate femoral-pelvic fusion (head status unknown) · Syme + knee fusion (too short) · immediate lengthening

Situation Treatment
Nondisplaced I (no dislocation), II, III, IV and <4 yr Closed reduction + abduction spica (rare) · OB: spica only <6 yr types III/IV

IV >⅔

5Management

Treatment by age & displacement

Age Acceptable alignment (non-op)
<10 yr Any angulation
10–12 yr Up to 60–75°
>12 yr Up to 45° or ⅔ displacement

Rockwood (OB)reduce ± fix if >50% displaced in >11 yr

Non-opsling ± swathe, immobiliser, coaptation splint · 7-yr Neer-Horowitz IV → sling + PT · 9-yr displaced → sling + follow-up X-rays
✗ Wrong options: CRPP · ORIF (higher complications)

Older adolescent (≥15, <1 yr growth) Neer-Horowitz III/IV → closed reduction + percutaneous pinning · 13-yr marked varus SH II → closed/open reduction + pins (varus = lost abduction)
✗ Wrong options: shoulder immobiliser · hanging arm cast · spica (redisplaces) · hemiarthroplasty

Outcome by ageolder patients with III/IV treated non-op → ↑ limitations in daily activities vs younger · long-term (Lähdeoja, 13 yr) no impairment vs controls, op = non-op
✗ Wrong options: nonunion · more displacement

Reductiontraction + 90° abduction + ER

Fixation2–3 lateral threaded pins (avoid axillary n. laterally, musculocutaneous anteriorly) · retrograde elastic nails · cannulated screws in older teens

Open reductionirreducible from interposed long head of biceps (most common), capsule, periosteum, deltoid · open fracture · vascular injury · intra-articular displacement · deltopectoral approach

Loss of reductionunstable fracture reduced without pins

Axillary nerve<1% from injury (neurapraxia, medially displaced shaft) · ↑ with pins → lateral pin below nerve (~5 cm below acromion in adults; = 2× humeral head height)

Othersvarus malunion → impingement · shortening (<3 cm tolerated <12 yr) · growth arrest rare · hypertrophic scar · pin-site infection 5–22%

Prognosisexcellent (remodeling + shoulder ROM)

Pediatrics · 90 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology<1% of pediatric fractures · 12–14 yr · high energy · varus/valgus or hyperextension
