Anatomy

Physisproximal tibia 6 mm/yr · knee = 15 of 23 mm/yr leg growth · closes posterior → anterior, medial → lateral, posteromedial → anterolateral

Buttressessuperficial MCL inserts below physis (medial buttress) · LCL to fibula (lateral buttress) · patellar tendon (resists posterior displacement) → physeal fractures are rare

Popliteal arterytethered to posterior proximal tibia by septa · trifurcation at physeal level → injury with displacement · geniculate arteries around popliteus

3Presentation

Examcan't bear weight · physeal tenderness · step-off · varus/valgus instability · thorough neurovascular exam

Normal X-ray + exquisite physeal tenderness after high-energy hit → may have displaced + reduced → splint, admit, frequent neurovascular / compartment checks (treat like knee dislocation) · MRI/CT to define
✗ Wrong options: cylinder cast + discharge · arthroscopy · prophylactic fasciotomy

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP, lateral ± obliques · stress views risk physis

CTdisplacement · best for SH III / IV

Salter-Harris classification

Type Features
I Mean age 12 · usually displaced (>50%)
II Mean age 14 · usually displaced (>67%) · medial gapping + lateral Thurston-Holland + proximal fibula fracture
III Exits epiphysis · usually tibial tubercle fractures
IV Physis + metaphysis + epiphysis

5Management

Fracture Treatment
Non-displaced (<2 mm), stable SH I/II Long leg cast, slight flexion, 6 wk · redisplacement common
Unstable SH I/II · redisplaced CRPP
Irreducible (periosteal flap) · displaced >2 mm SH III/IV · vascular injury ORIF

Fixationcrossed smooth pins: transphyseal for SH I/II with small Thurston-Holland · extraphyseal for SH III/IV · cannulated screws parallel to physis for SH II with large metaphyseal fragment or III/IV · cast in slight flexion 4–6 wk

Approachanterior midline (patella → tubercle) · medial approach if vascular injury

Popliteal artery injury & vascular monitoring

Hyperextension physeal fracture → popliteal artery most at risk
✗ Wrong options: tibial n. · peroneal n. · PCL

6Complications

Growth disturbance 25% (LLD, angulation; ↑ open fractures) · loss of reduction · compartment syndrome · ligament instability

How it's asked

"9-yr hyperextension proximal tibial physeal fracture — at risk?"popliteal artery

Radial Head and Neck Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 93 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology5–10% of pediatric elbow fractures · 1% of all · 3rd most common elbow fracture (OB) · median age 9–10 · M = F

Site90% physis or metaphysis (neck) · ~50% metaphyseal, 50% SH I/II · articular head fracture only 4–7% with open physes (52–96% after closure)

MechanismFOOSH with extension + valgus · elbow dislocation

Associated (30–50%)elbow dislocation · medial epicondyle · olecranon · condyles · forearm compartment syndrome

Anatomyradial head ossifies 3–5 yr (may be bipartite) · fuses 16–18 · annular ligament covers epiphysis + physis → stress riser at metaphysis → neck fractures · thick epiphyseal cartilage resists articular extension · head blood supply mainly metaphyseal

3Presentation

Examlateral swelling · pain with pronation/supination · may refer to wrist · watch for forearm compartment syndrome (rising forearm pain overnight)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral · radiocapitellar (Greenspan) view: elbow 90°, thumb up, beam 45° proximal

Linesradiocapitellar line (unreliable in young, esp. AP) · lateral humeral line (tangent to lateral condyle, lies lateral to radial neck) — more reliable in young children

Pitfallsnondisplaced hard to see · radial head flipped 180° · posterior fat pad always pathologic · neck partly extra-articular → effusion / fat pad may be absent

CTcomminuted head in older child · MRI — rare (unossified elbow, anterior head compression with ligament injury)

Classification

O'Brien Angulation
I <30°
II 30–60°
III >60°
Judet Angulation
I Undisplaced
II <30°
III 30–60°
IVa 60–80°
IVb >80°

Chambersgroup 1 primary radial head displacement (most common; valgus: SH I/II, SH III/IV, metaphyseal; dislocation: reduction / dislocation injury) · group 2 radial neck displacement (Monteggia variant) · group 3 stress (OCD)

5Management

Pediatric radial neck fracture
  • <30° and <3 mm translation→long arm cast/splint, no reduction (7–21 days, then ROM)
  • >30°→closed reduction (Patterson, Israeli, Neher-Torch, Esmarch)
    (stable once reduced — fixation usually not needed)
  • Residual >30° / >3–4 mm / <45° pro-supination→percutaneous reduction (K-wire joystick, Metaizeau) ± pin
  • Can't get <45°→open reduction (lateral approach, forearm pronated)

Treatment by angulation (closed, percutaneous, open)

Closed reduction45° or 35° angulation → attempt closed reduction · >60° unlikely to close-reduce (OB) · some tolerate up to 60° (Radomisli) · >50° often needs fixation (Nicholson & Skaggs)
✗ Wrong options: cast without reduction · percutaneous first · open

TechniquesPatterson: elbow extended, traction, supination, varus + direct radial head pressure · Israeli (Kaufman): elbow 90°, pronate the supinated forearm with thumb on head · Neher-Torch: extension, supination, traction, varus; assistant pushes shaft lateral, surgeon pushes head medial · Esmarch wrap → spontaneous reduction

PercutaneousK-wire joystick (push posterolateral / lever) · Metaizeau: retrograde flexible nail across fracture, rotate to reduce · hardware out at ~8 wk · after failed ED reduction with >30° (e.g. 62°) → percutaneous reduction ± pin / ESIN
✗ Wrong options: cast 6 wk · CT · ORIF first · plate · epiphysiodesis

Openwidely displaced head fracture with radial subluxation → ORIF · lateral approach, pronate forearm to protect PIN · fix only if unstable · no transcapitellar pins

Outcomebetter if younger, less angulation, isolated neck · open reduction → more stiffness, AVN, synostosis

6Complications

Complications & prognosis

Complication Fact
↓ ROM Most common (10–31%) · pronation > supination
Radial head overgrowth 20–40% · rarely matters
Osteonecrosis 10–20% · up to 70% after open reduction
PIN palsy ~15% after surgery
Physeal arrest → cubitus valgus
Synostosis Most serious · open reduction, extensive dissection, delay
Malunion (intra-articular) Radiocapitellar instability, pain, arthritis
Forearm compartment syndrome Increasing pain + swelling overnight

Worse outcomeage >10 · intra-articular (50% complications, 25% revision vs 0% extra-articular)
✗ Wrong options: BMI · dominance · sex

PIN injury

PINbranch of radial nerve wrapping radial neck · loss of thumb IP extension (EPL), finger extension incl. small finger (EDM), partial wrist extension · supplies posterior compartment (except anconeus) + ECRB · pins posterolateral with arm in maximal pronation

✗ Wrong options: annular ligament reconstruction · repeat closed

"6-yr radial neck fracture, increasing forearm pain overnight?"forearm compartment syndrome

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

Pediatrics · 98 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidencemost common adolescent hip disorder · 10 per 100,000

Whoobese (single greatest risk) · males (2:1.4 Orthobullets; ~2× TO) · African American, Pacific Islander, Latino · rapid growth 10–16 yr · boys 12–13.4, girls 11.2–12.2 · left hip more common (2× TO)

Bilateral17–50%, average 25% (Orthobullets) · 25–40% (TO) · 20–30% at presentation (TO) · second slip usually within 12–18 months

Risk factorsobesity · acetabular + femoral retroversion (↓ anteversion, ↓ neck-shaft angle) · prior radiation · ↑ leptin (4.9× odds, independent of obesity) · Down syndrome · open triradiate

Pathophysiology

Slipmetaphysis moves ANTERIOR + externally rotates · epiphysis stays in acetabulum, posterior/inferior to neck

Planethrough the hypertrophic zone (✓) · renal SCFE through secondary spongiosa

Why adolescentsperichondral ring thins · mammillary processes unlock · physis still vertical (160° birth → 125° maturity) → shear · epiphyseal tubercle pivot

vs SH I fractureantecedent epiphysiolysis, slower, periosteum intact (chronic) · type I transepiphyseal fracture = high energy, young child, M = F (TO)

Histopathology

Chronic SCFE histologygranulation tissue between columns in hypertrophic zone · ↓ perichondral ring thickness · ↓ physeal undulations · abnormal proteoglycan accumulation · ↑ hypertrophic zone height
✗ Wrong options: vascular invasion of proliferative zone · thick ring

Endocrine & metabolic associations

Endocrinehypothyroidism (most common non-idiopathic; ↑ TSH) · renal osteodystrophy (↑ BUN, creatinine) · GH deficiency · panhypopituitarism (pituitary adenoma) · Loder: hypothyroidism 40%, GH deficiency 25%, all hypothyroid → bilateral

Endocrine work-up if<10 yr · weight <50th percentile · prepubertal / short · labs: TSH, free T4, BUN, creatinine

Atypical SCFE<10 or >16 yr (TO) · renal failure, radiation, hypogonadism, Down

Blood supply

Lateral epiphyseal artery (MFCA) = main supply · LFCA anterior ring · ligamentum teres insignificant · posterosuperior hardware endangers vessels

Painhip 52%, thigh 35%, groin 14% · knee pain 15–50% (23% Matava; obturator nerve referral) · hip pain still more common than knee
✗ Wrong options: "knee more often than hip"

Delay in diagnosisknee pain · stable slip · Medicaid · severity · 88% of unstable slips had ~42 days of prior symptoms

Examantalgic / Trendelenburg / out-toeing gait · obligatory ER with hip flexion (Drehmann sign) · ↓ IR, abduction, flexion · sits with leg crossed · tender Scarpa triangle (TO)

Obese teen with knee pain + normal knee X-rays → examine hip + AP pelvis/frog-lateral
✗ Wrong options: knee MRI · arthroscopy · labs · PT

Unmanipulated severe SCFE on AP → leg lies in external rotation

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + frog-lateral of both hips · lateral best for subtle slip · unstable → cross-table lateral (not frog)

Klein linealong superior neck · normally cuts lateral epiphysis · SCFE: intersects less / not at all · ≥2 mm asymmetry improves sensitivity 40% → ~80% (TO)

Type Definition AVN
Stable (85–95%) Can walk ± crutches <10% (~0%)
Unstable (5–15%) Can't walk even with crutches 24–47% (Orthobullets) · 47–50% · 25–50% · 15–50% · up to 60% (OB) · 2–5× stable

Temporalacute <3 wk · chronic >3 wk · acute-on-chronic (no prognostic value)

Southwick (epiphyseal-shaft) angleseverity · frog lateral (± AP) · affected minus normal · bilateral reference 145° AP / 10° lateral (Orthobullets) · 12° (TO)
✗ Wrong options: presence · AVN prognosis · chronicity

Severity Orthobullets OB / TO
Mild <30° <30°
Moderate 30–50° 30–60°
Severe >50° >60°

% displacement gradeI 0–33% · II 34–50% · III >50%

5Management

SCFE
  • Stable→single central screw in situ (no reduction), WB after
  • Unstable → urgent bed rest→in situ fixation ± 2nd screw, ± decompression/capsulotomy, TDWB
  • High-risk contralateral→prophylactic pinning
  • Residual deformity→osteochondroplasty (<30°) / Imhauser osteotomy (>30–45°)

In situ fixation technique

Rulepercutaneous in situ fixation for stable AND unstable · no forceful reduction (↑ AVN) · serendipitous positional reduction OK

Screwsingle cannulated screw usually (↓ AVN vs multiple) · 2 screws more stable (some for unstable) · not inverted triangle (adult neck fracture, ↑ penetration + AVN)

Placementstart on ANTERIOR femoral neck → perpendicular to physis → centre-centre of epiphysis on AP + lateral · not medial to intertrochanteric line (screw head impinges, labral tear) · severe slip → more oblique from intertrochanteric region

Depth≥5 threads across physis (<5 → 41% progression vs 0%) · tip ~5 mm from subchondral bone · partially threaded: 40–60% of threads in epiphysis strongest · approach-withdraw fluoroscopy to exclude penetration

Post-opstable WB · unstable TDWB · young child: short-thread screw not crossing physis (TO)

Stable mild slip in 13-yr → single-screw in situ fixation
✗ Wrong options: spica (chondrolysis) · ORIF · NWB · closed reduction

Stable SCFE seen only on MRI → in situ fixation
✗ Wrong options: observation · labral repair

Unstable SCFE & AVN

Unstable slip → strict bed rest + urgent surgery (within hours; 8 h OB, 24 h OB) on affected hip
✗ Wrong options: MRI · elective · NSAIDs trial

AVN risk factorsinstability (greatest) · initial displacement · forceful / over-reduction, reduction of chronic slip · posterosuperior (superolateral) hardware · multiple pins · femoral neck osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: age, sex, obesity · single screw · in situ without reduction

Capsulotomy / decompressionunstable ICP ~2× normal · may ↓ AVN (low evidence) · TO advocates routine capsulotomy in acute unstable · ICP probe monophasic waveform → decompress hip, then capsulotomy if still monophasic

Modified Dunn (surgical dislocation, capital realignment)unstable + severe · posterior retinacular flap carries blood supply · remove posterior callus · AVN ~26% vs 24% in situ · complications 37% · steep learning curve

Most dreaded complicationAVN (TO); MFCA injury

Contralateral prophylactic pinning

Indication NOT an indication
Age <10 (girls <10, boys <12–12.5) Unstable presenting slip
Open triradiate cartilage Chronicity / duration of symptoms
Endocrinopathy (hypothyroid, renal, GH, pituitary adenoma) Height >95th percentile
Obesity (BMI >95th) / obese males African American ethnicity
Posterior sloping angle >12° (TO) / >14.5° (OB) Elite athlete · DI · weight 40th percentile
Modified Oxford score 16–18 (~98% risk; 24 = 0%) Closed triradiate
Weight <10th or >90th percentile · unreliable follow-up Continued slipping after fixation (TO)

Contralateral slipmost common complication after unilateral fixation · 20–80% · up to 36% high-risk · ↓ with weight loss · more common in YOUNGER children
✗ Wrong options: older (TO false statement)

Prophylactic pinning risk2–6% complications

Both hips involved / silent grade 1 on other side / pre-slip on MRI → pin both

Chronic deformity, osteotomy & natural history

Residual deformity↑ α-angle, pistol-grip, cam FAI · sequelae: shortening, ↓ flexion, ↓ IR, out-toeing

Deformity Procedure
Mild–moderate (<30°) cam FAI Osteochondroplasty (arthroscopy, limited anterior arthrotomy, surgical dislocation)
Severe (>30–45°), painful, no OA/AVN Imhauser intertrochanteric osteotomy — flexion + internal rotation + valgus (most used; AVN 2–7%)
Southwick subtrochanteric osteotomy
Greatest correction Femoral neck (subcapital) cuneiform osteotomy — AVN 37%, OA 37% · sole indication Southwick >60° (TO)

Natural historymost well tolerated · ~5% THA at 20 yr · realignment not proven to prevent OA · closed reduction worse
✗ Wrong options: 25%

Spinal Muscular Atrophy

Pediatrics · 99 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiologymost common genetic cause of death in childhood · 1 in 10,000

Pathologyprogressive loss of α-motor neurons in the anterior horn (✓ SMN protein deficiency) · weakness proximal > distal, LE > UE, symmetric

Genetics & pathophysiology (SMN1, SMN2)

Inheritanceautosomal recessive

Genehomozygous telomeric deletion of SMN1, chromosome 5 · in 90% (Orthobullets) · 95–98% (OB) · SMN protein: RNA metabolism, apoptosis

Severityall lack SMN1 protein · number of functional SMN2 copies sets severity (✓ SMN2 correlates with severity) · type I has 1 SMN2 copy

Gene (distractors) Disease
SMN1 SMA
Dystrophin (↑ CPK, DTRs present, calf pseudohypertrophy) Duchenne
PMP22 duplication CMT (70–80%)
Androgen receptor CAG repeat Spinobulbar (Kennedy)
Frataxin GAA repeat Friedreich ataxia
β-galactosidase Morquio B
COMP / COL1A1 Pseudoachondroplasia / OI
Sphingolipid (glucocerebroside) Gaucher
Fetal ACh receptor, non-progressive contractures Arthrogryposis

One SMN1 deletion → any of the 3 types (✓ "any of the above")

Types

Type Name Onset Function Prognosis
I Acute Werdnig-Hoffmann <6 months Floppy, poor head control, feeding difficulty, tongue fasciculations, absent DTRs Death by ~2 yr
II Chronic Werdnig-Hoffmann 6–12 months Sits but can't walk · LE worse To 5th decade
III Kugelberg-Welander 2–15 yr Walks as child, wheelchair as adult · proximal weakness Normal life expectancy ± respiratory support

3Presentation

Examabsent DTRs · fasciculations · hypotonia · normal CPK + aldolase
✗ Wrong options: Duchenne (present)

4Diagnosis & Classification

DiagnosisDNA testing (positive test usually avoids biopsy) · muscle biopsy · prenatal possible

X-rayscoliosis series · pelvis

5Management

Medical therapy - nusinersen

Nusinersenantisense oligonucleotide · alters SMN2 splicing to include exon 7 → full-length SMN · intrathecal (doesn't cross BBB) · FDA-approved

Othersrisdiplam (same mechanism, oral small molecule) · Zolgensma (onasemnogene, IV gene replacement of SMN1) · albuterol (adjunct)
✗ Wrong options: prednisone (Duchenne)

Scoliosis management

Curvealmost universal (100% type II) · from age 2–3 · long C-shaped thoracolumbar, very flexible · progresses despite brace · curve size correlates with ambulatory status

Bracingmay delay, not prevent surgery (<10 yr)

SurgeryPSF to pelvis for progressive curve (>30–40°, OB; >50–60° with sitting/pulmonary decline, OB) · goals: sitting balance, free the hands, slow pulmonary decline · release hip / LE contractures first for seating · leave a lower lumbar laminectomy window unfused for intrathecal nusinersen

Anterior + posterioronly curves >100° or very young (crankshaft) · avoid with poor lungs · typically NOT needed · growing rods only if young
✗ Wrong options: anterior alone (secondary progression)

Post-optemporary ↓ upper-limb function (e.g. ↓ self-propelling wheelchair)
✗ Wrong options: better strength · walking · contracture improvement

Hip subluxation - observation

Hip instabilitysubluxation/dislocation in 62% of type II, less in III · usually painless · open reduction redislocates

Treatmentobservation (leave dislocated) = standard
✗ Wrong options: adductor/psoas release · varus osteotomy · PAO · spica · abduction brace

Contractureship + knee (± ankle equinus in non-walkers) · PT · release controversial (rarely helps non-walkers, recurs)

SMA Duchenne
Lesion Anterior horn cell Muscle (dystrophin)
DTRs Absent Present
CPK Normal Very high
Fasciculations Yes (tongue) No
Inheritance AR X-linked recessive

Sprengel's Deformity

Pediatrics · 101 / 112

1Basics

Diagnosis & associations (Klippel-Feil)

Definitioncongenital elevation of a small, hypoplastic scapula from failure of caudal migration · most common congenital shoulder anomaly

DemographicsM:F 1:3 (Orthobullets) · equal (TO) · left more common (TO) · bilateral 10–30% (10% TO)

Causeinterrupted embryonic subclavian supply (subclavian, internal thoracic or suprascapular) · Poland = subclavian interruption proximal to internal thoracic, distal to vertebral

Omovertebral connectioncartilage/fibrous/bony bar from superomedial scapula to lower cervical spine · 30–50% (Orthobullets) · ~30% (OB) · ~½ (TO) · limits abduction to ~90°

AssociationsKlippel-Feil (most common associated finding: cervical spine anomalies) · congenital scoliosis · fused/cervical ribs · torticollis · diastematomyelia · myelomeningocele · kidney disease · UE anomalies · iniencephaly (TO)

Overlap Rate
Klippel-Feil patients with Sprengel ~⅓ (Orthobullets) · 35% (OB) · 20% (TO)

Klippel-Feil (TO)

Triad (~50%)short neck · low posterior hairline · ↓ neck motion · fusion C2–C3 most common (71%) · gene chromosome 8 · fetal alcohol → 50% fusions

Associatedscoliosis 60% (most common orthopaedic) · renal anomaly · VSD · deafness · synkinesis · respiratory · occipitalization, hemivertebrae, basilar impression · symptomatic → posterior C3–C7 fusion ± decompression

3Presentation

Examscapula high-riding, medially rotated (inferior pole medial) · small equilateral-triangle shape, loss of long medial border · abduction most limited + forward flexion · short, broad, webbed-looking neck (Turner-like) · often referred for "scoliosis"
✗ Wrong options: adduction · rotation

DifferentialFSHD (no omovertebral bone) · Turner · torticollis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Classification & surgery (Cavendish, Woodward)

Cavendish4-grade cosmetic classification of congenital elevation of scapula
✗ Wrong options: torticollis · radial head dislocation · clavicle pseudarthrosis

Rigault (TO) Superomedial angle
1 Below T2, above T4 transverse process
2 Between C5 and T2
3 Above C5

Pre-op imagingMRI or CT for omovertebral bar

5Management

Operative criteria

Observeno significant cosmetic or functional problem

Operatesevere cosmesis or abduction <110–120° · ideal age 3–8 (soon after 3) · >8 yr → brachial plexus risk
✗ Wrong options: defer until after 8 (TO false statement) · wait for maturity

Procedure Essence
Woodward Detach + reattach medial parascapular muscles (trapezius + rhomboid origins shifted distally at spinous processes) → scapula descends, rotates to abduction · modified: + superomedial border resection
Schrock / Green Extraperiosteal detachment of muscles at scapular insertion, scapula pulled down with traction, reinserted
Clavicle osteotomy / morcellation Severe deformity, before scapular descent → protect brachial plexus (2 cm midclavicular if >8 yr, 1 cm younger) (✗ Wrong options: mild deformity)
Bony resection Extraperiosteal superomedial prominence (cosmesis)
Mears Most abduction gain (TO)

Outcomeabduction +40–50° (Orthobullets) · ~40° (TO) · +38° (Farsetti)

Complicationbrachial plexus palsy = most severe and most common (TO) · SSEP monitoring

Supracondylar Fracture - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 102 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiologymost common pediatric elbow fracture (50–80%) · age 5–7 · M = F · FOOSH

Typeextension 95–98% (98% TO) · flexion <5% (2–4%) — fall on olecranon

Associatedipsilateral distal radius / forearm 5–10% (TO) · vascular compromise 5–17% · nerve injury 10–20%

Elbow ossification order

Centre Appears (yr) Fuses (yr)
Capitellum 1 12–14
Radial head 3 14–16
Medial (internal) epicondyle 5 (6 in Orthobullets text) 16–18 — LAST to fuse (16–19 OB)
Trochlea 7 12–14
Olecranon 9 15–17
Lateral (external) epicondyle 11 — last to appear 12–14

3Presentation

Nerve injuries (AIN, radial, ulnar)

Pattern Nerve Deficit
Extension (overall most common) AIN (median branch) Can't flex thumb IP (FPL) + index DIP (FDP) · no "OK" sign · PQ
Extension, posteromedial displacement Radial (2nd most common) Wrist drop, no thumb/MCP extension (PIN: EPL, ECU) · dorsal hand numbness
Extension, posterolateral displacement Median nerve, brachial artery Volar index sensory loss
Flexion Ulnar (C8–T1) Intrinsics: can't cross fingers / abduct index (FDI) · small-finger numbness
Medial pin Ulnar (iatrogenic) Can't cross fingers

Ratesextension neurapraxia 11% · flexion 17% · pre-op deficit ~20% in displaced extension (OB)

Managementexamine before any reduction · observe · recovery 6–12 wk, complete 3–6 months (2–3 months OB)
✗ Wrong options: EMG · exploration · neurolysis · nerve repair

Recovery (TO)radial 100% · median 88% · ulnar only 25% fully recover
✗ Wrong options: "majority recover in 3 months" (TO false statement)

Obese childrenmore pre- and post-op nerve palsy (TO)

Vascular exam

Assesspulse (palpation, Doppler) + perfusion (warm, pink vs cold, pale, CRT >2 s) · decision to explore is based on perfusion, not pulse · radial pulse absent at presentation 7–12%

Brachialis signantecubital ecchymosis, dimpling/puckering, palpable bone → proximal fragment buttonholed through brachialis → more arterial injury, swelling, harder reduction

4Diagnosis & Classification

Classification & radiographic assessment

Gartland Description Treatment
I Nondisplaced (beware medial comminution → varus) Long arm cast 3–4 wk, X-ray at 1 wk
II Displaced in 1 plane, posterior cortex/hinge intact (IIA no rotation, IIB rotation) CRPP (US standard) · cast only if AHL hits capitellum, little swelling, no medial comminution
III Displaced in 2–3 planes, no cortical contact CRPP ± open
IV Periosteum completely disrupted — unstable in flexion AND extension (found under EUA) CRPP ± open
Medial comminution Medial column collapse, ↓ Baumann CRPP (valgus force) — else cubitus varus
Flexion type Distal fragment anterior CRPP, more often open

Fat padsposterior fat pad = occult fracture · anterior "sail" sign (TO) = effusion · most common cause: supracondylar (child), radial head (adult)

Anterior humeral linethrough middle ⅓ of capitellum >5 yr · <5 yr: anterior and middle ⅓ about equally, posterior ⅓ in a few normal kids · capitellum visible from ~1 yr · extension type → capitellum posterior to line · compare other side
✗ Wrong options: always fracture

Baumann anglehumeral shaft vs lateral condylar physis on AP · 70–75° · deviation >5–10° unacceptable

Angiographynot indicated (lesion is at fracture)

5Management

Treatment indications - CRPP

Supracondylar fracture — timing by neurovascular status
  • Pulseless + POORLY perfused (cold, pale)→EMERGENT CRPP (hours, override NPO)
  • Pulseless + well perfused, sensory deficit, swelling, brachialis sign, open, floating elbow→URGENT (same day, 6–8 h)
  • Warm, perfused, neuro intact (± isolated AIN)→next day (splint 30–40°, elevate)

OperativeGartland II, III, IV · flexion type · medial comminution · displaced type II with medial impaction (3-yr) → CRPP
✗ Wrong options: cast (varus) · hyperflexion cast (compartment syndrome)

Floating elbow (supracondylar + forearm / distal radius) → pin BOTH (✗ Wrong options: casting either (compartment risk up to 33%)) · watch for compartment syndrome · ↑ nerve injury (✗ Wrong options: ↑ vascular · ↑ open)

Isolated AIN palsy → not a reason for overnight surgery

Pin configuration & iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury

Reduction (extension type)traction, correct coronal/rotation, hyperflexion · posteromedial → pronate · posterolateral → supinate (try opposite if fails)

Construct Use
2 lateral pins Type II · test stability
3 lateral pins Type III / IV, comminution (medial column) · = crossed-pin stability · construct of choice (AAOS)
Crossed (medial + lateral) Strongest in torsion (experimental) · ulnar nerve injury 3–8%

AAOS2–3 lateral pins, avoid medial pin (weak recommendation) · no Level 1 evidence that lateral is superior (RCT: equal outcomes) — the INCORRECT statement · lateral = fewer ulnar injuries, equal radiographic + ROM outcomes

Pin tipsmaximise separation at fracture, engage both columns, cross proximal to fracture · 3rd lateral pin ↑ stiffness with medial comminution or residual IR

Elbow position for pinningflexion for extension type · extension for flexion type

Medial pin safetyplace with elbow extended (ulnar nerve subluxes anteriorly in flexion) · small incision · anterior-to-posterior sagittal angle ↑ injury

Post-op ulnar palsy after crossed pins → observe + avoid hyperflexion >90° (TO) · resolves 1–7 months
✗ Wrong options: remove medial pin now · exploration/transposition

Open reductionfailed closed · open fracture · irreducible with gap (entrapped vessel/nerve) · flexion type more often · coronal displacement >7 mm predicts it · approach anterior (pulseless / median injury) or medial/lateral where periosteum torn · never posterior (AVN)

Pulseless hand & vascular management

Situation Action
Pulseless + cold/pale at presentation Emergent CRPP → reassess (✗ Wrong options: angiogram · splint and wait · explore first)
Pink pulseless (warm, brisk CRT ± Doppler) Urgent CRPP · after: if still pink (± triphasic Doppler) → long arm splint + admit 48 h observation · pulse returns 24–48 h in most
Pulseless + still cold/pale after CRPP Explore antecubital fossa (✗ Wrong options: observe · re-pin · fasciotomy)
Perfused hand becomes pale/pulseless after CRPP Remove pins, re-displace, reassess → still bad → open exploration (✗ Wrong options: medial pin · CT angiogram · warm and wait)
Irreducible + anterior gap + poor perfusion Vascular exploration (entrapped artery)

Pulseless + poorly perfused after CRPP → brachial artery injury up to 82%

Postoperative care (pin removal, PT, pin infection)

Pinsremove at 3 (–4) wk in clinic, stop immobilisation
✗ Wrong options: 3 more wk cast

ROM~94% by 6 months · no routine PT (no functional or motion benefit)

Pin infection1–2.4% · only proven risk: age <4.5 yr · oral antibiotics
✗ Wrong options: delay >24 h · no antibiotics · late follow-up; daily pin care ↑ infection

6Complications

Compartment syndrome

Rate0.1–0.3% (TO) · <1% · ↑ with floating elbow, splint >90°, type III, vascular injury, delay

Signs in children3 A's: anxiety, agitation, ↑ analgesic need · rising narcotic need overnight → emergent surgery ± fasciotomy
✗ Wrong options: rely on 6 P's

Volkmann ischemic contracturedeep volar compartment · casting in >90° flexion

Cubitus varus

Cubitus varus (gunstock)most common complication (OB) · Orthobullets lists pin migration (~2%) as most common · malreduction / malunion (medial collapse, IR, extension) — NOT growth arrest
✗ Wrong options: medial physeal arrest · lateral overgrowth

Effectsmainly cosmetic, function normal · posterolateral rotatory instability · forearm IR deficit · tardy ulnar palsy (anterior nerve subluxation most common, then FCU bands)

Osteotomyfor cosmesis · lateral closing wedge → lateral prominence · reverse V, step-cut, dome, medial opening with medialisation avoid it

Tarsal Coalition

Pediatrics · 104 / 112

1Basics

Prevalence1–2% (symptomatic ~1%) · **~75% asymptomatic** · bilateral ~50% · 2 coalitions in 10–20% (OB) · extra coalition on CT ~5% (Orthobullets)

Embryology - failure of segmentation

Causefailure of mesenchymal differentiation + segmentation (✓ both CN and TC) · bridge fibrous → cartilage → bone
✗ Wrong options: failure of formation · ischemic necrosis · microtrauma · peroneal hypertonicity

Interface Name
Fibrous Syndesmosis
Cartilaginous Synchondrosis
Bony Synostosis

Acquired (less common) — trauma, degeneration, infection

Genes & lab markers

Non-syndromicautosomal dominant (sibling history)

Syndromicfibular hemimelia · carpal coalition · FGFR1/2/3 craniosynostosis (Apert, Pfeiffer, Crouzon, Jackson-Weiss, Muenke) · TN coalition: Apert, Nievergelt (TO)

Site Incidence Symptom age Interface
Calcaneonavicular (CN) Most common (Orthobullets) · ~45% (TO) 8–12 yr (10–14 OB) Synchondrosis / syndesmosis
Talocalcaneal (TC), middle facet ~45% (TO) 12–15 yr (12–16 TO) Synchondrosis → synostosis
Talonavicular 1–2% Infancy Synostosis
Calcaneocuboid · naviculocuneiform <1% Variable / adult —

Symptoms start when the bar ossifies (CN earlier than TC)

2Mechanism

Mechanicssubtalar joint normally internally rotates ~10° in stance → blocked → flat arch, forefoot abduction, hindfoot valgus, peroneal spasm ("peroneal spastic flatfoot" — coalition = leading cause)

Pain sourcesossification of bar · microfracture at interface · chondral damage · stress on other joints

3Presentation

Presentation & diagnosis (imaging, anteater sign)

Historyrecurrent ankle sprains · activity pain · calf pain (peroneal spasm) · uneven ground

Pain sitesinus tarsi / below fibula → CN · distal to medial malleolus / medial foot → TC

Examrigid pes planus · hindfoot valgus that doesn't swing into varus on toe-rise · arch doesn't reconstitute · ↓ subtalar motion · heel cord contracture · reverse Coleman block for subtalar rigidity

Deformity associationrigid pes planus
✗ Wrong options: cavus · rocker-bottom · varus

Ball-and-socket anklefrom large neonatal TC coalition (develops by ~5 yr)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP · standing lateral · 45° internal oblique (best for CN) · Harris axial heel

Coalition Sign
CN "Anteater (nose)" sign — elongated anterior calcaneal process (lateral/oblique) · "comma" sign (TO) · ± talar beaking
TC "C-sign" — talar dome to posteroinferior sustentaculum (lateral) · talar (talonavicular) beaking — dorsal talar lip remodeling from altered motion, not OA · irregular middle facet on Harris · dysmorphic, rounded sustentaculum (Oestreich)

CTpre-op: size, location (TC % of posterior facet on coronal), rule out 2nd coalition, arthritis · gold standard in adults

MRIfibrous / cartilaginous coalition (normal X-rays + suspicion) · STIR for inflammation

Normal X-rays, rigid valgus heel, sinus tarsi pain, repeated sprains → suspect coalition → MRI
✗ Wrong options: Sever · Kohler · Iselin · flexible flatfoot surgery

5Management

Symptomatic tarsal coalition
  • First→short-leg walking cast 4–6 wk + NSAIDs (then orthosis / UCBL)
  • Recurs — CN→resection + EDB or fat interposition
  • Recurs — TC <50%→resection + fat / split FHL interposition ± deformity correction
  • TC >50%, no arthritis→flatfoot reconstruction (OB) / subtalar fusion (Orthobullets)
  • Failed resection / diffuse arthritis→triple arthrodesis

Initial nonoperative treatment - cast immobilisation

First line (every first presentation)below-knee walking cast 4–6 wk (6 wk Orthobullets · 4 wk OB) ± NSAIDs · up to 30% pain-free (Orthobullets) · very high short-term relief (OB) · inserts may hurt rigid feet · UCBL after
✗ Wrong options: resection first · arthrodesis · CT/MRI first if diagnosis clear · sinus tarsi injection

Pain recurs after good cast → surgery
✗ Wrong options: repeat cast · NWB cast · orthotic · more PT · quit sport

Calcaneonavicular coalition resection with interposition

Procedureresect bar + interpose EDB muscle or fat (or bone wax) · resection alone ↑ recurrence · lateral oblique incision over sinus tarsi between EXTENSOR and PERONEAL tendons · protect superficial peroneal + sural nerves · ~1 cm gap · NWB cast 3–4 wk

Addcalcaneal osteotomy / lengthening for marked valgus · heel cord lengthening if DF < neutral · mild flatfoot → no osteotomy

Outcome80–85% pain relief · full return to sport (87%, Mubarak) · ↑ subtalar motion (74%), ↑ plantar flexion (82%) · repeat resection ~5%
✗ Wrong options: subtalar fusion · arthroereisis · manipulation

Contraindicationsadvanced degeneration · multiple coalitions → arthrodesis

Talocalcaneal coalition - resection vs arthrodesis/reconstruction

Operative criteria

TC situation Treatment
≤50% of subtalar width (coronal CT), acceptable alignment, no OA Resection + fat / split FHL interposition ± valgus correction
>50%, joints healthy Bony flatfoot reconstruction WITHOUT resection (OB220914) · subtalar arthrodesis (Orthobullets, OB3016) — read the options
>50% + heel valgus >16° Poor results with resection (Wilde)
Failed resection, >50%, or diffuse TN/CC arthritis Triple arthrodesis

TC approachmedial, curved incision over sustentaculum, between FDL and neurovascular bundle (Orthobullets) · between FDL and FHL (OB) · find normal anterior + posterior facets, resect with burr, check inversion/eversion · NWB cast 3 wk

Subtalar fusionavoid in young (10–12 yr) — limits foot growth (OB)

Poor outcomesresecting >50% · uncorrected hindfoot valgus · degenerative change

Adults (TO)usually ossified + secondary arthritis → CT · accommodative orthosis, AFO, injections · resection only if small bar and normal joints · otherwise subtalar / double / triple arthrodesis ± gastrocnemius recession

6Complications

Listincomplete resection · recurrence · residual pain / stiffness (malalignment, arthritis, missed 2nd coalition → pre-op CT)

Interposition EDB / fat Fat / split FHL

Type Findings
1a No proximal tibia on X-ray · extensor mechanism absent · hypoplastic distal femoral epiphysis
1b Proximal tibia ossifies later, extensor mechanism works · distal femoral epiphysis normal
2 Proximal tibia present at birth, short tibia

Operative criteria

Finding Procedure
Complete tibial absence · no active knee extension (most cases) Knee disarticulation + prosthesis
Proximal tibia present, intact extensor mechanism, minimal flexion contracture Tibiofibular synostosis + modified Syme
Ankle diastasis Syme / Boyd amputation
Brown (fibula centralized under femur) No longer recommended — high failure

Good below-knee resultfull functional quadriceps + no knee flexion contracture · otherwise knee disarticulation
✗ Wrong options: 35° flexion contracture · absent synostosis · bilateral · family history

Tibial Eminence Fracture

Pediatrics · 106 / 112

1Basics

Definitionintra-articular avulsion of the bony ACL attachment (tibial spine) · ages 8–14 · 2–5% of pediatric knee injuries with effusion

Why bone failseminence incompletely ossified → weaker than ACL · fails through deep cancellous bone · may extend into plateau (medial most common)

Anatomynon-articular area between plateaus · ACL → medial spine (lateral aspect) · insertion 9 mm behind intermeniscal ligament, beside anterior horns · PCL doesn't attach to spines

Associated injuries (~40%)meniscal · collateral ligament · capsular · osteochondral · MRI: 15–37% intra-articular pathology

Adult equivalent - ACL avulsion

Equivalent in skeletally matureACL tear · with fracture → Segond (lateral capsule)
✗ Wrong options: PCL tear · patellar tendon rupture · lateral meniscus tear

Adult tibial ACL avulsionbony fragment on MRI + arthroscopy
✗ Wrong options: midsubstance ACL tear · PCL avulsion · bucket-handle

2Mechanism

Mechanismrapid deceleration, hyperextension / rotation (sport) · fall from bike (hyperextension) · same mechanism as adult ACL tear

3Presentation

Findingsimmediate effusion (hemarthrosis) · knee held flexed · can't bear weight · +anterior drawer / Lachman · motion block after analgesia → meniscus or entrapped fragment

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP · lateral (best for displacement) · intercondylar notch · oblique (plateau extension)

CTpre-op planning · displacement unclear on X-ray

MRIligament / meniscal injury (better than CT) · not routine once X-ray confirms
✗ Wrong options: MRI as next step

Classification & closed reduction in extension

Modified Meyers & McKeever Description
I Nondisplaced (<3 mm)
II Anterior displacement, intact posterior hinge
III Completely displaced
III+ Type III + rotation
IV Completely displaced, rotated, comminuted

OB variantIIIa comminution · IIIb rotation

5Management

Tibial eminence fracture
  • Type I→long-leg cast in extension
  • Type II→aspirate + closed reduction in extension
    • reduces→long-leg cast in extension, close X-ray follow-up
    • doesn't reduce→arthroscopic / open reduction + fixation
  • Type III→arthroscopic / open reduction + fixation

Closed reductionaspirate tense hemarthrosis + lidocaine · full extension / hyperextension · cast at 0° (or 10–20° flexion — debated) · 3–4 wk (Orthobullets) · 4–6 wk then hinged brace (OB) · lateral X-ray to confirm + serial films · CT/MRI if unclear · <5 mm displacement → closed (OB)

Trapscast in extension (✗ Wrong options: 90° flexion) · reduce before immobilizing (✗ Wrong options: knee immobilizer + NWB) · 1–2 wk cast too short
✗ Wrong options: immediate WB · ACL reconstruction · fragment excision (ACL attached)

Meniscal entrapment blocking reduction

Block to reductionanterior horn of medial meniscus (most common) > intermeniscal ligament > anterior horn lateral meniscus
✗ Wrong options: ACL · PCL · fat pad

Kocher (80 cases)medial meniscus 36 · intermeniscal 6 · lateral meniscus 1 · entrapment in 26% type II, 65% type III · meniscal tear 3.8%

Lowelateral meniscus + ACL pull fragment in opposite directions (not entrapment)

Associated with type IImeniscal entrapment
✗ Wrong options: compartment syndrome (tibial tubercle fracture) · patellar dislocation · growth arrest

Operative fixation

Operative criteria

Indicationstype III · irreducible type II · block to extension · failed closed reduction · late displacement

Treatmentarthroscopic (or open) reduction + internal fixation of eminence · anatomic reduction
✗ Wrong options: ACL reconstruction · tibial tubercle ORIF

Suture Screw
Pros Minimal physeal damage · growth breaks non-absorbable sutures · biomechanically superior in type II (OB) Easier · earlier motion
Cons Technically demanding Needs large fragment · impingement · iatrogenic comminution · physeal damage · remove only if malpositioned

Post-opcast in extension 7–10 days (variable) → early controlled ROM

6Complications

Outcomes (laxity, arthrofibrosis)

Loss of motionvery common, esp. extension (fragment impinges in notch)

Arthrofibrosismore common after surgery · adolescents / adults → counsel stiffness · concomitant ACL injury = independent risk factor for return to OR for MUA
✗ Wrong options: nonunion · physeal closure · compartment syndrome

ACL laxity38–100%, more after surgery · common but rarely symptomatic (even after anatomic fixation — ligament stretched at injury) · ACL reconstruction later 15–25%

Growth arrestiatrogenic at surgery

Prognosisgood · 85% return to prior sport

✗ Wrong options: 90° flexion

Tibial Shaft Fractures - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 107 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology3rd most common pediatric long-bone fracture · 15% of pediatric fractures · boys > girls · mean age 8 yr · 39% mid-diaphysis · fibula fractured in 30%

NAT2nd most common bone fractured in non-accidental trauma · suspect abuse in non-ambulatory child

Anatomytriangular, apex anterior · anteromedial border subcutaneous · distal flare mostly cancellous · posterior tibial a. → nutrient + periosteal vessels · anterior tibial a. at risk through interosseous membrane · fibula carries 6–17% of load

2Mechanism

Adolescentpedestrian vs vehicle (50%) · direct blow

Toddlerlow-energy twist / fall → spiral or oblique ("toddler's fracture")

3Presentation

Findingspain, bruising · refuses to bear weight · tenderness · pain on ankle dorsiflexion · always think compartment syndrome

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP + lateral tib/fib · image ipsilateral knee + ankle · ± contralateral · toddler's fracture may be normal initially → repeat at 2 wk for callus / periosteal reaction

CTphyseal / intra-articular extension (distal third) · pathologic lesion

MRIpathologic / stress fracture · occult fracture

Bone scanoccult fracture

Pattern Description
Incomplete Greenstick of tibia ± fibula
Complete Tibia ± fibula fracture or plastic deformation
Toddler's fracture Nondisplaced spiral / oblique tibia, intact fibula, age <2.5 yr

Toddler's fracture

Typicalafebrile · normal WBC / ESR / CRP · distal tibial tenderness · X-rays often negative · usually unwitnessed

Treatmentlong leg cast · heals 3–4 wk
✗ Wrong options: MRI · aspiration · vitamin D / metabolic labs · child services · chromosomal analysis

Notosteomyelitis / subperiosteal abscess (afebrile, normal labs) · NOF · NAT (age + story fit)

5Management

Operative criteria

Acceptable alignmenttranslation 50% (Orthobullets, OB: <50% = >50% cortical overlap) · shortening <1 cm · angulation <5–10° sagittal + coronal (Orthobullets) · <10° (OB210163) · <5° (OB218688) — read the options

Method Indication
Long leg cast Toddler's · greenstick
Closed reduction + long leg cast Most traumatic fractures with acceptable reduction
External fixator Extensive soft-tissue injury · length unstable · polytrauma
Flexible IM nails Open / closed in skeletally immature · multiple long bones · floating knee
Percutaneous pins Noncomminuted unstable oblique (± cast)
Rigid IM nail At / near skeletal maturity (✗ Wrong options: open physes)
Plate Physeal / articular extension · length unstable · nonunion / malunion

Reasons to operate (Ho)open fracture · obesity · compartment concern · segmental · polytrauma · floating knee · failed non-op

Treatment - casting vs flexible nailing

Casting techniquesedation / GA · cast to groin, knee flexed 30°, molded · ± bivalve · loss of reduction → cast wedging

Early weight bearingWB at 1 wk in long leg cast (knee ~10°) is safe and may speed healing (Jenkins: +0.3 days healing per day delayed)
✗ Wrong options: NWB 4–6 wk · short leg cast · flexible nails first

Distal tibia fractureshigh secondary displacement → follow-up within 1–2 wk · most non-op
✗ Wrong options: >1 month

Casting vs flexible IMNonly real difference: casting = prolonged immobilization (>3 months) · compartment syndrome more with IMN (up to 20%) · union, malunion, LLD similar

Elastic nailsperiod of casting / splint + NWB after (nails don't control rotation, bending) · no 50-kg contraindication (unlike femur) · open fractures OK
✗ Wrong options: soft dressing + WBAT · added ex-fix

Complication Rate
Ex-fix nonunion ~2% · refracture · pin tract infection
Flexible nail nonunion ~10%

Valgus deformity

Fibula Drift
Intact Varus
Fractured (both bones) Valgus + recurvatum (procurvatum, OB)

Why valguslateral compartment pull + pes anserinus · gentle varus mold (too much → varus malunion) · residual → wedging

6Complications

Compartment syndrome

Compartment syndromeless common than adults · open + closed · signs in kids: 3 As — analgesia ↑, anxiety, agitation · firm leg with pulses → 4-compartment fasciotomy
✗ Wrong options: more narcotics · nerve block · PCA · observe

LLDage <10 · comminution → overgrowth · pins → growth arrest, recurvatum from tibial tubercle arrest

Angular deformitycomplex · valgus + apex posterior · physeal extension · osteotomy for rotational malunion / symptomatic

Nonunion25% of open fractures · ↑ age, wound severity · hypertrophic → graft + rigid fixation

Healing3–4 wk toddler's · 6–8 wk others

Tibial Tubercle Fracture

Pediatrics · 108 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology<1% of pediatric fractures · males >> females · 12–15 yr (near skeletal maturity) · basketball, football, sprinting, high jump · growth hormone weakens physis

Ossification2 centers: primary (proximal tibial physis) + secondary (tubercle apophysis, patellar tendon insertion)

Physeal closureposterior → anterior, proximal → distal · tubercle last to fuse → vulnerable in older adolescents

Vesselrecurrent anterior tibial artery at lateral border of tubercle → lacerated → retracts under fascia → anterior compartment syndrome

2Mechanism

Mechanism

Mechanismknee flexion + quadriceps contraction · concentric quad contraction at jump take-off · eccentric quad contraction in forced knee flexion
✗ Wrong options: hamstring · gastrocnemius · direct blow

3Presentation

Findingssudden pain at jump / sprint start · can't walk · effusion / hemarthrosis (type III) · tubercle tenderness · extensor lag / can't straight-leg raise (II–III; retinaculum may allow some extension) · patella alta · palpable defect · watch anterior compartment

Associatedcompartment syndrome · meniscal tears with type III · cruciate / collateral / patellar injuries uncommon (OB7708, OB210101) · patellar / quadriceps tendon avulsion, ligament tears to assess (OB1487)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP + lateral · internal rotation view (tubercle in profile) · contralateral comparison (younger) · widening / hinging of apophysis · patella alta · anterior swelling only → type V sleeve

CTintra-articular / posterior extension · arteriogram if popliteal concern
✗ Wrong options: delay fasciotomy

MRInot routine · nondisplaced type II extension or type V

Ogden classification (modified Watson-Jones)

Type Fracture
I Secondary ossification center near patellar tendon insertion
II Propagates proximally between primary and secondary centers
III (most common) Coronal, extends posteriorly across primary center → intra-articular
IV Through entire proximal tibial physis
V Periosteal sleeve avulsion of extensor mechanism from secondary center
Modifier A nondisplaced · B displaced

5Management

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Type I / displacement <2 mm / acceptable after closed reduction Long leg cast in extension 6 wk
Displaced, types II–IV ORIF ± arthrotomy / arthroscopy (joint surface, meniscus)
Type V Soft-tissue (periosteal) repair
Compartment syndrome Emergent fasciotomy + ORIF (± prophylactic fasciotomy)

Treatment - ORIF

ORIFmidline incision · remove interposed periosteum (blocks closed reduction) · anatomic reduction · 4.0 cancellous partially threaded screws (or headless compression) · smooth K-wires if >3 yr from maturity · cannulated screws better than CRPP (OB) · NWB long leg cast / brace 4–6 wk · sport ≥3 months

Arthrotomy / arthroscopyintra-articular (type III) → visualize joint, evacuate hematoma, meniscus repair

Soft-tissue repair (V)heavy suture of periosteum to secondary center · cast 8–10 wk

Traps✗ Wrong options: long leg cast for displaced · patellar tendon bearing cast · CRPP · ligament reconstruction · spanning ex-fix (temporizing only) · patellar tendon repair (tendon intact, deforming) · fragment excision · MRI / CT if X-ray clear

6Complications

Compartment syndrome - anterior tibial recurrent artery

Rate4% (Orthobullets, OB) · 4–5% (OB) · up to 10% (OB) — read the options · high with type III

Vesselanterior tibial recurrent artery
✗ Wrong options: peroneal · posterior tibial · middle geniculate (ACL) · medial / lateral inferior geniculate · popliteal (knee dislocation)

Signsrising analgesic need, anxiety, distress, swelling overnight → emergent fasciotomies + ORIF
✗ Wrong options: observe · vascular exploration · ORIF alone

Otherstiffness · refracture

Complication Fact
Bursitis Most common after surgery · screw prominence → removal
Recurvatum Anterior arrest, posterior growth → ↓ slope · more common than LLD (LLD low — age) · unusual (near maturity)
Popliteal artery injury Over distal metaphyseal fragment (physeal types)

✗ Wrong options: ACL disruption · popliteal artery · patella baja

✗ Wrong options: peroneal · middle geniculate · saphenous

✗ Wrong options: inferior geniculates

✗ Wrong options: LLD · varus · procurvatum

"Displaced type III, noncontact — more likely?"compartment syndrome
✗ Wrong options: ACL + MCL · patella dislocation · peroneal palsy

"13-yr ↑ analgesia — vessel in figure?"recurrent anterior tibial artery (lateral border of tubercle)

"13-yr admitted for morning ORIF, ↑ narcotics, swollen leg?"emergent fasciotomies + ORIF
✗ Wrong options: ORIF only · observe · vascular exploration

"12-yr basketball, anterior tibial pain at 6 h — artery?"recurrent branch of anterior tibial artery
✗ Wrong options: popliteal

"14-yr volleyball, type III, anxious overnight?"recurrent anterior tibial artery

"14-yr can't straight-leg raise, displaced tubercle?"ORIF
✗ Wrong options: long leg cast · PTB cast · CRPP

"13-yr displaced intra-articular tubercle?"ORIF
✗ Wrong options: MRI · cast · fasciotomy

"10-yr cheerleader, palpable defect, patella elevated, ligament retracted >2 cm?"ORIF
✗ Wrong options: MRI · CT · excision · cast

"14-yr CT shows articular extension — definitive?"ORIF (± arthrotomy)
✗ Wrong options: spanning ex-fix · percutaneous screws · tendon repair

✗ Wrong options: quadriceps rupture · Osgood-Schlatter · ACL tear

Tillaux Fractures

Pediatrics · 109 / 112

1Basics

DefinitionSalter-Harris III of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis · transitional fracture (physis closing) · entirely epiphyseal

Epidemiology3–5% of pediatric ankle fractures · more common in girls · 12–14 yr (12–15 OB) · within ~1 yr of complete distal tibial closure (18-month transitional window) · older than triplane (triplane ~10–12, OB)

Associateddistal fibula fracture (SH I/II) · ipsilateral tibial shaft fracture

Distal tibial physeal closure pattern

Ordercentral → anteromedial → posteromedial → lateral (Orthobullets, TO, OB) · central → posterior → medial → anterolateral (OB3880) · central → medial → lateral (OB) · central → anteromedial → posterolateral (TO17124838)

Last to fuseanterolateral (TO) → open lateral physis avulsed by AITFL
✗ Wrong options: anteromedial · posteromedial · posterolateral

Distal tibial physis35–40% of tibial growth · 15–20% of lower-limb growth · 3–4 mm/yr · growth until 14 girls / 16 boys

Anatomy - AITFL avulsion

Ligamentanterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL) · Chaput tubercle (anterolateral tibial epiphysis) → Wagstaffe tubercle (anterior distal fibula) · part of syndesmosis (+ PITFL)
✗ Wrong options: PITFL · ATFL (ankle sprain) · PTFL · CFL · deltoid

Same ligament injured inhigh ankle sprain (syndesmosis)
✗ Wrong options: low ankle sprain (ATFL) · Weber A (below syndesmosis) · Gosselin (V-shaped plafond fracture) · subtalar dislocation

Axial CTdisplaced fragment = anterolateral region (AITFL)
✗ Wrong options: posterolateral · medial malleolus

2Mechanism

Mechanism

Mechanismsupination / eversion – external rotation → AITFL tension → anterolateral avulsion
✗ Wrong options: pronation/eversion–ER (SH II lateral tibia + suprasyndesmotic fibula) · supination–plantarflexion (posterior tibia) · axial compression (SH V) · supination–inversion (ankle sprain)

vs triplaneno coronal fracture in posterior metaphysis = Tillaux

3Presentation

Findingspain · can't bear weight · slight swelling · focal anterolateral joint-line tenderness · deformity rare (fibula blocks displacement)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP · lateral · mortise = best view · SH III anterolateral epiphysis

CTfracture pattern · articular displacement · intramalleolar / medial variants · after closed reduction → CT for residual step-off
✗ Wrong options: discharge without CT

5Management

CT & surgical indications (>2 mm step-off)

Operative criteria

After closed reduction Treatment
<2 mm displacement (rare) Long leg cast 3–4 wk → short leg cast / boot 2–4 wk
>2 mm residual step-off CRPP or ORIF

Not indicationsage, sex, any step-off <2 mm
✗ Wrong options: age >12 · male · any step-off

Closed reductioninternal rotation of foot (or dorsiflex pronated foot then IR) · long leg cast controls rotation · early X-rays

CRPPK-wire joystick · fluoro / arthrogram · K-wire or cannulated screw · crossing physis OK (little growth left) · good outcome if residual <2.5 mm

ORIFanterolateral approach · reduce with internal rotation · intraepiphyseal or transphyseal wires / screws · long leg cast 3–4 wk → short leg walking cast 2 wk

Post-reduction carelow compartment risk · long leg > short leg cast
✗ Wrong options: admit + splint

6Complications

Growth arrestrare (physis already closing) · ↓ with anatomic reduction

Early arthritis↑ with articular displacement · degenerative change as early as 4 yr

X vs Y

Tillaux Triplane
Salter-Harris III IV (as described by OB)
Age Older, nearer maturity Younger (~10–12, OB)
Posterior metaphyseal coronal fracture Absent Present

✗ Wrong options: PITFL · ATFL · CFL

✗ Wrong options: posterolateral · deltoid

✗ Wrong options: deltoid · calcaneofibular

✗ Wrong options: ATFL · long plantar

✗ Wrong options: PITFL · PTFL · CFL

✗ Wrong options: low ankle sprain · Weber A · Gosselin

"Strongest indication for fixation after reduction?"articular step-off >2 mm
✗ Wrong options: age · male sex · any step-off

Transient Synovitis of Hip

Pediatrics · 110 / 112

1Basics

Definitionnonspecific inflammation + hypertrophy of synovium · most common cause of pediatric hip pain · diagnosis of exclusion vs septic arthritis

Epidemiology3% of children 3–10 yr · peak 4–8 yr · M:F 2:1 · hip most common joint · recurrence up to 20%

Diagnosis & preceding viral illness

Causelargely unknown · viral upper respiratory infection (most cited) · bacterial (poststreptococcal toxic synovitis) · trauma · ↑ interferon · allergy

Preceded byinfectious respiratory illness
✗ Wrong options: hematogenous bacterial inoculation (septic arthritis) · hypothyroidism (SCFE) · secondhand smoke (Perthes) · LLD (painless limp)

Genes & lab markers

Lab Transient synovitis
WBC Normal / slightly ↑
CRP <20 mg/L — most important to RULE OUT septic arthritis · CRP >20 = independent risk factor for sepsis
ESR Usually <20 mm/h (can be ↑ — 35 with normal CRP + rapid improvement still synovitis)
Synovial WBC Near normal · >50,000 → treat as septic

3Presentation

Historyrecent URI or trauma · mild / no fever · acute or insidious groin / thigh pain · refuses to bear weight → better later in day (limps by evening) · muscle spasm

Examhip in flexion, abduction, external rotation (lowest intracapsular pressure) · not toxic · ↓ internal rotation = most sensitive ROM sign · painless arc → synovitis > sepsis · log-roll guarding · spine + knee non-tender · toe-walking / cavus / claw toes → neurological limp

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP + frog-leg / lateral · ± spine · usually normal

USeffusion (accurate) · synovial thickening · can't separate synovitis from sepsis, but no effusion → infection unlikely

MRImyositis / osteomyelitis suspicion · markedly ↑ labs

Aspirationif septic suspicion (clinical / Kocher criteria)

Differentialseptic hip · osteomyelitis (point tenderness, swelling, ↑ markers) · SCFE (10–16 yr, visible on AP) · Perthes (visible on X-ray) · leukemia (normal CBC rules out) · JIA (rarely hip) · fracture (no trauma)

5Management

Low septic suspicionIV / PO NSAIDs + close observation 24 h · minimize walking · ± traction · improves on NSAIDs → synovitis

Coursemarked improvement 24–48 h · resolves <1 wk (Orthobullets treatment) · 1–2 wk (prognosis)

6Complications

Recurrence~20%

Perthes0–10% (controversial; most series no sequelae)

X vs Y

Transient synovitis Septic arthritis
Fever Mild / none Higher
CRP <20 mg/L >20
Course Rapid improvement on NSAIDs Doesn't improve
Synovial WBC Near normal >50,000

How it's asked

"8-yr hip pain, CRP 1.8, ESR 35, walking after 24 h ketorolac?"transient synovitis
✗ Wrong options: septic arthritis · leukemia · JIA

"5-yr recent URI, CRP 9, ESR 20, limited IR?"transient synovitis
✗ Wrong options: septic · SCFE · Perthes

"5-yr limp, normal labs — what preceded?"infectious respiratory illness
✗ Wrong options: bacterial inoculation · hypothyroidism · secondhand smoke

"2-yr improving, afebrile, normal CRP, US effusion?"toxic synovitis
✗ Wrong options: septic · osteomyelitis · leukemia

Traumatic Hip Dislocation - Pediatric

Pediatrics · 111 / 112

1Basics

Epidemiology80% posterior · more common than hip fracture in children

Mechanism<10 yr: low-energy sport / trip and fall (lax ligaments, cartilaginous acetabulum; <6 yr minimal force, OB) · >10 yr: high-energy (MVA)

Associatedacetabular fractures less common than adults (posterior wall most common) · femoral head / neck / proximal femoral physis fracture · missed ipsilateral femoral shaft fracture (OB) · AVN ↑ if not reduced within 6 h

3Presentation

Direction Limb position
Posterior (most common) Slight flexion, adduction, internal rotation · LLD (large posterior wall fragment → short without malalignment)
Anterior Slight flexion, abduction, external rotation
Inferior External rotation + extension

Nervessciatic or gluteal palsy (rare) · usually resolves after reduction

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP pelvis (most diagnosed) · lateral (anterior vs posterior; check femoral neck before reduction) · post-reduction films → joint incongruity / nonconcentric reduction

MRIstudy of choice for abnormal post-reduction films (joint widening) · less radiation · best for interposed soft tissue, entrapped labrum / capsule

CT2nd choice · osteochondral fragments (older children) · soft-tissue interposition hard to see

5Management

Pediatric hip dislocation
  • First→urgent closed reduction under GA / sedation, within 6 h (85% succeed)
  • Post-reduction films normal→spica / abduction splint (<10 yr) or protected WB (older)
  • Nonconcentric / fragment / irreducible→MRI or CT, then open reduction
    • Approach→in direction of dislocation (usually posterior)

Closed reductionadequate anesthesia mandatory (avoid displacing unrecognized proximal femoral epiphyseal fracture) · under fluoroscopy (epiphyseolysis risk) · traction in flexion + gentle rotation · test stability before waking · post-reduction imaging

Aftercarespica / bed rest with abduction splint 4 wk if <10 yr · brace + 6–12 wk protected WB in older

Operative criteria

Open reduction indications
Nonconcentric reduction
Intra-articular fragment
Unstable acetabular rim fracture · femoral head / neck fracture
Irreducible closed

Non-concentric reduction - arthrotomy

Persistent incongruitysoft-tissue interposition (torn labrum + lateral acetabular apophysis) · osteochondral fragment → hip arthrotomy via POSTERIOR approach (posterior structures already torn)
✗ Wrong options: anterior approach · repeat closed reduction · traction 1 month · WBAT

6Complications

AVN with delayed reduction

AVN3–15% (Orthobullets) · 0–43% (OB) · ↓ under age 5 · less than adults (without neck fracture) · only complication linked to delay in reduction · >24 h → 66% (OB)
✗ Wrong options: coxa magna · redislocation · chondrolysis · HO (not time-dependent)

Complication Fact
Coxa magna 20%, radiographic, no functional limit
Redislocation Rare · prolonged immobilization → capsulorrhaphy if recurrent
Nerve Sciatic / gluteal, usually resolves
Other (OB) Femoral head deformity · premature physeal fusion · degenerative arthritis · chondrolysis

Prognosisgood when treated promptly · most return to high-demand activity

How it's asked

"10-yr post-reduction CT — joint widened, fragment?"hip arthrotomy via posterior approach
✗ Wrong options: anterior approach · repeat closed reduction · traction

"3-yr MVC hip dislocation — delayed concentric reduction ↑ risk of?"avascular necrosis
✗ Wrong options: coxa magna · recurrent dislocation · chondrolysis · HO

Mechanism

Pattern Mechanism
Lateral triplane Supination–external rotation (like Tillaux)
Medial triplane Adduction

Plane Structure Seen on
Sagittal Epiphysis (lateral) AP X-ray → SH III

CTusually required (pattern + articular congruity) · after closed reduction · all 3 planes · "Mercedes-Benz sign" · 4-part only seen on CT

Parts Fragments
2-part (1) anterolateral + posterior epiphysis with posterior metaphyseal fragment · (2) anteromedial epiphysis with rest of tibia
3-part (1) anterolateral epiphysis · (2) posterior epiphysis + posterior metaphyseal fragment · (3) anteromedial epiphysis + rest of tibia

Pattern Epiphysis Metaphysis Note
Lateral Sagittal Coronal Most common · looks like Tillaux on AP → SH II on lateral distinguishes
Medial Coronal Sagittal —

Displacement Treatment
<2 mm Closed reduction + long leg cast 3–4 wk → short leg cast / boot 2–4 wk · ideal for 2-part

Closed reductionreduce fibula first · lateral → internal rotation · medial → eversion (closed) / external rotation (operative) · post-reduction CT
